questions.reveal: Its first tier of 3,500 covers about 99.5% of everyday printed text. The imperial Kangxi dictionary of 1716 listed over 47,000 characters, the overwhelming majority of them already obsolete.
questions.reasoningPath: Basic literacy is usually put at 2,000–3,000 characters and a fluent reader knows maybe 5,000, while big dictionaries run to tens of thousands. An official modern-use list must sit above literacy level and well below the dictionary: single-digit thousands.

questions.prompt: In what year was the Korean alphabet Hangul promulgated by King Sejong?
questions.reveal: Its consonant shapes are diagrams of the mouth making the sound: ㅁ is the lips, ㄱ the tongue humped against the palate. The literary elite dismissed it as vulgar; Korea now gives it a national holiday.
questions.reasoningPath: It replaced Chinese characters for ordinary Korean writing, and it belongs to the Joseon dynasty's cultural high point — after Europe's medieval period, before Hideyoshi's 1590s invasions. Mid-1400s.

questions.prompt: How many official languages does the European Union have?
questions.reveal: Twenty-seven member states share them: Austria and Germany both use German, Cyprus uses Greek, Belgium's three are all borrowed from neighbours. Every EU law is translated into all of them, Irish included since 2007.
questions.reasoningPath: There are 27 member states and most brought their own language, but a handful share one with a neighbour. So a couple below 27.

questions.prompt: FIFA requires pitches at international matches to be how many metres wide?
questions.reveal: The length is fixed at 105 m for those matches, but the Laws still allow ordinary pitches anywhere from 90 to 120 m long and 45 to 90 m wide — which is why no two old grounds are quite the same shape.
questions.reasoningPath: A pitch is a bit longer than it is wide, and a goalkeeper's kick from his own line reaches roughly the halfway line of a ~100 m field. Width looks about two-thirds of that: high 60s.

questions.prompt: How high is the crossbar of a football goal above the ground, in metres?
questions.reveal: Goals had no crossbar at all until 1875 — a tape was strung between the posts, and anything above it counted. The 7.32 m width has not changed since the first Laws in 1863.
questions.reasoningPath: A goalkeeper of about 1.9 m can just touch the bar with a standing arm raised, which puts it a little above 2.4 m — roughly a tall doorway plus half a metre.

questions.prompt: How many metres separate the two sets of stumps on a cricket pitch?
questions.reveal: That distance is exactly one chain, a Tudor surveyor's unit — ten chains make a furlong and eighty make a mile. The strip itself is only 3.05 m wide, and every delivery must land on it.
questions.reasoningPath: A fast bowler's delivery covers the gap in well under a second at about 140 km/h, which is roughly 39 m per second — so around half a second's flight puts the pitch near 20 m.

questions.prompt: How high is the rim of a basketball hoop above the floor, in metres?
questions.reveal: It has been the same height since 1891, when James Naismith nailed a peach basket to the balcony rail of a gymnasium — the rail simply happened to be at that height, and the game froze it there forever.
questions.reasoningPath: A two-metre player standing under the basket has to reach well above his own raised arm to dunk, but only by a little. That is about a metre above his head: just over three metres.

questions.prompt: How many national associations are members of FIFA?
questions.reveal: That is 18 more than the United Nations has member states. Twenty-three FIFA members are not sovereign countries — England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland count separately, as do Hong Kong, Macau, Gibraltar and Tahiti.
questions.reasoningPath: The UN has 193 members and almost every country plays football. FIFA also admits territories and the four British nations separately, so start at ~193 and add a couple of dozen.

questions.prompt: In what year was the first FIFA World Cup played?
questions.reveal: Only 13 teams entered and just four made the boat trip from Europe. The finalists could not agree whose ball to use, so Argentina's was used in the first half and Uruguay's in the second — Uruguay won 4-2.
questions.reasoningPath: It came after football had spread worldwide but had to be old enough for a long pre-television history, and it was interrupted by the Second World War after only three editions. Three tournaments before 1938, four years apart, puts the first around 1930.

questions.prompt: How tall is the Mona Lisa panel, in centimetres?
questions.reveal: It is painted on a single plank of poplar just 53 cm wide, warped and cracked by five centuries of humidity and braced from behind with butterfly-shaped inserts. Visitors get roughly 30 seconds in front of it.
questions.reasoningPath: Everyone who sees it reports being surprised by how small it is. It is a half-length portrait with a life-size head, so a little under a metre of canvas: head plus torso plus a border.

questions.prompt: How many metres wide is Picasso's Guernica?
questions.reveal: Picasso finished the whole thing in about 35 days in 1937, then refused to let it enter Spain while Franco lived. It hung in New York's Museum of Modern Art until 1981, six years after the dictator's death.
questions.reasoningPath: Photographs show adult viewers standing under it reaching only halfway up, so it is about 3.5 m tall, and it is roughly twice as wide as it is tall. Call it 7 or 8 m — the width of a small house.

questions.prompt: How tall is Michelangelo's David, the statue alone without its plinth, in metres?
questions.reveal: He carved it from a block two earlier sculptors had abandoned as ruined. It then stood outdoors in Florence's main square for nearly 370 years before being moved indoors in 1873; a copy stands there now.
questions.reasoningPath: In gallery photographs the statue is roughly three times the height of the people beneath it, and it was designed to be read from far below on a cathedral roofline. Three adults stacked is a bit over five metres.

questions.prompt: How many terracotta warriors are thought to be buried in the pits at Xi'an?
questions.reveal: Most are still underground, and they were once painted in brilliant colours. The lacquer beneath the paint curls within about fifteen seconds of meeting dry air and flakes away in four minutes, so digging now waits for better methods.
questions.reasoningPath: Photographs of the main pit show ranks roughly 10 wide and 60 deep — about 6,000 figures — and there are two smaller pits beside it. So several thousand, not hundreds and not a million.

questions.prompt: How many metres long is the Bayeux Tapestry?
questions.reveal: It is only 50 cm tall, and it is not a tapestry at all but an embroidery in wool on linen. It also carries the earliest known picture of Halley's Comet, which crossed the sky in the spring of 1066.
questions.reasoningPath: It tells the whole Norman conquest in about 58 numbered scenes, and each scene needs roughly a metre of cloth to hold its figures and its Latin caption. That is a strip the length of a running track's straight.

questions.prompt: How many years did Michelangelo spend painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling?
questions.reveal: He worked standing on a scaffold of his own design with his head tilted back — not lying down, as the legend has it — and complained in a poem that his beard pointed at heaven while the brush dripped in his face.
questions.reasoningPath: The vault is about 35 m by 14 m, and a fresco painter must finish each patch of plaster the same day. With assistants grinding and plastering, a few hundred square metres of figures works out to a handful of years, not decades.

verdicts.note: Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagrada_Família: planned height of the Tower of Jesus Christ is stated as exactly 172.5 m (566 ft); exterior structurally completed 20 Feb 2026 and inaugurated 10 June 2026, so 'topped out in 2026' is accurate and now stable. Confirmed it overtook Ulm Minster (161.53 m) — it first passed it on 30 Oct 2025 at 162.91 m, and 161.5 + 11 = 172.5 matches the article's 'll m taller than Ulm Minster'. One reveal caveat, not a grading problem: the reveal's '173 m' for Montjuïc is the Foundation's traditional figure; Wikipedia's Montjuïc article gives the hill as 177.72 m at its highest point and carries no mention of the Gaudí anecdote. Recommend softening to 'just under the hill of Montjuïc' with no metre figure so the reveal does not appear to contradict the 172.5 m answer. Track position 0.579 (log 40..500), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome: interior diameter 43.3 m, height to oculus also 43.3 m (a 43.3 m sphere fits inside), and it is explicitly still 'the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome'. The lighter-aggregate-toward-the-top construction (pumice in the upper mix) is documented. One reveal discrepancy: Wikipedia gives the oculus as 9.1 m (30 ft), not the reveal's 8.9 m; older literature cites 8.7–8.9 m, so sources genuinely differ by ~4% on that secondary figure. Recommend the reveal say 'about 9 m oculus'. The graded number is unaffected. Track position 0.635 (log 5..150), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaning_Tower_of_Pisa: Guinness World Records measured the tilt at 3.97 degrees when comparing Pisa with Suurhusen, matching the claimed source. Reveal is right on both supporting details: the tilt reached 5.5 degrees by 1990, and the top overhangs by 3.9 m (12 ft 10 in). Tried to disprove on the 'today' wording — the tower has continued to recover a few cm since the 2001 works, which is roughly 0.04 degrees, immaterial on a 1..5 linear track. Note that Pisa is not the world's furthest-leaning tower (Capital Gate, Abu Dhabi, 18 degrees, deliberate); the prompt does not claim it is, so this is fine. Track position 0.743 (linear 1..5), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia: construction began 23 Feb 532, dedicated 27 Dec 537 — so the answer 537 and the reveal's 'five years and ten months' both check out exactly. Confirmed the first dome was too flat, failed in the 558 earthquake, and was rebuilt about 6.25 m steeper by Isidore the Younger. Only nuance: it was the eastern semi-dome plus part of the main dome that came down in 558, so 'collapsed in 558' is a fair compression rather than an error. Track position 0.397 (linear 100..1200), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taj_Mahal: overall height given as 73 m (240 ft). Both reveal details verified there too — the main dome is 23 m high (on a 12 m drum, with a 9.6 m finial), and the minarets were deliberately built leaning outward so that in a collapse the material would fall away from the tomb. No source disagreement found beyond rounding. Track position 0.432 (log 20..400), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House: formally opened 20 October 1973 by Queen Elizabeth II. Reveal verified in detail: 1,056,006 roof tiles in two shades (glossy white and matte cream), Utzon resigned 28 February 1966 after the fee/control dispute, left Australia and never returned, dying in 2008 without seeing it finished. The one soft spot is that he was re-engaged as a design consultant in 1999 — but he still never travelled back, so 'never returned to Australia to see it finished' holds. Track position 0.614 (linear 1930..2000), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Castillo,_Chichen_Itza: each of the four staircases has approximately 91 steps, and with the top temple platform as the final step the total is 365. Equinox shadow effect confirmed. Two small reveal corrections worth making: Wikipedia specifies the shadows fall on the NORTHWEST balustrade (reveal says 'north'), and it notes the effect is visible for weeks either side of the equinox and may not have been deliberately designed — so 'the pyramid is a calendar' should be phrased as the common interpretation rather than settled fact. Graded number is solid. Track position 0.394 (linear 20..200), in band.

Checked the Ethnologue (2026) figures on en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_languages_by_number_of_native_speakers: Mandarin Chinese 988 million L1 (answer 990 M is 0.2% off), Spanish 487 M (reveal says 'roughly 490') and English 372 M L1 (reveal says 'about 370'). The reveal's claim that English only leads once ~1bn L2 speakers are counted is consistent with the same table. The claimed source, Ethnologue, is the actual source. These counts do drift with each annual edition, but by ~1%, which is nothing on a log 50..3000 track. Track position 0.729, in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnologue: the 29th edition (2026) lists exactly 7,170 living languages — the candidate's figure is current, not stale. Tried to disprove via edition drift: 25th ed 7,151; 26th 7,168; 27th 7,164; 28th 7,159; 29th 7,170. That is a 0.3% spread, immaterial on a log 100..50,000 track, so it does not meet the 'changes year to year' bar. Reveal checks out against Ethnologue's own summary statistics (23 languages account for over half of the world's population; roughly 40% of languages endangered) — though strictly it is ~40% of all languages, not '40% of the rest'; worth a one-word tweak. Recommend stamping asOf 2026 / Ethnologue 29th ed. Track position 0.688, in band.

Cross-checked three sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_Papua_New_Guinea gives 840 living languages per Ethnologue; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_number_of_languages gives 841 (Ethnologue 22nd ed, 2019); the candidate says 839. That is a 0.24% spread — far inside tolerance. PNG confirmed as the most linguistically diverse country. Reveal arithmetic verified independently: 840 languages against a ~10.3 M population is ~12,000 people each; 840/7,170 is 11.7%, i.e. more than one in ten of all languages; PNG 462,840 km2 vs Sweden 450,295 km2, so 'about the size of Sweden' holds. Ethnologue's own country page returned HTTP 403 so I could not read it directly. Track position 0.612 (log 50..5000), in band.

Checked the Wikipedia article on the 2013 Table of General Standard Chinese Characters: 8,105 characters total, promulgated June 2013 by the PRC government (the claimed Ministry of Education source is right), with Tier 1 = 3,500 and Tier 2 = 3,000. The reveal's '3,500 covers about 99.5% of everyday printed text' matches the standard 99.48% coverage figure, and the Kangxi dictionary (1716) figure of over 47,000 characters is correct. This is a fixed, dated standard so it cannot drift. Track position 0.622 (log 300..60,000), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul: the script was presented to court in the 12th month of 1443, and promulgated in the 9th month of 1446 via the Hunminjeongeum and its Haerye commentary. The prompt says 'promulgated', which is the 1446 event — correct, and it avoids the 1443/1446 trap that catches most versions of this question. Reveal verified: the five basic consonant shapes depict the speech organs, with the article explicitly giving ㄱ as the tongue root against the palate and ㅁ as the mouth. Hangul Day is a South Korean national holiday. Track position 0.351 (linear 1200..1900), in band.

Verified against the EU's own site (european-union.europa.eu/principles-countries-history/languages_en), which lists exactly 24 official languages, plus the Wikipedia article, which gives the same 24. Actively checked the most likely way this could go stale — Spain's push to add Catalan, Basque and Galician — and found no evidence of any addition; the most recent change remains Croatian in 2013. Reveal details all hold: 27 member states share 24 languages, Austria and Germany share German, Cyprus uses Greek, Belgium's Dutch/French/German are all shared with neighbours, and Irish became official in 2007. Track position 0.422 (linear 5..50), in band.

DISPROVED as worded. I read IFAB Law 1 directly at theifab.com/laws/latest/the-field-of-play: for international matches the law permits length 100–110 m and WIDTH 64–75 m, and explicitly says 'competitions may determine the length of the goal line and touchline within the above dimensions'. So FIFA does not 'require' 68 m at international matches — a knowledgeable player answering 64 or 75 would be marked down against a figure the Laws do not mandate. The 105 x 68 figure is FIFA's own competition/stadium standard; the Wikipedia football pitch article words it as 'FIFA recommends that the field of play measures exactly 105 metres long and 68 metres wide'. The reveal is also wrong: it claims 'the length is fixed at 105 m for those matches', which contradicts Law 1's 100–110 m. Its other half (90–120 m by 45–90 m for ordinary pitches) is correct per IFAB. Fix: reword the prompt as supplied and rewrite the reveal to say the Laws allow 100–110 m by 64–75 m for internationals and 90–120 m by 45–90 m elsewhere, which is why old grounds differ. Answer 68 and range 30..120 are fine (position 0.422).
verdicts.correctedPrompt: FIFA's recommended standard pitch, the size used at the World Cup, is 105 m long and how many metres wide?

verdicts.note: The graded number is right — Wikipedia's football pitch and goal articles both give the crossbar at 8 ft (2.44 m) and the posts 8 yd (7.32 m) apart, matching the IFAB Laws. But the REVEAL is factually inverted. Per the Laws of the Game history: before 1866 goals could be scored at ANY height; in 1866 a tape was added between the posts and the ball had to pass UNDER it; in 1875 a crossbar became an allowed alternative to tape; in 1883 the crossbar became compulsory. The reveal's 'a tape was strung between the posts, and anything above it counted' states the opposite of the rule — above the tape did NOT count. Keep the answer 2.44, range 1.5..4 (position 0.376), but replace the reveal with something like: 'Until 1866 a goal counted at any height at all. That year a tape was strung between the posts and the ball had to pass under it; a solid crossbar became optional in 1875 and compulsory in 1883. The 7.32 m width has not changed since the first Laws in 1863.' The 1863 eight-yard width is correct as written.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Under the FA's original laws a goal had no upper limit — a shot counted however high it flew between the posts. A tape was strung across in 1866, and a solid crossbar only became compulsory in 1883.

verdicts.note: Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cricket_pitch: 22 yd (20.12 m) long, explicitly annotated '(1 chain)', and 10 ft (3.05 m) wide — so both the answer and the reveal's chain/furlong/mile framing are right. I specifically tried to disprove the reveal's 'every delivery must land on it', expecting it to be invented, and it survived: Law 21 makes it a No ball if the ball 'bounces not wholly within the 10 foot width of a full pitch' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-ball). Strictly a full toss lands nowhere and is legal, so 'must land on it, if it lands at all' would be the precise phrasing, but the claim is substantively correct. Metric figure is a conversion of 22 yards, but it is the figure the MCC Laws themselves print, so it does not need imperial units to make sense. Track position 0.432 (linear 5..40), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball_court: 'the baskets are always 10 feet (3.05 m) above the floor' under both FIBA and NBA rules, so the claimed FIBA source is right. The Naismith article confirms the 1891 peach baskets were mounted about 10 feet from the floor, secured to the inside of the gallery railing. One reveal caveat: the article frames the height as a deliberate design choice (placing the goal above players' heads to make it unguardable), which sits in tension with the reveal's 'the rail simply happened to be at that height'. That accidental-railing story is the popular telling rather than settled fact — recommend softening to 'he nailed it to the gym's balcony rail, ten feet up, and the game has never moved it'. Track position 0.35 (linear 2..5), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA: 211 national associations, and the article states directly that FIFA 'has admitted associations from 23 non-sovereign entities as members in their own right', naming the four Home Nations and Hong Kong and Macau — so the reveal's '23' is sourced, not invented. I tried to disprove it by counting independently (UN members absent from FIFA: UK, Monaco, Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Nauru, Kiribati, Tuvalu, Palau) which suggests a figure nearer 26 depending on how Palestine, Kosovo and Taiwan are classed; since FIFA's own framing and Wikipedia both say 23, and the graded answer 211 is not affected, this is a reveal nuance only. 211 − 193 = 18 checks out, and Gibraltar and Tahiti are both members. Track position 0.644 (linear 50..300), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1930_FIFA_World_Cup: held in Uruguay 13–30 July 1930. Every reveal detail verified: 13 teams entered (7 South American, 4 European, 2 North American), only Belgium, France, Romania and Yugoslavia made the Atlantic crossing, and the two-ball dispute was settled by FIFA ruling Argentina's ball for the first half and Uruguay's for the second, with Uruguay winning 4–2. Track position 0.364 (linear 1890..2000), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mona_Lisa, which carries the Louvre's catalogue dimensions of 77 cm x 53 cm, oil on a white poplar panel — matching both the answer and the reveal's 53 cm width. The reveal's structural detail is verified: a crack developed near the top of the panel running down to the figure's hairline, and two butterfly-shaped walnut braces were inserted into the back to about a third of the panel's thickness (one fell out between 1888 and 1905). The '30 seconds' viewing figure is the widely reported Louvre estimate and is a soft claim, but it is not the graded number. Track position 0.317 (linear 20..200), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernica_(Picasso): 349.3 cm x 776.5 cm, so the true width is 7.765 m and the answer of 7.8 m is 0.45% high — a rounding, well inside tolerance, and the Reina Sofía is the correct source. Reveal verified: Picasso worked 35 days and finished 4 June 1937; the painting hung at MoMA and only reached Spain in September 1981, six years after Franco's death in 1975, going to the Reina Sofía in 1992. If you want maximum precision, set the answer to 7.77. Track position 0.686 (log 1..20), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(Michelangelo): the statue measures 5.17 m (17 ft 0 in), which is the figure alone as the prompt specifies — I specifically looked for a with-plinth conflation, the usual failure mode here, and the article gives no separate plinth-inclusive total. Reveal verified: the block had been abandoned by two earlier sculptors, and the statue was removed from the Piazza della Signoria to the Accademia in 1873 (transported 30 July–10 August), which is 369 years outdoors from 1504 — 'nearly 370' is right — with a replica now standing in the square. Track position 0.351 (log 2..30), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army: 2007 estimates put more than 8,000 soldiers in the three pits, alongside 130 chariots with 520 horses and 150 cavalry horses. Since the prompt asks specifically about warriors, 8,000 is the right target and does not collide with the horse/chariot counts. The reveal's striking numbers are verified verbatim in the same article: the lacquer under the paint 'can curl in fifteen seconds once exposed to Xi'an's dry air and can flake off in just four minutes', which is why excavation is deferred, and most figures remain unexcavated. Not a duplicate of the existing history-category question on the 1974 discovery year. Track position 0.634 (log 100..100,000), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayeux_Tapestry: 68.38 m long and 0.5 m tall, so the answer of 68 m is 0.6% low and the reveal's 50 cm height is exact. Reveal verified on both other points: it is embroidery in wool on linen (stem stitch and laid work) rather than a true tapestry weave, and the star with a streaming tail is the first known depiction of Halley's Comet, which appeared in spring 1066. Track position 0.767 (log 5..150), in band.

Checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistine_Chapel_ceiling: painted between 1508 and 1512, approximately four years. Reveal verified against the same article: Vasari records that he worked 'with his head tilted backwards', standing on scaffolding of his own design rather than lying down, and Michelangelo's own poem to Giovanni da Pistoia describes his beard turning up to heaven and the brush dripping on his face. Track position 0.158 (linear 1..20) — low but above the 0.08 floor, so the range is acceptable; tightening hi to 15 would centre it better if you want more separation.

questions.prompt: The glass pyramid outside the Louvre in Paris is built from how many panes of glass?
questions.source: Wikipedia (Louvre Pyramid): 603 rhombi plus 70 triangles, confirmed by the Louvre
questions.reveal: A rumour that it has exactly 666 panes has followed it since the 1980s, when the official brochure published during construction cited that number twice. Architect I. M. Pei's office says President Mitterrand never specified any number of panes.

questions.prompt: Highest a bird has ever been confirmed to fly: a Rüppell's vulture reached what altitude, in metres?
questions.source: Guinness World Records; 1973 Abidjan bird-strike report
questions.reveal: It was established the hard way: the bird hit an airliner over Ivory Coast in 1973 and wrecked an engine. Its haemoglobin grips oxygen so tightly it can work on air that would knock a climber unconscious.
questions.reasoningPath: Airliners cruise around 11 km and birds are normally far below them, but soaring vultures ride thermals for hours. Put the record above the highest mountain (8.8 km) and near jet cruising height — so about 10,000 m, not 3,000 and not 30,000.

questions.prompt: A naked mole-rat's heart keeps beating for how many minutes in air with no oxygen at all?
questions.reveal: It switches its cells to burning fructose, a fuel pathway otherwise seen in plants, then gets up and carries on as if nothing had happened.
questions.reasoningPath: A human brain fails in about four minutes and a champion breath-hold diver manages ten. An animal adapted to stale, crowded burrows should beat both, but not by orders of magnitude — tens of minutes, not hours.

questions.prompt: A hibernating Arctic ground squirrel lets its core body temperature fall to roughly what, in Celsius?
questions.reveal: Its blood stays liquid by supercooling — below freezing with nothing to seed an ice crystal. Every two or three weeks it shivers itself back up to 37 °C for a day, then lets go again.
questions.reasoningPath: Ordinary hibernators drop to about 5 °C. The point of this animal is that it goes further than anyone thought a mammal could, so aim just past the freezing point rather than at 10 °C or -30 °C.

questions.prompt: Whatever the weather outside, honeybees hold their brood nest at what temperature in Celsius?
questions.source: apiculture literature: brood nest maintained at 34-35 °C
questions.reveal: Brood raised even one degree cooler emerges with measurably worse memory and navigation, so the colony is effectively incubating its own intelligence.
questions.reasoningPath: Developing insects need warmth close to mammal body heat, and a hive is famously hot inside. Human body temperature, 37 °C, is the obvious anchor; the answer sits just under it.

questions.prompt: Tracked in the wild, African elephants sleep how many hours a day?
questions.reveal: They often go 46 hours without sleeping at all, walking 30 km in the meantime. Elephants in zoos, with food delivered and no lions about, sleep two to three times longer.
questions.reasoningPath: Big grazing animals must eat almost constantly and stay alert for predators, so they sleep far less than we do. Horses and giraffes get by on three or four hours; the largest land animal should be at or below that.

questions.prompt: Highest voltage ever measured coming out of an electric eel, in volts?
questions.source: de Santana et al., Nature Communications, 2019
questions.reveal: The record-holder, Electrophorus voltai, was only recognised as a separate species in 2019. Four-fifths of the animal's body is battery: stacked cells each contributing a fraction of a volt.
questions.reasoningPath: Enough to knock a horse off its feet, but not to arc across a room. Mains electricity is 220 V and a stun gun runs into the thousands; the eel sits between them, nearer the lower end.

questions.prompt: A mantis shrimp's club goes from rest to what speed when it strikes, in metres per second?
questions.reveal: The punch is so fast the water ahead of it boils, and the collapsing bubble lands a second blow — the shrimp can stun prey even when the club misses.
questions.reasoningPath: Fast enough to crack aquarium glass, but it is a limb a few centimetres long moving through water. A thrown baseball is about 40 m/s; the strike belongs in that neighbourhood, nowhere near a bullet.

questions.prompt: A one-square-kilometre locust swarm eats as much food in a day as how many people?
questions.reveal: Locusts are ordinary solitary grasshoppers until crowding brushes their hind legs together; within hours they change colour, shape and behaviour, and start marching.
questions.reasoningPath: Such a swarm holds tens of millions of insects, and each eats roughly its own body weight — a couple of grams — every day. Tens of millions of grams is tens of tonnes, and a person eats about a kilogram a day.

questions.prompt: A modern commercial laying hen produces roughly how many eggs in a year?
questions.source: poultry industry averages, 285-300 eggs per bird per year
questions.reveal: Her wild ancestor, the red junglefowl, lays 10 to 15 a year in a single clutch. A hen ovulates about every 25 hours, so laying drifts later each day until she skips one and resets.
questions.reasoningPath: A hen lays at most one egg a day and takes the occasional day off, so 365 is a hard ceiling and the answer has to sit a little under it.

questions.prompt: A male emperor penguin goes how many days without food while seeing the egg through the Antarctic winter?
questions.source: Antarctic research programmes; standard figure ~115 days
questions.reveal: He loses about 40% of his body weight, then feeds the newly hatched chick a milk-like secretion from his own oesophagus while waiting for the female to walk back from open water.
questions.reasoningPath: The Antarctic winter is dark for months and the open sea is a long march away, so the fast has to be measured in months rather than weeks — three to four months is the plausible band.

questions.prompt: The only blue whale heart ever preserved for a museum weighed how many kg?
questions.reveal: It took four people to lift and six months to plastinate. The aorta is about 23 cm across — wide, but not the crawl-through tunnel of legend.
questions.reasoningPath: A heart runs to roughly half a percent of body mass in large mammals. A blue whale is 100 to 150 tonnes, so half a percent of that is a couple of hundred kilograms.

questions.prompt: Largest bird wingspan ever verified, on a wandering albatross, in centimetres?
questions.reveal: It was caught from a research ship in the Tasman Sea in 1965. A shoulder tendon locks the wings open, so gliding costs an albatross barely more energy than sitting still.
questions.reasoningPath: Photographs show an albatross clearly wider than a tall person is high, but not twice as wide. Somewhere between three and four metres, so a few hundred centimetres.

questions.prompt: Darwin's bark spider slings a web across rivers. How many metres can its bridge line span?
questions.reveal: Nobody has watched how the first line gets across; the leading guess is that the spider pays out silk into the wind and waits. That silk is the toughest biological material ever measured.
questions.reasoningPath: A garden web bridges a metre or two between bushes. Spanning a river means a stream you could not jump but could throw a stone across — tens of metres, not hundreds.

questions.prompt: General Sherman, the largest tree on Earth by volume, holds how many cubic metres of wood?
questions.reveal: It is neither the tallest tree alive nor the widest. It wins by refusing to taper, holding nearly its full girth 30 metres above the ground.
questions.reasoningPath: Treat the trunk as a cylinder: about 80 m tall with an average radius near 2.5 m gives pi times 6 times 80, which lands around 1,500 cubic metres.

questions.prompt: The largest leaf ever measured, a Raphia palm frond in Congo, ran how many metres long?
questions.source: Hallé's measurement of Raphia regalis, 25.9 m
questions.reveal: The palm itself is barely taller than a person — almost the whole plant is leaf, and one frond carries around 180 leaflets on each side.
questions.reasoningPath: A banana leaf reaches three metres and already looks startling. A record palm frond should beat that several times over while still being something one person could drag — tens of metres, not hundreds.

questions.prompt: The deepest tree roots ever found reached how many metres below the surface?
questions.reveal: Well-drillers hit them by accident in the Kalahari. The tree above ground is a modest shepherd's tree you could walk past without noticing.
questions.reasoningPath: Most tree roots stay in the top two metres of soil. A desert tree chasing fossil water has to reach the water table, which in the Kalahari is tens of metres down — the height of a twenty-storey building.

questions.prompt: The Svalbard seed vault, cut into Arctic rock, can hold how many seed samples?
questions.reveal: It holds about 1.3 million today. The mountain stays below freezing on its own, so the seeds would outlast both the refrigeration and, in principle, the country running it.
questions.reasoningPath: It is an insurance policy for the world's gene banks, which between them hold a few hundred thousand crop varieties, and it was built with room to spare — millions, not thousands and not billions.

questions.prompt: How many litres of maple sap must be boiled down to make one litre of maple syrup?
questions.source: maple producers' standard 40:1 ratio (Jones' Rule of 86)
questions.reveal: A single tap yields about 40 litres in a season, so a tree gives roughly one bottle a year. Boiling it off takes more energy than every other step combined.
questions.reasoningPath: Sap tastes barely sweet — about 2% sugar — while syrup is roughly two-thirds sugar. Dividing 66 by 2 gives the concentration ratio directly.

questions.prompt: The world's largest plant, a single seagrass clone off Australia, covers how many km²?
questions.source: Edgeloe et al., Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2022
questions.reveal: It grew from one seed about 4,500 years ago and has cloned sideways ever since at roughly 35 cm a year. It also carries twice the normal number of chromosomes.
questions.reasoningPath: It is described as stretching 180 km along a bay, but as a ribbon of meadow rather than a solid block. A long strip a kilometre or so wide comes out in the low hundreds of km².

questions.prompt: Averaged across the whole world, one hectare of wheat yields how many kg of grain?
questions.source: FAO: ~799 Mt of wheat from ~223 million ha, 2023
questions.reveal: The same hectare gave about 1,100 kg in 1961. Nearly all the gain came from breeding shorter plants that put their growth into grain instead of straw.
questions.reasoningPath: A hectare feeds a handful of people for a year and a person eats roughly 150 kg of grain annually. Hundreds of kilos would mean famine, tens of tonnes is impossible — a few thousand kilos fits.

questions.prompt: Highest air temperature ever officially recorded on Earth, in Celsius?
questions.source: WMO World Weather & Climate Extremes Archive
questions.reveal: Set at Furnace Creek in 1913, it has survived repeated attempts by meteorologists to strike it off as a misreading. Its nearest modern rival, 54.4 °C, comes from the same valley.
questions.reasoningPath: Hot deserts routinely hit 50 °C, so the record must beat that — but it cannot approach the temperature of a hot bath. The high fifties is the only plausible band.

questions.prompt: The heaviest hailstone on record, which fell in Bangladesh in 1986, weighed how many grams?
questions.source: WMO World Weather & Climate Extremes Archive
questions.reveal: Holding a stone that heavy aloft while it grows takes an updraft well over 150 km/h. That storm killed 92 people.
questions.reasoningPath: Eyewitnesses described stones the size of melons. A grapefruit of ice is a few hundred grams and a melon is around a kilogram, so the record sits near a kilogram.

questions.prompt: Without any greenhouse gases, Earth's average surface would be how many degrees Celsius colder?
questions.reveal: Water vapour does about half of the warming and CO2 roughly a fifth. Strip it away and the oceans freeze, after which no water vapour could circulate to bring it back.
questions.reasoningPath: The planet averages about 15 °C today, and a bare rock at this distance from the Sun would sit well below freezing, near -18 °C. The gap between those two numbers is the answer.

questions.prompt: On average, how many days does a water molecule spend in the atmosphere before falling as rain?
questions.source: van der Ent & Tuinenburg, HESS, 2017 (8.9 ± 0.4 days)
questions.reveal: The whole sky holds about 13,000 cubic kilometres of water at any moment — barely a week and a half of global rainfall — so it has to be recycled roughly forty times a year.
questions.reasoningPath: Weather systems form, travel and rain out within a week or so, and the atmosphere holds only a few centimetres of water spread over the globe. Days, then, not hours and not months.

questions.prompt: How many kilograms does Earth's entire atmosphere weigh?
questions.reveal: Half of that mass sits below 5.5 km, which is why the summit of Everest offers roughly a third of the oxygen you get at the beach.
questions.reasoningPath: Sea-level pressure means about 10 tonnes of air pressing on every square metre, and Earth has 510 million square kilometres of surface. Multiply the two.

questions.prompt: At any given moment, roughly how many thunderstorms are in progress worldwide?
questions.reveal: Together they push around 1,000 amps into the upper atmosphere, sustaining a permanent difference of some 300,000 volts between the ground and the ionosphere.
questions.reasoningPath: Lightning flashes somewhere on Earth roughly 50 to 100 times a second, and a single storm flashes every few seconds. Dividing one by the other lands you in the low thousands.

questions.prompt: Outside a jet cruising at 11 km, the air is at roughly what temperature in Celsius?
questions.reveal: Above 11 km the cooling stops and the temperature holds flat for another 9 km — the base of the stratosphere, where ozone soaks up sunlight and warms the air back up.
questions.reasoningPath: Air cools about 6.5 °C for every kilometre of altitude. Start from 15 °C at the ground and subtract eleven times that.

questions.prompt: World record rainfall in 24 hours, set on Réunion in 1966, in millimetres?
questions.source: WMO World Weather & Climate Extremes Archive
questions.reveal: The gauge sat at 2,990 m on a volcano directly in a cyclone's path, so the air was forced up the slope and wrung dry. It averaged 76 mm an hour for a full day.
questions.reasoningPath: A very wet temperate city collects about 1,000 mm in a whole year. A record day under a tropical cyclone should deliver something on the order of a year's worth at once.

questions.prompt: Averaged over 2025, CO2 at Mauna Loa measured how many parts per million?
questions.source: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory (2025 annual mean 427.35 ppm)
questions.reveal: The record began in 1958 at 315 ppm. Its year-to-year saw-tooth is the Northern Hemisphere's forests inhaling every summer and exhaling every winter.
questions.reasoningPath: The pre-industrial value was 280 ppm, and the figure is usually described as having risen by about half again since. Add a bit over 100 ppm to 280.

questions.prompt: Arica in Chile once went how many consecutive months without a drop of measurable rain?
questions.reveal: The town is trapped between the Andes and a cold offshore current, so the air arrives dry from both directions. When rain finally returned in 2015 it caused deadly floods.
questions.reasoningPath: To be the driest inhabited place on Earth the run has to beat any ordinary drought by a wide margin — years rather than seasons, so well over a hundred months.

questions.prompt: The oldest mineral grain ever dated on Earth formed how many billion years ago?
questions.source: Valley et al., Nature Geoscience, 2014 (4.374 billion years)
questions.reveal: It is a zircon from Western Australia smaller than a grain of sand, and its chemistry shows liquid water already existed on Earth when it crystallised.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth is 4.54 billion years old and the surface stayed molten for a stretch after that, so the oldest surviving crystal must sit just below the planet's own age.

questions.prompt: The 1980 eruption of Mount St Helens removed how many metres from the mountain's summit?
questions.reveal: It did not so much blow its top as slide off it — the largest landslide in recorded history carried the north flank away first, uncorking the magma underneath.
questions.reasoningPath: Before-and-after photographs show a mountain with roughly its top eighth gone. It stood just under 3,000 m, so an eighth of that is a few hundred metres.

questions.prompt: The 2011 Tohoku earthquake shifted Japan's main island eastward by how many centimetres?
questions.source: USGS; Geospatial Information Authority of Japan (2.4 m)
questions.reveal: The seafloor directly above the fault moved about ten times further. The quake also nudged Earth's axis and shortened the day by a couple of millionths of a second.
questions.reasoningPath: Plates creep a few centimetres a year and a great earthquake releases centuries of stored strain in one go. A few hundred years of a few centimetres gives metres, not kilometres.

questions.prompt: Going down a deep mine, the rock warms by how many degrees Celsius per kilometre?
questions.reveal: South Africa's deepest gold mines sit in rock near 60 °C and have to be refrigerated before anyone can work in them. The gradient flattens sharply below the crust, or the mantle would be entirely molten.
questions.reasoningPath: Caves a few hundred metres down stay cool, yet mines at three or four kilometres need air conditioning against rock at about 60 °C. That works out to tens of degrees per kilometre.

questions.prompt: The world's longest cave system has how many km of surveyed passage?
questions.reveal: It is in Kentucky and it is more than twice the length of the runner-up. Surveyors add a few kilometres most years, so the record partly measures how much walking has been done.
questions.reasoningPath: It is a maze in flat-lying limestone rather than one long tunnel, and it has been surveyed for two centuries. Hundreds of kilometres is the right order — weeks of walking, not years.

questions.prompt: The largest gem diamond ever found, the Cullinan, weighed how many grams when it was dug up?
questions.reveal: That is 3,106 carats. It was cut into nine major stones, the largest of which now sits in a royal sceptre.
questions.reasoningPath: Photographs show a stone about the size of a clenched fist — perhaps 150 to 200 cubic centimetres. Diamond is roughly 3.5 times denser than water, so several hundred grams.

questions.prompt: Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia, the largest salt flat on Earth, covers how many km²?
questions.reveal: It varies by less than a metre in height across its whole width, so satellites use it to calibrate their altimeters. Beneath the crust lies brine holding much of the world's lithium.
questions.reasoningPath: Photographs and driving times suggest roughly 100 km across, though not a neat square. A hundred kilometres by a hundred is 10,000 km².

questions.prompt: The longest continuous ice core drilled so far reaches back how many years?
questions.reveal: The bubbles in it are literal samples of ancient air, which is how we know CO2 never passed 300 ppm across that entire span.
questions.reasoningPath: The ice sheet is around 3 km thick and accumulates a few centimetres a year, compressing sharply with depth. Even at an average of a millimetre a year, 3 km buys hundreds of thousands of years.

questions.prompt: At the peak of the last ice age, global sea level sat how many metres below today's?
questions.reveal: Britain was joined to Europe and Siberia to Alaska. The shorelines of that world are still down there, drowned, with river channels and settlement sites on them.
questions.reasoningPath: The vanished ice sheets were up to 3 km thick but covered perhaps a tenth of the ocean's area, and their meltwater spread across the whole ocean. That gives tens of metres, approaching a hundred.

questions.prompt: Over the past million years, ice ages have returned on a cycle of roughly how many years?
questions.reveal: The pacemaker is the shape of Earth's orbit, which stretches and rounds on that rhythm. Before about a million years ago the beat ran at 41,000 years instead, and nobody fully knows why it changed.
questions.reasoningPath: The last one ended about 12,000 years ago and there have been several — not dozens — in the past million years. A million divided by roughly ten gives the spacing.

questions.prompt: At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, water pressure is how many times that at sea level?
questions.source: computed from the 10,935 m depth of Challenger Deep
questions.reveal: Fish stop appearing below about 8,200 m, apparently a chemical limit: the molecule they use to keep proteins folded under pressure would have to reach concentrations that wreck their cells.
questions.reasoningPath: Every 10 m of water adds one atmosphere of pressure. The trench is roughly 11,000 m deep, so divide.

questions.prompt: The highest wave ever recorded, in an Alaskan bay in 1958, ran up the far slope to how many metres?
questions.reveal: A rockfall dropped 30 million cubic metres of mountain into the water at one end. The height was read afterwards from the trim line where the forest had been scoured away.
questions.reasoningPath: This was a landslide into a narrow inlet, not an ocean wave, so the water had nowhere to spread sideways. Expect something far past any storm wave — hundreds of metres rather than tens.

questions.prompt: Highest wave ever measured by an ocean buoy, in the North Atlantic, in metres?
questions.reveal: Buoys report significant wave height — the average of the biggest third — so individual crests that night were higher still. It was measured between Iceland and Britain.
questions.reasoningPath: Ships in a severe North Atlantic storm describe seas as high as the bridge, so 15 to 20 metres. A record should sit at the top of that range rather than double it.

questions.prompt: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch spreads across roughly how many km² of ocean?
questions.reveal: Almost half its mass is discarded fishing gear rather than consumer plastic, and most of the rest is fragments smaller than a grain of rice — you could sail straight through and see almost nothing.
questions.reasoningPath: It is described as several times the area of France, and France is about 550,000 km². That puts it in the low millions.

questions.prompt: The oldest seafloor anywhere on Earth is roughly how many million years old?
questions.source: global seafloor age maps; Jurassic crust, western Pacific
questions.reveal: Continental rock is forty times older. Subduction keeps swallowing the seafloor, and the oldest surviving patch lies in the western Pacific, right beside the trenches consuming it.
questions.reasoningPath: The Atlantic widens a few centimetres a year and is about 5,000 km across, which works out to roughly 200 million years of spreading. No ocean floor can be much older than that.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the world's land area is covered by forest?
questions.reveal: Half of it sits in just five countries: Russia, Brazil, Canada, the United States and China. About 90% is naturally regenerated rather than planted.
questions.reasoningPath: Deserts, ice, grassland, farmland and cities take most of the land between them, so forest cannot be half — but it is plainly more than a tenth. Around a third.

questions.prompt: All life on Earth adds up to how many gigatonnes of carbon?
questions.reveal: Plants are 82% of it and bacteria most of the remainder. Every animal on the planet together comes to about 2 gigatonnes — under half a percent.
questions.reasoningPath: Forests carry a few hundred tonnes of dry matter per hectare and cover some 40 million km². That alone gives hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon, and plants are the bulk of all life.

questions.prompt: How many million tonnes of Saharan dust settle on the Amazon basin each year?
questions.source: NASA CALIPSO analysis, 2015 (27.7 Mt per year)
questions.reveal: Much of it comes from a single dried-up lakebed in Chad, and it carries about 22,000 tonnes of phosphorus — close to exactly what the rainforest loses to its rivers each year.
questions.reasoningPath: Satellites put total dust leaving the Sahara near 200 million tonnes a year, and only a slice of that plume survives the Atlantic crossing to South America — a tenth or so.

questions.prompt: The world's marine fishing fleets land how many million tonnes of catch a year?
questions.source: FAO, The State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture 2024
questions.reveal: The figure has barely moved since the late 1980s despite far bigger boats and better electronics — the ceiling is the fish, not the fleet. Farmed production overtook it in 2022.
questions.reasoningPath: Eight billion people eating roughly 20 kg of seafood a year is about 160 million tonnes, and half of that now comes from farms rather than the open sea.

questions.prompt: The Amazon's drainage basin covers how many million km²?
questions.reveal: Rain falling on it may be recycled through the forest five or six times before reaching the sea, each tree breathing it back out for the next one downwind.
questions.reasoningPath: South America is about 18 million km², and the basin takes in a broad band across its northern half — somewhere between a third and 40% of the continent.

verdicts.prompt: Highest a bird has ever been confirmed to fly: a Rüppell's vulture reached what altitude, in metres?
verdicts.note: Opened Guinness 'Highest flying birds' plus secondary coverage: 11,300 m (37,000 ft), Gyps rueppellii, struck an airliner over Abidjan, Ivory Coast, 29 Nov 1973, engine shut down, plane landed safely; remains identified by Roxie Laybourne. Reveal checks out on all three claims (engine wrecked, Ivory Coast 1973, high-affinity haemoglobin). Recomputed position on log 800..40000 = 0.677, matches author claim, in band.

verdicts.prompt: A naked mole-rat's heart keeps beating for how many minutes in air with no oxygen at all?
verdicts.note: Checked Park et al., Science 356:307-311 (2017) abstract and Science/LiveScience/CBC coverage: 'survive 18 minutes of total oxygen deprivation (anoxia) without apparent injury', via GLUT5/KHK fructose-driven anaerobic glycolysis to lactate in the brain. 18 min confirmed. Reveal's 'fuel pathway otherwise seen in plants' is the press framing the researchers themselves used ('turn into plants'); loose but not false. Position log 1..600 = 0.452, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: A hibernating Arctic ground squirrel lets its core body temperature fall to roughly what, in Celsius?
verdicts.note: Barnes, Science 244 (1989) measured -2.9 °C abdominal temperature in Spermophilus parryii; supercooling without ice nucleation and periodic arousals to euthermia every 2-3 weeks both confirmed in the hibernation literature. Reveal accurate. Position linear -20..15 = 0.486, matches claim, in band. Note the linear scale with negative lo is handled correctly by valToPos in tools/assemble.js.

verdicts.prompt: Whatever the weather outside, honeybees hold their brood nest at what temperature in Celsius?
verdicts.note: Apiculture literature is consistent at 34-35 °C brood nest, tightly regulated; 35 °C is the top of the band and the usual single-number citation, so no >10% source disagreement. Reveal's cognitive claim traces to Tautz et al. (PNAS 2003), where bees pupated one degree cooler showed measurably impaired short-term memory and dance/navigation behaviour — verified, not folklore. Position linear 0..50 = 0.700, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: Tracked in the wild, African elephants sleep how many hours a day?
verdicts.note: Gravett et al., PLOS ONE 12(3) 2017 (actiwatch + gyroscope collars on two wild matriarchs, Chobe): mean 2 h sleep/day, longest recorded waking bout ~46 h covering ~30 km, and captive elephants sleep 4-6 h. Every number in the reveal is from that paper. Position log 1..24 = 0.218, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: Highest voltage ever measured coming out of an electric eel, in volts?
verdicts.note: de Santana et al., Nature Communications 10:4000 (2019) split Electrophorus into three species and recorded 860 V from E. voltai — the highest discharge ever measured from any animal. Reveal's '2019 new species' and 'four-fifths of the body is electric organ' both check out against the paper and standard Electrophorus anatomy. Position log 20..6000 = 0.659, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: A mantis shrimp's club goes from rest to what speed when it strikes, in metres per second?
verdicts.note: Patek, Korff & Caldwell, Nature 428:819-820 (2004): peak strike speed 23 m/s in Odontodactylus scyllarus, with cavitation bubbles producing a measurable second impact force — so the reveal's 'water boils' and 'stuns prey even when the club misses' are both from the primary source. Position log 1..300 = 0.550, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: A one-square-kilometre locust swarm eats as much food in a day as how many people?
verdicts.note: Opened FAO Locust Watch FAQ: verbatim 'a swarm the size of one square kilometre contains about 40 million locusts, which eat the same amount of food in one day as about 35,000 people'; FAO also gives ~2 g/day per locust. Single authoritative origin but it is the UN body that owns the figure, not a lone unreliable source. Gregarious-phase change on tactile stimulation of the hind femur is well documented, so the reveal holds. Position log 10000..10000000 = 0.181, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: A modern commercial laying hen produces roughly how many eggs in a year?
verdicts.note: DEDUPE FLAG ADJUDICATED: genuine duplicate, not a shared template. The sibling everyday candidate 'A modern commercial laying hen produces how many eggs in a year?' differs only by the adverb 'roughly'; identical subject, identical unit, identical answer (300 egg). Two questions that a player cannot tell apart and that score identically. Dropping the nature copy so the everyday one survives — poultry production reads as an everyday/food topic, and nature already carries fowl-adjacent items (nature13 ostrich egg, nature36 queen honeybee eggs, nature54 sunfish eggs). Not dropped for any factual defect; 300/yr is sound.

verdicts.prompt: A male emperor penguin goes how many days without food while seeing the egg through the Antarctic winter?
verdicts.note: Cross-checked Antarctic programme sources and the fasting-physiology literature (Groscolas; Robin et al.): males fast an average ~115 days (up to ~120) across courtship plus incubation, losing ~40% of body mass, and secrete an oesophageal 'crop milk' of protein and fat if the chick hatches before the female returns. All three reveal claims verified. Position log 7..500 = 0.656, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: The only blue whale heart ever preserved for a museum weighed how many kg?
verdicts.note: Answer independently confirmed, but the verifier identified a defective reveal and supplied no replacement text. Dropped rather than shipped with a known-bad reveal. Recoverable as a fresh candidate in a later batch. Original note: First verifier was RIGHT to flag ambiguity, HALF-RIGHT on the fix. Confirmed the fork is real and matters: this is a bracket game, so a player who draws a narrow band around one published figure is burned by another. Documented readings for this one object: 175 kg fresh (Journal of Plastination), '400 pounds'/180 kg as-removed (Smithsonian, CBC, Korea Times headline 'World's biggest heart: 180kg'), '200-kilogram organ' (Wired/ScienceAlert), 600 lb = 272 kg with blood and supporting structure (Vice), plus a heavier post-plastination mass after steel mesh insertion. Pinning the prompt to the as-removed organ is the necessary fix and I have kept it. BUT I reject the answer change to 175. 386 lb and 400 lb are the same measurement at different roundings; 175 appears essentially only in the one peer-reviewed paper, while 180 is the dominant public figure. 180 strictly dominates: a bracket built from the journal (170-180) still catches 180, while a bracket built from '400 pounds' (~178-185) misses 175. Reverting to the candidate's 180. On the reveal, the first verifier was right to delete both original claims - 'six months to plastinate' is flatly wrong (Vice: over a year in Germany, more than four months in the vacuum chamber alone) and 'four people to lift' is a garble of Smithsonian's 'four staff onsite plus myself to push the heart out of the thoracic cavity'. But its replacement imports a contested number: 3,200 litres traces to a single Wired-derived sentence, while the peer-reviewed paper says 600 L of stock formaldehyde and Smithsonian says 2,800 L - the same class of error it had just flagged. That sentence also calls the organ 200 kg, in tension with the 175 it chose. My reveal uses only figures I could corroborate: four days of extraction, over a year of plastination in Germany with four-plus months in the vacuum chamber (Vice), and the 23 cm aorta (confirmed, 'about nine inches'). MISSED BY BOTH VERIFIERS: the reasoning path is arithmetically broken. 0.5 percent of 100-150 tonnes is 500-750 kg, not 'a couple of hundred kilograms'; the actual heart-to-body ratio here is ~0.15 percent. A solver who follows that path lands roughly 3x high. There is no schema field for it, so flagging here - the path should be rewritten to something like 'a heart is a few tenths of a percent of body mass in the largest mammals' before ship. Range 50..20000 log unchanged; 180 sits at position 0.214, comfortably in band.

verdicts.prompt: Largest bird wingspan ever verified, on a wandering albatross, in centimetres?
verdicts.note: Opened the Guinness 'Largest wingspan for a bird species (living)' record: male Diomedea exulans, 3.63 m (11 ft 11 in), caught by the crew of the Antarctic research ship USNS Eltanin in the Tasman Sea on 18 September 1965. Ship, sea and year in the reveal all match. The shoulder-lock tendon that holds the wing extended with almost no muscular cost is standard albatross anatomy. Position log 80..1200 = 0.558, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: Darwin's bark spider slings a web across rivers. How many metres can its bridge line span?
verdicts.note: Answer independently confirmed, but the verifier identified a defective reveal and supplied no replacement text. Dropped rather than shipped with a known-bad reveal. Recoverable as a fresh candidate in a later batch. Original note: First verifier was right that 25 m is a lake figure (Agnarsson, Kuntner & Blackledge, PLOS ONE 5(9):e11234, 2010: Perinet rivers avg 3.5+/-1.5 m, Ranomafana 10-14 m, 'bridgeline threads reached 25 m (N = 3) across a lake'), but it certified the reveal as accurate when the reveal is the real defect. The reveal claims nobody has watched the first line get across and that wind-borne silk is only a 'leading guess'. That was the 2010 paper's own hedge ('as yet unknown... likely involves bridging'), but Gregoric, Agnarsson, Blackledge & Kuntner published the direct observation a year later (PLOS ONE 6(11):e26847, 2011): spiders descend on a dragline and release tens of threads that fuse into a single line over ~18-25 s, carried downwind to the far bank. Reveal rewritten to report the resolution instead of the mystery. Prompt widened to 'rivers and lakes' and asked for the longest measured, so the 25 m record is the thing being asked for; note the 2010 abstract does say 'anchor threads as long as 25 meters' to riverbanks, so the original framing was defensible and this is polish, not the load-bearing fix. Answer, range and log position (0.817) unchanged and in band. Toughness record (354+/-93 J/cm3, >10x Kevlar) still stands.

verdicts.prompt: General Sherman, the largest tree on Earth by volume, holds how many cubic metres of wood?
verdicts.note: NPS/Guinness figure 52,508 cubic feet = 1,487 m³, confirmed by the Sequoia & Kings Canyon NPS page and Guinness 'Largest living tree (volume)'. Sources agree exactly; no spread. Reveal verified: it is not the tallest (Hyperion, 116 m — already in the pack as nature26) and not the widest, and the low taper is precisely why it wins on volume. Position log 200..100000 = 0.323, matches, in band. Checked against nature26 for overlap: different tree, different quantity, no dedupe issue.

verdicts.prompt: The largest leaf ever measured, a Raphia palm frond in Congo, ran how many metres long?
verdicts.note: Confirmed Francis Hallé's Raphia regalis specimen in the Republic of Congo: 25.91 m total, of which 16.47 m blade and 9.44 m petiole — the largest leaf recorded on any plant. Reveal's ~180 leaflets per side and the near-stemless (acaulescent) habit of R. regalis both check out. Position log 0.5..50 = 0.858, matches, in band though close to the top edge; still clear of the 0.90 cut and of assemble.js's 0.08 margin.

verdicts.prompt: The deepest tree roots ever found reached how many metres below the surface?
verdicts.note: Concur with verifier 1 on the diagnosis, but its fix was incomplete. Both records verified independently: 68 m for Boscia albitrunca, central Kalahari Botswana, from Jennings (1974) via Canadell et al. 1996 Oecologia 108:583 — the deepest MEASURED root in the literature; and Guinness 'Greatest root depth', which I fetched directly, listing a CALCULATED 120 m for a wild fig (Ficus natalensis) at Echo Caves, Ohrigstad, Mpumalanga, with no mention of the shepherd's tree. The collision is real because the candidate prompt reuses Guinness's own phrasing ('deepest... ever found'), and Guinness is what a player finds first. Verifier 1's 76% figure overstates the damage — on the log band 5..500 the answers sit at 0.567 and 0.690, roughly a tenth of the span apart, so 120 is penalized but not crushed — yet the ambiguity is worth a cheap tightening rather than a drop. The actual defect in verifier 1: its writeup claims it fixed this by 'pinning the prompt to soil and naming the tree', but it supplied only a correctedReveal and NO correctedPrompt. A reveal fires after the answer is committed, so it cannot disambiguate at answer time — the 120-answering player is still marked down and only then told why, which is the exact 'feeling cheated' outcome verifier 1 said it was preventing. Supplying the prompt fix it described but omitted. I declined its suggestion to name the tree in the prompt: 'shepherd's tree' is the reveal's payoff, and hoisting it into the question spoils the beat. Pinning to 'measured' and 'down through soil' excludes the fig on its own, since that figure is calculated and follows cave voids. Reveal keeps verifier 1's rewrite with 'calculated' added, matching Guinness's own wording and sharpening the contrast. Answer 68 and range 5..500 unchanged and correct; position 0.567, comfortably in band. Reasoning path (fossil water, water table tens of metres down) survives the rewording intact.
verdicts.correctedPrompt: Growing down through soil, the deepest tree roots ever measured reached how many metres below the surface?
verdicts.correctedReveal: Well-drillers hit them by accident in the central Kalahari in 1974, and the tree above ground is a modest shepherd's tree you could walk past without noticing. Guinness lists a deeper figure — a calculated 120 m for a wild fig at South Africa's Echo Caves — but those roots were following cave voids rather than pushing through soil.

verdicts.prompt: The Svalbard seed vault, cut into Arctic rock, can hold how many seed samples?
verdicts.note: Crop Trust / NordGen / seedvault.no all give a design capacity of 4.5 million seed samples (~500 seeds each, ~2.25 billion seeds) with more than 1.3 million samples deposited as of the mid-2020s. Capacity is a fixed engineering number, so no year-to-year drift in the answer even though the deposit count in the reveal creeps up. Permafrost keeping the chamber below freezing without power is documented. Position log 40000..20000000 = 0.760, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: How many litres of maple sap must be boiled down to make one litre of maple syrup?
verdicts.note: Confirmed the first verifier independently. puzzles.js key everyday73 (line 6621-6631) is 'How many litres of maple sap boil down into one litre of syrup?' with answer 40, unit L, scale log — identical quantity, unit, answer and scale — and its reveal already contains both of the candidate's reveal facts (the 2%-sap/66%-syrup sugar framing and the one-tap-yields-about-that-much-per-season line). tests/published-schedule.json line 493 places everyday73 in days[69] with its prompt hash at line 1189, inside the range frozen through day index 118. One correction to the first verifier's framing: it is not yet answered by returning players — epoch 2026-07-27 with playedThroughDayIndexAtFreeze 38 puts today at day 38 and day 69 on 2026-10-04 — but the frozen schedule cannot be rewritten, so the collision is guaranteed to reach players regardless. Verdict unchanged. Separately, the candidate is not rescuable on accuracy grounds either: the 40:1 ratio and the Jones' Rule of 86 citation are correct, but the stated reasoning path is wrong — 66/2 is 33, not 40. The rule divides 86 (from syrup being about 86.3% solids by weight, together with the density difference) by the sap Brix, so 86/2 is about 43, which rounds to the familiar 40:1. Sources: UVM Extension 'The Jones Rule of 86 revisited', Northern Woodlands 'Sugar Content', The Maple News.

verdicts.prompt: The world's largest plant, a single seagrass clone off Australia, covers how many km²?
verdicts.note: Edgeloe et al., Proc. R. Soc. B 289:20220538 (2022), confirmed via the journal page and UWA release: one Posidonia australis clone, 200 km² of Shark Bay meadow, spanning 180 km, ~4,500 years old, polyploid with double the normal chromosome count. Checked the reveal's arithmetic tension (0.35 m/yr for 4,500 yr ≠ 180 km): the paper itself derives the age from a conservative 0.15-0.35 m/yr rhizome extension and notes seagrass branches in many directions rather than expanding linearly, so the reveal is faithful to the source rather than wrong. Position log 30..5000 = 0.371, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: Averaged across the whole world, one hectare of wheat yields how many kg of grain?
verdicts.correctedPrompt: Averaged across the whole world, one hectare of wheat yields how many kg of grain?
verdicts.correctedReveal: The same hectare gave about 1,100 kg in 1961. The tripling took two things at once: semi-dwarf breeding that pushed growth into grain instead of straw, and the heavy nitrogen and irrigation that short, stiff stems could finally absorb without the crop falling over.
verdicts.note: First verifier was right on the number, wrong to wave the reveal through. Answer and range confirmed independently: FAO 2023 gives ~799 Mt on ~220-223 Mha = 3.58 t/ha; the FAO 2016-2020 world mean is 3.48 t/ha; the Our World in Data/FAOSTAT series has Asia 3.63 and Europe 4.21 t/ha in 2024. 3,500 kg sits between those, log position 0.423 on 500..50000 (recomputed: ln(7)/ln(100) = 0.4226). Reveal sentence one also checks out — FAOSTAT 1961: 222 Mt on ~204 Mha = 1.09 t/ha, so 'about 1,100 kg' is right. Sentence two is the problem the first verifier missed. 'Nearly all the gain came from breeding shorter plants' is not what the literature says, and it fails an arithmetic check the verifier never ran: the semi-dwarf harvest-index shift is ~0.3 to ~0.5, a factor of 1.67, while world yield rose by a factor of 3.2. Partitioning alone cannot cover 'nearly all' of that; the rest is nitrogen, irrigation, and agronomy. Published attributions bear this out and vary widely by system — irrigated spring wheat in Mexico 1968-1990 was 28% genetic vs 48% N fertilizer, dryland Kansas 1977-2006 was 79% vs 21%. The standard framing is that semi-dwarf stature was what made heavy fertilizer usable without lodging, not that it was the gain by itself. Corrected reveal keeps the 1961 hook and the straw-to-grain mechanism but restores the fertilizer/irrigation half. Separately, and not fixable through these fields: the reasoning path is internally inconsistent. 'A hectare feeds a handful of people' times 'roughly 150 kg per person' lands near 750 kg, which the same path then dismisses as famine territory. The path argues a player toward the wrong order of magnitude; the ratio is ~23 people per hectare, not a handful. Worth flagging to whoever owns the path text even though the answer stands.

verdicts.prompt: Highest air temperature ever officially recorded on Earth, in Celsius?
verdicts.note: WMO World Weather & Climate Extremes Archive: 56.7 °C, Furnace Creek (Greenland Ranch), Death Valley, 10 July 1913 — still the standing official record despite repeated challenges to its validity, with 54.4 °C from the same valley (2020/2021) as the nearest modern reading. Reveal is accurate including the 'survived attempts to strike it off' framing. Unit is Celsius and the record is a global superlative, so no US-centrism or imperial dependence. Position linear 20..70 = 0.734, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: The heaviest hailstone on record, which fell in Bangladesh in 1986, weighed how many grams?
verdicts.note: WMO extremes archive (Table_Records, current PDF) and Guinness both give 1.02 kg, Gopalganj district, Bangladesh, 14 April 1986, with 92 deaths — matching the reveal exactly. FLAG FOR THE AUTHOR: the claimed position 0.607 is wrong; I recomputed log(1020/20)/log(30000/20) = 0.538. Still comfortably in the 0.10-0.90 band, so no range change needed, but the author's position arithmetic is unreliable here and in two other entries (36, 49).

verdicts.prompt: Without any greenhouse gases, Earth's average surface would be how many degrees Celsius colder?
verdicts.note: Standard radiative-balance result reproduced in IPCC assessments: ~15 °C observed versus ~-18 °C effective radiating temperature, a 33 °C greenhouse effect. Reveal's attribution split matches Schmidt et al. (2010) — water vapour ~50%, clouds ~25%, CO2 ~20% — so 'about half' and 'roughly a fifth' are right, and the runaway-icehouse consequence is the textbook one. Not a drifting or brand-dependent figure. Position linear 10..150 = 0.164, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: On average, how many days does a water molecule spend in the atmosphere before falling as rain?
verdicts.note: van der Ent & Tuinenburg, HESS 21:779-790 (2017): global mean atmospheric residence time 8.9 ± 0.4 days. Checked the reveal's arithmetic myself: ~12,900 km³ of atmospheric water against ~500,000 km³/yr of global precipitation gives ~39 turnovers a year, so 'roughly forty times' is right and internally consistent with 9 days. Position log 1..1000 = 0.318, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: How many kilograms does Earth's entire atmosphere weigh?
verdicts.note: 5.15 x 10^18 kg is the standard value and I re-derived it independently: 101,325 Pa / 9.81 m/s² = 10,330 kg/m² over 5.10 x 10^14 m² = 5.27 x 10^18 kg, agreeing to ~2% once topography and gravity variation are accounted for. Reveal verified: the 5.5 km half-mass level is the standard scale-height result, and Everest's summit pressure is ~33% of sea level, so 'roughly a third of the oxygen' is right. Position log 1e16..1e20 = 0.678, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: At any given moment, roughly how many thunderstorms are in progress worldwide?
verdicts.note: I did not take this on trust because the global-electric-circuit literature quotes a range. Fetched NOAA NSSL Severe Weather 101 directly: 'at any given moment, there are roughly 2,000 thunderstorms in progress' — verbatim, and the prompt says 'roughly', matching the source's own hedge. The reveal's circuit numbers are the low end of a real spread (literature gives ~1,000-1,800 A total current; ~300 kV ionosphere-ground potential is firm), so 'around 1,000 amps' is defensible but is the loosest claim in this entry. Position log 500..200000 = 0.231, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: Outside a jet cruising at 11 km, the air is at roughly what temperature in Celsius?
verdicts.note: International Standard Atmosphere gives exactly -56.5 °C at 11,000 m, and I re-derived it from the reveal's own method: 15 °C - (6.5 °C/km x 11 km) = -56.5 °C. The isothermal layer from 11 to 20 km and its ozone-heating explanation are both correct ISA/stratosphere facts. A defined standard, so there is no source-disagreement or drift risk at all. Position linear -100..40 = 0.314, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: World record rainfall in 24 hours, set on Réunion in 1966, in millimetres?
verdicts.note: WMO extremes archive: 1,825 mm at Foc-Foc, Réunion, 15-16 January 1966 during Tropical Cyclone Denise. Reveal checks out — the Foc-Foc gauge sits at 2,990 m, orographic lift on the volcano's windward slope is the mechanism, and 1825/24 = 76 mm/h exactly as stated. Checked against nature77 (Mawsynram annual rainfall): different quantity, different timescale, no dedupe conflict. Position log 50..5000 = 0.781, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: Averaged over 2025, CO2 at Mauna Loa measured how many parts per million?
verdicts.note: NOAA GML: 2025 annual mean 427.35 ppm at Mauna Loa (May 2025 peak 430.2 ppm, the first month above 430). Reveal verified: the Keeling record opens in 1958 near 315 ppm and the seasonal saw-tooth is Northern Hemisphere vegetation. I considered dropping this for drift and decided against it — the prompt is explicitly stamped 'Averaged over 2025', which freezes the target, unlike an unstamped 'current CO2' question. Position linear 300..1000 = 0.181, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: Arica in Chile once went how many consecutive months without a drop of measurable rain?
verdicts.note: First verifier was correct that the answer holds and correct to fix rather than drop, but its replacement reveal is itself wrong. Answer re-verified independently: Guinness World Records ('Longest sustained dry period', and cross-referenced on its 'Driest place' page) and the WMO both give 172 months / 14.42 years, October 1903 to January 1918. Log position 0.477 in 15..2500 — mid-band, no anchoring problem. Original reveal's 'when rain finally returned in 2015' is indeed a chronological error (the streak broke in January 1918; the March 2015 Atacama floods were centred on Copiapo and Chanaral, over a thousand km south), so 'fix' was the right call and a drop would have wasted a good question. However the first verifier's correctedReveal adds two fresh errors: (1) 'the lowest of any inhabited place on Earth' contradicts Guinness itself, which awards the 'Driest place' record to Quillagua, Chile at 0.5 mm/yr (1964-2001), recognised by the Direccion Meteorologica de Chile — Arica's 0.76 mm is the runner-up; (2) 'even now Arica averages well under a millimetre' is unsupported — the 0.76 mm figure comes from a pre-1968 59-year series, while the 1971-2000 normal is 1.46 mm (Christopher Burt, Weather Underground), roughly double. My corrected reveal keeps the verified 1918 end date, keeps the mechanism (rain shadow plus Humboldt Current, both true), and swaps the unsafe superlative for the accurate one: Arica holds the duration record, Quillagua holds the lowest-average record.
verdicts.correctedReveal: The town is trapped between the Andes and the cold Humboldt Current, so the air arrives dry from both directions. The run finally broke in January 1918 — and while Arica still holds the duration record, nearby Quillagua has since posted the lowest yearly rainfall average of any weather station on Earth.

verdicts.prompt: The oldest mineral grain ever dated on Earth formed how many billion years ago?
verdicts.note: Valley et al., Nature Geoscience 7:219-223 (2014): 4.374 ± 0.006 Ga Jack Hills zircon from Western Australia, confirmed grain-by-grain with atom-probe tomography to rule out lead mobility — so this is not a single shaky measurement. Oxygen-isotope evidence for liquid water at crystallisation is from the same body of work. Reveal accurate. Position linear 0..5 = 0.880: in band, but it is the tightest entry in the batch (0.12 from the top edge), so any later answer revision upward would push it out.

verdicts.prompt: The 1980 eruption of Mount St Helens removed how many metres from the mountain's summit?
verdicts.note: USGS: 2,950 m (9,677 ft) before, 2,549 m (8,363 ft) after — a 400-401 m loss depending on rounding, so the answer is right to within a metre. Verified the reveal's strongest claim separately: USGS and Britannica both describe the north-flank collapse as the largest debris avalanche/landslide in recorded history, and the sequence (landslide first, decompressing the cryptodome, then the lateral blast) is the accepted mechanism. Position log 10..800 = 0.842, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: The 2011 Tohoku earthquake shifted Japan's main island eastward by how many centimetres?
verdicts.note: Answer confirmed: GSI/USGS report ~2.4 m eastward coseismic displacement of Honshu; log position in 20..20000 is 0.360, in band. The first verifier was WRONG on its central claim. The original reveal's 'ten times' is accurate: Sato et al., Science 332:1395 (2011) - literally titled 'Displacement Above the Hypocenter of the 2011 Tohoku-Oki Earthquake' - measured ~24 m ESE and ~3 m up at seafloor GNSS-acoustic station MYGI directly above the focal region, exactly 10x the 2.4 m onshore figure. The first verifier's >50 m figure is Fujiwara et al., Science 334:1240 (2011), differential bathymetry at the TRENCH AXIS (38 deg 05' to 38 deg 35' N) - the shallowest, most seaward edge of the rupture, a different place from above the hypocenter. Both numbers are real; verifier one swapped locations and then called the original an error, so its 'fix' rests on a false premise and would have replaced a correct statement. The one genuine weakness is that 'directly above the fault' is ambiguous (the trench is also above the fault), which is precisely what misled verifier one. My correction keeps the correct 10x, pins it to the hypocenter, and gives the 24 m / 3 m numbers so it is checkable. Also swapped 'a couple of millionths of a second' for the concrete NASA/JPL figure: Gross computed 1.8 microseconds (later revised to 1.4), plus a 17 cm shift of Earth's figure axis toward 133E. Prompt, answer, and range unchanged.
verdicts.correctedReveal: The seafloor directly above the hypocenter moved about ten times further - a GPS-acoustic station off Miyagi jumped roughly 24 metres east-southeast and 3 metres up. The quake also nudged Earth's figure axis about 17 centimetres and shortened the day by nearly two millionths of a second.
