verdicts.prompt: Going down a deep mine, the rock warms by how many degrees Celsius per kilometre?
verdicts.note: DROP CONFIRMED, but the first verifier's reasoning is wrong on the load-bearing point and its disposition leaves a broken question in the batch. FIRST VERIFIER SAID 'No factual defect - 25-30 C/km is the correct continental average.' That is true of the continental average and irrelevant to this prompt, which anchors the question to a MINE. Real deep mines do not have a 25 C/km gradient. Peer-reviewed source: 'Virgin rock temperatures and geothermal gradients in the Bushveld Complex' (J. Southern African Inst. Mining & Metallurgy, scielo.org.za/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S2225-62532018000700004) gives Witwatersrand Basin gold-reef gradients of 9.6-12.9 K/km, Carletonville (the Mponeng/TauTona field) at 11.7 K/km, and states Bushveld platinum gradients are 'approximately double the gradients in rocks overlying gold reefs' at 16.5-20.7 K/km; Venetia diamond mine 19.5 K/km. The Witwatersrand sits on the Kaapvaal craton with heat flow of 33-43 mW/m2, among the lowest on Earth, roughly half the continental average - which is exactly why its gradient is roughly half of 25. THE QUESTION REFUTES ITSELF ON THE REVEAL SCREEN: Wikipedia Mponeng Gold Mine confirms the reveal's own figures (over 4 km deep, rock at 66 C, ice-slurry refrigeration holding air below 30 C), and (66 - ~17 surface) / ~3.9 km = ~12.5 C/km. The reasoning path is worse still: '60 C at three or four kilometres' derives 15-20, not 25. So a player who follows the supplied reasoning path lands at 12-15 and is scored against 25 - a factor of two, 13 points of a 0..100 linear track - and then reads a reveal whose numbers vindicate their answer, not the scored one. That is precisely the Rule 2 trust failure ('being scored wrong on a number you can defend'). Fixable only by stripping the mine framing (e.g. 'Beneath the continents, how much hotter does rock get per kilometre of depth?') plus a rewritten reveal that does not present 60 C at 4 km as evidence for 25 - but that fix is barred here because the space sibling already occupies the subject. DEDUPE FLAG: I agree it is a genuine duplicate. Same subject, setting, unit and answer; the 50% token score is an artefact of 'the rock warms by'/'temperature rises by' and 'kilometre'/'km'. Drop stands on both grounds. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE FIRST VERIFIER'S SUPPORTING CLAIMS, neither changing this verdict but both affecting which twin survives. (1) ACTION REQUIRED ON THE SIBLING: 'Going down a deep mine, temperature rises by how many C per km of depth?' with answer 25 carries the identical defect. Dropping the nature copy and shipping the space copy unchanged ships the bug. The sibling must be re-verified: either reword it to the continental crust and rewrite its reveal, or set the answer to ~12 C/km if the mine framing is kept. Do not treat this dedupe as resolved by deletion alone. (2) 'The geothermal gradient is a better fit under space/earth-science' is backwards for this deck. In data/verified.json, 'space' is 'Space & Science' / 'Space & Physics' (astronomy, chemistry, human biology), while solid-earth science lives in NATURE: group 7 carries the Kola Superdeep Borehole, the deepest explored cave, Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreading, mean ocean depth, Krakatoa and Bay of Fundy tides. On category fit alone nature is the better home, so the choice of which twin to keep was made on a false premise. Also, the cited 'nature84' does not appear to be the deep-cave item: nature indices run 0-54 (group 0), 55-79 (group 6), 80-104 (group 7), putting the deepest-cave question near nature 89 and nature 84 at the cumulus-cloud item - a sign the sibling reference was not checked against the file. Verified independently: Wikipedia Geothermal gradient ('about 25-30 C/km near the surface in the continental crust'; mantle 'of the order of 0.5 kelvin per kilometer'), so the reveal's second sentence about the gradient flattening below the crust is sound - 25 C/km sustained to the core-mantle boundary would give tens of thousands of degrees. It is the first sentence's inference that fails.

verdicts.prompt: The world's longest cave system has how many km of surveyed passage?
verdicts.note: Answer 686 km re-verified and correct: NPS Park Statistics gives 426 miles (685 km); Wikipedia's longest-caves list gives 685.6 km. Log position 0.268 on 200..20000, comfortably in band. The first verifier was right that the original reveal's 'more than twice the runner-up' fails, but its replacement is itself wrong: it names Sistema Sac Actun as 'the next longest in the world' at 'under 400 km'. Sac Actun (387 km) is about FOURTH, not second. The actual runner-up is Sistema Ox Bel Ha in Quintana Roo at 541.7 km as of February 2026 (Wikipedia, corroborated by Live Science/ScienceAlert coverage of CINDAQ surveys; 524 km in April 2026 reporting, still climbing). Shuanghedong in China (441 km) also outranks Sac Actun. So the true Mammoth-to-runner-up ratio is 1.27x, not the 1.8x the first verifier computed and not the original 2x. Corrected reveal names Ox Bel Ha, gives an approximate figure flagged as growing so it does not rot as the survey extends, and keeps the honest survey-effort note. Prompt and answer unchanged.
verdicts.correctedReveal: It is Mammoth Cave in Kentucky, at about 686 km. The runner-up is Mexico's flooded Sistema Ox Bel Ha, past 540 km and still growing. Surveyors add a few kilometres most years, so the record partly measures how much walking has been done.

verdicts.prompt: The largest gem diamond ever found, the Cullinan, weighed how many grams when it was dug up?
verdicts.note: 3,106.75 carats x 0.2 g = 621.35 g — I did the conversion myself rather than trusting the source line, and Wikipedia/Britannica/Cape Town Diamond Museum all agree on the rough weight (Premier No. 2 mine, 26 January 1905). Reveal verified: nine major stones (1,055.89 ct total) plus 96 minor brilliants, and Cullinan I, the largest, is set in the Sovereign's Sceptre. The prompt asks in grams and the answer is metric, so the carat unit is a bonus in the reveal rather than a units dependency. Position log 15..1500 = 0.809, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia, the largest salt flat on Earth, covers how many km²?
verdicts.note: Second verifier: the first verifier's drop is CORRECT, and I confirmed it independently rather than taking its word. puzzles.js line 6033 defines geography65 = 'Area of Salar de Uyuni, the world's largest salt flat, in km²?', answer 10582, unit km², scale log — identical subject, quantity, unit, scale and number to this candidate, differing only in prompt wording and lo (1000 vs 500). It is not merely sitting in the bank: geography65 appears in puzzles.js's day list at line 8314 and in tests/published-schedule.json (line 835, the final day, index 118) with promptHash 80f90b9b7cda, i.e. it is inside the frozen published schedule that tools/freeze-schedule.js refuses to alter. So the existing copy cannot be removed to make room, and shipping this candidate re-deals a question players have already been given. The candidate's reveal is also a near-paraphrase of the published one ('varies by less than a metre... satellites... calibrate') with a lithium sentence appended, which makes the collision more obvious, not less, to a returning player. Note the candidate arrives tagged category 'nature' while the twin lives under geography — a same-category-only dedupe would have missed it; tools/check-batch.js does compare against all shipped questions (line 144-165), so it should catch this too. On the facts, nothing is wrong: Wikipedia gives 'approximately 10,582 square kilometres (4,086 sq mi)', 'elevation variation is less than 1 meter', describes it as one of the most effective natural calibration sites for Earth-observing satellites, and confirms lithium brine at ~0.3% under the crust with Bolivia holding ~22% of global reserves as of 2024. I also re-ran the first verifier's arithmetic: log position on 500..500000 is 0.4419 (its 0.442 is right, the author's claimed 0.613 is wrong); the published entry's 1000..500000 gives 0.3796, matching the 0.38 recorded in data/verified.json. Those are secondary — the duplication alone is disqualifying and unfixable, since no rewording changes that the answer is the same number about the same place.

verdicts.prompt: The longest continuous ice core drilled so far reaches back how many years?
verdicts.note: Agree with verifier 1 on the answer: 800,000 (EPICA Dome C, 2004) was superseded in January 2025 when Beyond EPICA - Oldest Ice reached bedrock at Little Dome C at 2,800 m and recovered a continuous record to ~1.2 Ma (AWI, Cambridge ESC, Univ. Bern releases; still the standing record in May 2026 coverage, cores delivered to European labs April 2026). Independently re-verified, not assumed. Nuance checked and accepted: the peer-reviewed flow-model paper (The Cryosphere 19, 4125, 2025) gives 1.12 Ma as the oldest ice meeting the 20 kyr/m resolution threshold, with a 200-250 m ambiguous basal layer - indistinguishable from 1.2 Ma on this log range, so the headline figure stands. BUT verifier 1's replacement reveal contains an error: it calls the new core 'roughly doubling' the 800-kyr record; 1.2 Ma / 0.8 Ma is 1.5x, not 2x. I corrected that phrase and kept its verified facts (bedrock Jan 2025, 2,800 m, up to 13,000 years per metre near the base - the last confirmed by the Beyond EPICA/AWI release). Position on the unchanged log 2000..20000000 range = 0.695, in band, so lo/hi stay. Also endorse verifier 1's build note: the source line must be hand-edited from 'EPICA Dome C, Antarctica' to 'Beyond EPICA - Oldest Ice, Little Dome C, 2025', since the schema carries no source field. The prompt itself is fine and portable - 'continuous ice core' correctly excludes the older discontinuous Allan Hills blue ice (~2.7 Myr) - though 'so far' means this question will need rechecking whenever the record moves again.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Beyond EPICA hit bedrock at Little Dome C in January 2025 after drilling 2,800 metres, pushing the continuous ice record from 800,000 years back to about 1.2 million. Near the bottom the ice is squeezed so hard that up to 13,000 years of snowfall fit into a single metre.

verdicts.prompt: At the peak of the last ice age, global sea level sat how many metres below today's?
verdicts.note: Palaeo sea-level reconstructions (Lambeck, Clark, Peltier ICE-6G and the coral-terrace records) converge on 120-135 m below present at the LGM ~21 ka, so 125 m is mid-range and the spread is within the tolerance for a log 10..2000 track. Reveal verified: Doggerland joined Britain to Europe and Beringia joined Siberia to Alaska at that lowstand, and drowned river channels and archaeological sites on those shelves are documented. Position 0.477, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: Over the past million years, ice ages have returned on a cycle of roughly how many years?
verdicts.note: Marine oxygen-isotope (LR04) stack: ~100 kyr glacial cycles through the late Pleistocene. Reveal verified against the Milankovitch literature — the ~100 kyr beat matches orbital eccentricity, and the mid-Pleistocene transition around 0.8-1.2 Ma switched the record from a 41 kyr (obliquity) rhythm, with the cause still genuinely unresolved. The prompt's 'roughly' and 'past million years' correctly scope it to the post-MPT regime, so the 41 kyr era is not a competing answer. Position log 4000..250000 = 0.778, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, water pressure is how many times that at sea level?
verdicts.note: Re-derived rather than trusted: 10,935 m at Challenger Deep, ~1 atm per 10.06 m of seawater, gives ~1,087 atm of water column plus the 1 atm above it — about 1,090, so 1,100 is right and robust against the 10,935 versus 10,984 m depth disagreement (that fork changes the answer by 0.4%). Reveal verified against Yancey et al. (PNAS 2014): fish disappear below ~8,200 m, and the proposed cause is that the TMAO concentration needed to stabilise proteins deeper would become osmotically intolerable. Position log 50..10000 = 0.583, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: The highest wave ever recorded, in an Alaskan bay in 1958, ran up the far slope to how many metres?
verdicts.note: Every element confirmed against USGS/Miller (1960), Wikipedia and NASA Earth Observatory: 9 July 1958 M7.8-8.3 Fairweather strike-slip quake, 30 million m³ rockslide into Gilbert Inlet, trees stripped to a maximum run-up elevation of 524 m (1,719 ft). The reveal's trim-line measurement method is exactly how Miller derived the figure. Note the prompt correctly says 'ran up the far slope' rather than calling it a 524 m wall of water — that distinction is what keeps this honest. Position log 20..5000 = 0.591, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: Highest wave ever measured by an ocean buoy, in the North Atlantic, in metres?
verdicts.note: WMO Commission for Climatology extremes committee: 19.0 m significant wave height, automated buoy at ~59°N 11°W between Iceland and the UK, 4 February 2013, behind a strong cold front; previous record 18.275 m (2007). Reveal verified: significant wave height is defined as the mean of the highest third, so individual crests were indeed higher, and the Iceland-Britain location is right. Checked it does not collide with candidate 41 — different record (buoy-measured sea state versus landslide run-up), different order of magnitude. Position log 8..300 = 0.239, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch spreads across roughly how many km² of ocean?
verdicts.note: Second verifier, independent check: first verifier was correct and its correction holds. Answer confirmed against Lebreton et al., Sci Rep 8:4666 (2018) — 'at least 79 (45-129) thousand tonnes of ocean plastic are floating inside an area of 1.6 million km2'. Log position in 10000..20000000 = ln(160)/ln(2000) = 0.668, comfortably in band. The reveal defect is genuine: the paper reports microplastics at 8% of total MASS but 94% of the ~1.8 trillion pieces, with over three-quarters of the mass carried by debris larger than 5 cm and at least 46% fishing nets. So 'most of the rest is fragments smaller than a grain of rice' is false on mass and contradicts the 46% fishing-gear clause sitting in the same sentence. Also spot-checked the gloss: the paper's microplastic class is 0.05-0.5 cm, and a rice grain is ~5-7 mm, so 'smaller than a grain of rice' is fair. The 'sail through and see almost nothing' punchline still lands on density grounds (79,000 t over 1.6M km2 is ~49 kg/km2), so I kept it. My corrected reveal carries the same verified numbers as the first verifier's but is tightened to the one-sentence shape used by the existing reveals in data/verified.json. Not a drop: the question is sound and the sole defect is repairable.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Almost half its mass is discarded fishing gear rather than consumer plastic, and the fragments smaller than a grain of rice are 94% of the pieces but only 8% of the weight — you could sail straight through and see almost nothing.

verdicts.prompt: The oldest seafloor anywhere on Earth is roughly how many million years old?
verdicts.note: Independently confirms the first verifier. Answer 180 Ma is solid: global age grids and ODP Hole 801C (Pigafetta Basin, western Pacific) put the oldest surviving ocean crust in the Jurassic, with Pacific accretion ~192 +/- 6 Ma and oldest dated basement 167.4 Ma; the standard statement is that no seafloor is much older than ~180 Ma. Log position 0.536 on 5..4000, mid-track, so the 167-200 Ma literature spread is harmless. The reveal's arithmetic is genuinely wrong as the first verifier found: the oldest continental rock is the Acasta Gneiss at 4.031 Ga, which is 22.4x older than 180 Ma, and the 4.4 Ga Jack Hills zircon (a mineral, not a rock) is only 24.4x; 'forty times' would require 7.2 Ga material, older than the Earth itself. The correction to 'more than twenty times' re-verifies as true against Acasta (22.4x), Jack Hills (24.4x), and the contested Nuvvuagittuq 4.28 Ga (23.8x), so it stays consistent with candidate 30 if both ship. Adopting the first verifier's corrected reveal verbatim. One thing the first verifier missed but which I judge non-fatal: Granot (2016, Nature Geoscience) claims ~340 Ma in-situ oceanic crust in the Herodotus Basin, eastern Mediterranean, so 'anywhere on Earth' technically invites that number. It is a single contested magnetic-stripe inference on crust buried under ~15 km of sediment, the mainstream teaching answer remains ~180 Ma, and on the log track 340 sits at 0.631 versus 0.536 for 180 -- a 0.095 gap that lands inside any reasonable tolerance band. The reveal also explicitly anchors the western Pacific, keeping the question internally consistent. Not a drop, and not worth a prompt rewrite.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Continental rock is more than twenty times older. Subduction keeps swallowing the seafloor, and the oldest surviving patch lies in the western Pacific, right beside the trenches consuming it.

verdicts.prompt: What percentage of the world's land area is covered by forest?
verdicts.note: DEDUPE FLAG ADJUDICATED: genuine duplicate, not a template collision — the sibling geography candidate is the same sentence word for word, with the same answer (31%). There is nothing to distinguish them. Dropping the nature copy: land-cover share is a geography quantity, and nature already carries the tree-side facts (nature92 three trillion trees, nature94 Pando). I separately verified the figure so the surviving geography copy is safe: FAO FRA 2020 gives 4.06 billion ha of forest = 31% of total land area, with 54% of it in Russia, Brazil, Canada, the USA and China, and 93% naturally regenerating (the reveal's 'about 90%' is slightly low but not wrong).

verdicts.prompt: All life on Earth adds up to how many gigatonnes of carbon?
verdicts.note: Bar-On, Phillips & Milo, PNAS 115(25):6506-6511 (2018): ~550 Gt C total, plants ~450 Gt C (82%, matching the reveal exactly) and animals ~2 Gt C. Checked the reveal's 'bacteria most of the remainder': the paper's remaining ~100 Gt C is bacteria ~70, fungi ~12, archaea ~7, protists ~4, animals ~2 — so bacteria are indeed the majority of what is left, and 2/550 is 0.36%, under half a percent as claimed. Position log 200..200000 = 0.146, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: How many million tonnes of Saharan dust settle on the Amazon basin each year?
verdicts.note: NASA Goddard / CALIPSO 2007-2013 analysis: 27.7 million tonnes reaching the Amazon annually, carrying ~22,000 tonnes of phosphorus — close to what the basin loses to runoff — with the Bodélé Depression in Chad as the dominant source. Every element of the reveal is from the NASA release. One correction to the reasoning line rather than the content: total dust leaving the Sahara is 182 Mt/yr, not 'near 200', making the Amazon share 15% rather than 'a tenth or so' — the reasoning is a hint, not player-facing, and the answer is unaffected. Position log 0.05..500 = 0.687, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: The world's marine fishing fleets land how many million tonnes of catch a year?
verdicts.note: FAO, The State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture 2024: 2022 capture production was 92.3 Mt total, of which 81 Mt marine and 11.3 Mt inland — so the answer matches the marine figure the prompt asks for, and the prompt correctly says 'marine' rather than conflating the two. Reveal verified: SOFIA 2024's headline finding is that aquaculture overtook capture fisheries for the first time in 2022, and marine capture has been flat since the late 1980s. Position log 20..3000 = 0.279, matches, in band.

verdicts.prompt: The Amazon's drainage basin covers how many million km²?
verdicts.note: ~7,050,000 km² is the standard basin area and is stable across sources. Checked the reveal's moisture-recycling claim: five to six recycling passes across the basin is the accepted figure from the flying-rivers literature (van der Ent and colleagues), consistent with candidate 23's residence-time work. Checked for collision with geography9 (Amazon length, 6,400 km) and nature90 (Amazon discharge, 209,000 m³/s) in puzzles.js — different quantities, no dedupe problem. FLAG FOR THE AUTHOR: the claimed position 0.671 is wrong; I compute log(7/3)/log(100/3) = 0.242. Still in band, so no range change, but this is the third position miscalculation in the batch (see 21 and 36).

questions.prompt: Ceres, the largest object in the asteroid belt, is how many km across?
questions.reveal: Ceres holds about a third of the entire asteroid belt's mass, and Dawn found bright salt deposits where briny water had seeped up through the crust and evaporated.
questions.reasoningPath: The Moon is 3,475 km across and Pluto 2,377 km. Ceres is a dwarf planet too, but the smallest one, and the whole asteroid belt together weighs far less than the Moon. So a fraction of Pluto: roughly a thousand km.

questions.prompt: Valles Marineris, the great canyon on Mars, runs how many km end to end?
questions.reveal: It was not carved by a river. It is a tectonic split in the crust, torn open as the neighbouring Tharsis volcanic bulge swelled.
questions.reasoningPath: Mars is about half Earth's diameter, so its circumference is near 21,000 km. Photographs show the canyon spanning roughly a fifth of the visible disc, which puts it in the thousands of km, far beyond the Grand Canyon's 450 km.

questions.prompt: Air pressure at the surface of Mars is what percentage of Earth's at sea level?
questions.source: NASA Mars fact sheet (610 Pa vs 101,325 Pa)
questions.reveal: That is below the triple point of water, so liquid water on the surface boils away rather than evaporating. It is why Mars has ice and vapour but no lakes.
questions.reasoningPath: Mars keeps a thin skin of CO2: enough for dust storms and parachutes, but nowhere near enough to breathe or to hold pressure suits at bay. That rules out tens of percent. The sky is not vacuum-black either, so it is well above a thousandth. Somewhere under one percent.

questions.prompt: Phobos, Mars's inner moon, completes one orbit in how many hours?
questions.reveal: It laps Mars three times in a Martian day, so seen from the ground Phobos rises in the west and sets in the east. It is also spiralling inward and will break apart in tens of millions of years.
questions.reasoningPath: Phobos circles only about 6,000 km above Mars, against our Moon's 384,000 km. Low orbits are fast: the ISS takes 90 minutes at 400 km above Earth, so a moon a few thousand km up around a smaller planet lands in single-digit hours.

questions.prompt: Sunlight takes 8 minutes to reach Earth. How many hours does it take to reach Neptune?
questions.source: computed from NASA planetary fact sheets
questions.reveal: That lag is why outer-system probes cannot be flown by joystick: every command sent to New Horizons or Voyager is already hours stale on arrival.
questions.reasoningPath: Neptune orbits about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth does. Thirty times 8.3 minutes is roughly 250 minutes, a little over four hours.

questions.prompt: Mars swings close to Earth on a repeating cycle. How many days pass between one close approach and the next?
questions.reveal: That rhythm sets every launch window: each rocket ever sent to Mars left inside one of these narrow gaps, which is why missions arrive in clusters.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth takes 1 year per lap of the Sun, Mars about 1.9. Earth gains roughly half a lap on Mars each year, so it needs a bit over two years to gain a whole lap and catch it again.

questions.prompt: Standing on the Moon, surface gravity pulls at how many m/s squared?
questions.reveal: Apollo crews found bunny-hopping easier than walking, and the suit and backpack that weighed 82 kg on Earth handled like 13 kg up there.
questions.reasoningPath: The Apollo footage shows astronauts falling slowly but definitely falling, bouncing rather than floating. Roughly a sixth of Earth's 9.8 puts it near 1.6.

questions.prompt: The asteroid that ended the dinosaurs is estimated at how many km across?
questions.source: Schulte et al., Science (2010) Chicxulub review
questions.reveal: The clue was iridium, rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids, found in a thin clay layer at the same depth on every continent.
questions.reasoningPath: The Chicxulub crater is around 180 km wide, and impact craters run roughly 10 to 20 times the size of the object that made them. That points to something in the low tens of km at most.

questions.prompt: How many grams of asteroid did OSIRIS-REx bring back from Bennu?
questions.reveal: The canister stayed sealed for three extra months because two of its 35 fasteners would not open with the tools permitted inside the airtight glovebox.
questions.reasoningPath: This was a touch-and-go scoop, not a mining run. Apollo's six crewed landings managed 382 kg with astronauts and shovels; a robotic tap on an asteroid brings home something you could hold in one hand.

questions.prompt: NASA's Opportunity rover drove how many km across Mars over its fourteen years?
questions.source: NASA/JPL Mars Exploration Rover mission summary
questions.reveal: It was designed for 1,000 metres and 90 days. Wind gusts kept scouring dust off its solar panels, and that accident is what bought it fourteen years.
questions.reasoningPath: Rovers crawl at a few centimetres per second and drive only part of each day, so a good day is tens of metres. Over roughly 5,000 days that totals tens of km, not hundreds.

questions.prompt: The Sun outweighs all eight planets put together by roughly what factor?
questions.source: computed from NASA planetary fact sheets
questions.reveal: Jupiter alone is about 70% of that planetary total, and the Sun's dominance is why the solar system's centre of mass barely strays outside the Sun's own surface.
questions.reasoningPath: The Sun is 333,000 Earth masses. Jupiter is 318 Earths and carries most of the planetary mass, with Saturn, Neptune and Uranus adding maybe 130 more. So 333,000 divided by something near 450.

questions.prompt: Earth's solid inner core is a ball how many km across?
questions.reveal: It is crystallising outward at roughly a millimetre a year, and the heat released as it freezes is what stirs the liquid outer core into a magnetic dynamo.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth is 12,750 km across and seismic maps put the whole core at about half that. The inner core is only the innermost part of the core, so think a fifth of Earth's diameter: about Pluto's size.

questions.prompt: Standing on the equator, how fast are you moving in km/h from Earth's spin alone?
questions.reveal: Launch sites hug the equator to pocket that speed for free, which is why Kourou in French Guiana and Sriharikota in India sit where they do.
questions.reasoningPath: The equator is 40,000 km around and one turn takes 24 hours. Divide and you get roughly 1,670 km/h, faster than an airliner.

questions.prompt: By how many degrees is Earth's axis tilted from the plane of its orbit?
questions.reveal: The tilt is what draws the tropics on a map: those two lines mark the furthest north and south the Sun can ever stand directly overhead.
questions.reasoningPath: The tilt gives us seasons but not extreme ones, and mid-latitudes never get Arctic-style permanent darkness. It is clearly not zero and nothing like the 98 degrees of Uranus, so a couple of tens of degrees.

questions.prompt: A sidereal day is how many seconds shorter than the 24-hour solar day?
questions.reveal: That gap is why a given star rises about four minutes earlier each night, and why the constellations return to the same place after exactly one year.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth has to turn one extra sliver each day to face the Sun again, and that sliver is 1/365th of a full turn. 86,400 seconds divided by 365 is about 236.

questions.prompt: Earth's axis wobbles like a spinning top. How many years does one full wobble take?
questions.reveal: Polaris has not always been the pole star. Five thousand years ago it was Thuban in Draco, and in twelve thousand years it will be Vega.
questions.reasoningPath: The zodiac signs have slipped by roughly one constellation, a twelfth of the circle, since they were named about 2,000 years ago. Twelve times 2,000 gives around 25,000 years for the whole loop.

questions.prompt: Standing on a beach with your eyes 1.7 m up, how many km away is the horizon?
questions.reveal: Climb a 30 m lighthouse and it stretches to about 20 km. Distance grows with the square root of height, which is what made the crow's nest worth the climb.
questions.reasoningPath: From the shore, a ship's hull disappears surprisingly soon: a few km, not tens. Earth's surface curves away about one metre over 3.5 km, so an eye height under two metres gives under five km.

questions.prompt: Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, lies how many light-years away?
questions.reveal: It is bright largely because it is near: Sirius puts out only about 25 times the Sun's light, while Rigel, a hundred times farther off, pumps out tens of thousands.
questions.reasoningPath: The nearest star of all, Proxima, is 4.2 light-years away. Sirius outshines everything else, and in astronomy that usually means close rather than colossal, so single digits to low teens.

questions.prompt: Crush the Sun into a black hole: its event horizon would have what radius, in km?
questions.reveal: Do the same to Earth and the radius is 9 mm, about a large marble. Neither can actually happen: both are far too light to collapse on their own.
questions.reasoningPath: A neutron star packs more than a solar mass into a sphere about 20 km across and sits just short of collapse. A black hole of the same mass must be smaller still, so single-digit km.

questions.prompt: How many stars across the whole sky are bright enough to see with the naked eye?
questions.source: Yale Bright Star Catalogue, magnitude 6.5 limit
questions.reveal: Only half the sky is above the horizon at once and haze eats into the rest, so even under perfect conditions you are seeing roughly 2,500 at a time.
questions.reasoningPath: Star charts label a few hundred stars, and even a dark sky never resolves into more than a few thousand distinct points before it turns to Milky Way haze. Catalogues to the eye's limit run to thousands, not millions.

questions.prompt: TRAPPIST-1, with its seven Earth-sized planets, sits how many light-years from us?
questions.reveal: All seven orbit closer to their star than Mercury does to the Sun, so the entire system would fit inside Mercury's orbit with room to spare.
questions.reasoningPath: It was found by a modest ground telescope watching a dim red dwarf that no one can see by eye, so it has to be a near neighbour: tens of light-years, well beyond Proxima's 4 but nothing like the galaxy's 100,000.

questions.prompt: The Andromeda Galaxy is falling toward the Milky Way at how many km/s?
questions.reveal: When the two discs meet, stars themselves will almost certainly never collide: the gaps between them are so vast that the galaxies will pass through each other like sparse mist.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth orbits the Sun at 30 km/s and the Sun circles the galaxy at about 230 km/s. Galaxies drifting toward each other move at the same sort of pace, so tens to low hundreds of km/s.

questions.prompt: How many watts of power does the Sun radiate in total?
questions.reveal: Earth intercepts less than half a billionth of it, and even that sliver is roughly 8,000 times all the power humanity uses.
questions.reasoningPath: Above the atmosphere, sunlight delivers 1,361 watts per square metre. Spread that over a sphere of radius 150 million km: the area is 4 pi r squared, about 2.8 x 10^23 square metres, and multiplying gives a few times 10^26.

questions.prompt: The Large Magellanic Cloud, visible by eye from southern skies, is how many light-years away?
questions.reveal: The last supernova bright enough to see without a telescope, SN 1987A, went off there. Its neutrinos reached Earth about three hours before its light did.
questions.reasoningPath: It is a satellite galaxy sitting outside the Milky Way's 100,000-light-year disc but far nearer than Andromeda at 2.5 million. That brackets it to the low hundreds of thousands.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the universe's ordinary matter, by mass, is helium?
questions.source: Big Bang nucleosynthesis, primordial helium fraction
questions.reveal: Almost all of it was forged in the first few minutes after the Big Bang. Thirteen billion years of stars have added only a couple of percent more.
questions.reasoningPath: Hydrogen dominates everything — the Sun alone is 73% hydrogen — and every element heavier than helium is a rounding error by mass. So helium takes almost all of what is left over: roughly a quarter.

questions.prompt: The solar wind streams past Earth at typically how many km/s?
questions.reveal: It takes two to four days to cross from the Sun, and that crossing time is the entire warning we get between spotting a flare and the geomagnetic storm arriving.
questions.reasoningPath: Solar material has to beat the Sun's surface escape velocity of 618 km/s but is nowhere near relativistic. Coronal ejections are reported as taking a few days to cover 150 million km, which works out to hundreds of km/s.

questions.prompt: The Parker Solar Probe set the record for the fastest human-made object: how many km/h?
questions.reveal: No engine did it. Seven Venus flybys bled off the probe's orbital energy so it could fall ever closer to the Sun and be slung around it.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth orbits at 30 km/s. A probe skimming the Sun's outer atmosphere, ten times closer in, must move several times faster at perihelion — call it 190 km/s. Multiply by 3,600 and you land near 700,000 km/h.

questions.prompt: Armstrong and Aldrin spent how many hours on the lunar surface before lifting off?
questions.reveal: Only about two and a half of those hours were spent outside. The rest was checks, a meal and a cold, cramped attempt at sleep on the cabin floor.
questions.reasoningPath: It was a one-shot demonstration with a single ascent engine and no backup, so nobody lingered. But they did try to sleep before leaving, so longer than a working day and well short of three days.

questions.prompt: The International Space Station masses how many tonnes?
questions.reveal: It was assembled across more than forty launches, because no rocket then flying could have lifted more than a fraction of it in one piece.
questions.reasoningPath: It spans roughly a football pitch but is mostly thin-walled modules and solar wings, not solid metal. A Shuttle could deliver about 16 tonnes per flight and it took dozens of flights, so hundreds of tonnes.

questions.prompt: How many metres across is the Hubble Space Telescope's main mirror?
questions.reveal: It was ground to the wrong curve by about a fiftieth of the width of a human hair, and astronauts had to fly up in 1993 to fit it with corrective optics.
questions.reasoningPath: It had to fit inside the Space Shuttle's payload bay, which is 4.6 m wide. Serious amateur mirrors reach half a metre; Hubble is much bigger but hard-capped by that bay, so a couple of metres.

questions.prompt: Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk in 1965. How many minutes was he outside?
questions.reveal: His suit ballooned in vacuum until he could not fit back through the airlock, and he had to bleed off its pressure to squeeze in — a decision he did not report to ground control until afterwards.
questions.reasoningPath: This was a first attempt from a cramped capsule with an inflatable fabric airlock and a tethered air supply. Long enough to count as a real demonstration, short enough to stay survivable: minutes, not hours.

questions.prompt: How many years did New Horizons take to fly from Earth to Pluto?
questions.reveal: It crossed the Moon's orbit nine hours after launch and passed Jupiter thirteen months in, then spent most of the remaining trip asleep in hibernation.
questions.reasoningPath: Pluto sits roughly 32 astronomical units out. The fastest launch ever managed about 16 km/s, a pace that covers one AU in a bit under a year, and a Jupiter gravity assist helps. So around a decade.

questions.prompt: Apollo 13's crew still hold the Apollo distance record: how many km from Earth at their farthest?
questions.reveal: The extra distance was forced on them. With the service module crippled they could not brake into lunar orbit, so they took the wide free-return loop behind the Moon instead.
questions.reasoningPath: The Moon averages 384,400 km away, and Apollo 13 swung around its far side rather than orbiting close in. So somewhat more than the Moon's distance, but nowhere near double it.

questions.prompt: How many missions did the Space Shuttle fly across the whole programme?
questions.reveal: Two were lost, Challenger and Columbia, a loss rate near one flight in 68 — nothing like the one-in-100,000 figure quoted when the vehicle was sold as a routine spaceplane.
questions.reasoningPath: The fleet flew from 1981 to 2011 with five orbiters, and in busy years managed roughly half a dozen launches, fewer after each accident grounding. Thirty years averaging four or five a year lands near 135.

questions.prompt: Carbon-14 has a half-life of how many years?
questions.reveal: Atmospheric nuclear testing in the 1950s nearly doubled the world's carbon-14, and the falling 'bomb pulse' since has been used to date wine fraud and even work out when individual human cells were born.
questions.reasoningPath: Radiocarbon dating works on archaeology out to roughly 50,000 years and no further, because after about ten half-lives too little is left to measure. Divide 50,000 by ten.

questions.prompt: Uranium-238 has a half-life of how many billion years?
questions.reveal: That near-match to Earth's own age means the planet still holds about half the uranium-238 it formed with, and the heat from its decay is a large part of what keeps the core molten.
questions.reasoningPath: Uranium is still common enough in the crust to mine after 4.54 billion years, so its half-life cannot be much shorter than that. But it does decay measurably in a laboratory, so it is not vastly longer either.

questions.prompt: Boiling one kg of water that is already at 100 °C into steam takes how many kilojoules?
questions.source: CRC Handbook, enthalpy of vaporisation at 100 °C
questions.reveal: That is over five times the energy needed to heat the same kilogram from freezing to boiling, which is why sweating cools so well and why steam scalds far worse than hot water.
questions.reasoningPath: Heating a kilogram of water from 0 to 100 °C takes about 420 kJ. Tearing the molecules apart entirely takes several times more than merely speeding them up, so a couple of thousand kJ.

questions.prompt: The Large Hadron Collider's ring measures how many km around?
questions.reveal: It reuses the tunnel dug in the 1980s for an earlier machine, LEP, and the whole ring is tilted 1.4 degrees so one side lies deeper beneath the Jura than the other.
questions.reasoningPath: It runs under the Swiss-French border near Geneva and passes beneath several villages, so it is a loop you could walk around in a few hours: tens of km, not hundreds.

questions.prompt: A skydiver falling flat, before the parachute opens, settles at what speed in km/h?
questions.reveal: Pull the arms and legs in and the same jumper passes 300 km/h. The speed is set by body area, which is why the spread-eagle pose is the standard one.
questions.reasoningPath: It is clearly faster than motorway driving and clearly slower than an airliner's 900 km/h. Free-fall footage and the fact that a jump from 4 km lasts under a minute both point to the low hundreds.

questions.prompt: What is the longest wavelength of light the human eye can see, in nanometres?
questions.reveal: Just past that edge sits the near-infrared a TV remote uses. A phone camera lacks the eye's filter, so point a remote at one and you can watch it blink.
questions.reasoningPath: Visible light spans roughly one octave of wavelength from violet to red, far below the millimetre scale but far above atomic sizes. Textbooks put the violet end near 400 nm, so the red end is a bit under double that.

questions.prompt: Yttrium barium copper oxide superconducts below what temperature, in kelvin?
questions.reveal: It mattered because it cleared 77 K, the boiling point of nitrogen. Cooling it needs only a flask of a liquid cheaper than milk, instead of scarce liquid helium.
questions.reasoningPath: It made headlines in 1987 as the first 'high-temperature' superconductor, but high-temperature still means cryogenic: far below room temperature, and the whole point of the fuss was clearing liquid nitrogen's 77 K.

questions.prompt: Pressure at the very centre of the Earth reaches how many gigapascals?
questions.reveal: Iron stays solid down there despite being hotter than the Sun's visible surface, because that squeeze pushes its melting point far above the 1,538 °C it has at sea level.
questions.reasoningPath: The deepest ocean trench manages only about 0.11 GPa. Diamond anvil cells in laboratories are built to reach a few hundred GPa specifically to mimic planetary cores, so hundreds of GPa.

questions.prompt: The Sun's core is compressed to what density, in kg per cubic metre?
questions.reveal: It still behaves as a gas rather than a solid: the temperature is so high that atoms are stripped bare of electrons and nothing can lock into a lattice.
questions.reasoningPath: The Sun averages 1,400 kg/m³, barely denser than water, but its mass is enormously concentrated inward. The core must beat any metal — osmium is 22,600 — so think several times that.

questions.prompt: Argon is the third most common gas in dry air. What percentage of it, by volume?
questions.reveal: Nearly all of it is argon-40, produced by potassium-40 decaying in the rocks and leaking out over billions of years. The atmosphere's noble gas is really radioactive exhaust.
questions.reasoningPath: Nitrogen takes 78% and oxygen 21%, which leaves about 1% for everything else combined. Argon is the bulk of that remainder, with carbon dioxide at 0.04% far behind it.

questions.prompt: The atmosphere presses down with the weight of how many tonnes on every square metre?
questions.reveal: It is also why a suction cup grips, and why no simple suction pump can lift water more than about ten metres: the air below is doing all the pushing.
questions.reasoningPath: Sea-level pressure is about 101,000 pascals, meaning 101,000 newtons on each square metre. Divide by gravity's 9.8 newtons per kilogram and you get roughly 10,300 kg.

questions.prompt: Oxygen is the commonest element in Earth's crust. What percentage of its mass?
questions.reveal: None of it is the air. It is locked into silicate minerals: quartz alone is two-thirds oxygen by atom count, and the crust is largely quartz and feldspar.
questions.reasoningPath: Rock is mostly silicates. In silicon dioxide the two oxygens weigh 32 against silicon's 28, so oxygen is already over half by mass there. Blend in heavier iron-bearing minerals and it settles a little under half.

questions.prompt: Going down a deep mine, temperature rises by how many degrees Celsius per km of depth?
questions.reveal: South Africa's deepest gold mines meet rock near 60 °C almost 4 km down, and are kept workable by sending hundreds of tonnes of ice underground every day.
questions.reasoningPath: Mines a few kilometres deep are famously hot but survivable with ventilation, meaning rock somewhere around 50 to 60 °C. Divide that rise by the few km of depth that produced it.

questions.prompt: Compress all the ozone above your head to sea-level pressure: how many mm thick is the layer?
questions.reveal: It is measured in Dobson units, each one a hundredth of a millimetre, and the Antarctic ozone hole is formally defined as anything below 220 of them.
questions.reasoningPath: Ozone is a trace gas at a few parts per million, spread through a column of air that would be about 8 km deep at sea-level density. A few millionths of 8,000 metres is a few millimetres.

questions.prompt: How many degrees does the Sun move across the sky in one hour?
questions.reveal: It is why time zones are drawn roughly 15 degrees of longitude wide, and why the hour lines on a sundial face are spaced by exactly that angle.
questions.reasoningPath: A full circle is 360 degrees and the Sun completes it in 24 hours. Divide one by the other.

questions.prompt: How many light-years from Earth is the centre of the Milky Way?
questions.reveal: Dust blocks the view completely in visible light. The black hole at the centre was only pinned down by tracking individual stars in infrared for nearly thirty years.
questions.reasoningPath: The galactic disc is about 100,000 light-years across, so the centre can be at most 50,000 away. The Sun sits in the outer half but nowhere near the rim, so roughly a quarter of the disc's width.

verdicts.prompt: Ceres, the largest object in the asteroid belt, is how many km across?
verdicts.note: Checked NASA Science Ceres facts: mean diameter 940 km (equatorial 964, polar 892) - answer confirmed. Position recomputed 0.613 on log 50..6000, matches. Dawn's bright Occator salt (sodium carbonate) deposits from evaporated brine confirmed. The reveal's 'about a third of the belt's mass' contradicts the cited source: NASA Science says 25%; Britannica says more than one-third; mass-budget arithmetic (9.4e20 kg of a ~2.4e21 kg belt) gives ~39%. Sources disagree well beyond 10% on that fraction, so I hedged it rather than assert a contested number. No collision in puzzles.js (Pluto, Ganymede and Moon diameters exist; Ceres does not).
verdicts.correctedReveal: Ceres holds somewhere between a quarter and a third of the entire asteroid belt's mass - estimates still differ - and Dawn found bright salt deposits where briny water had seeped up through the crust and evaporated.

verdicts.prompt: Valles Marineris, the great canyon on Mars, runs how many km end to end?
verdicts.note: Opened USGS Astrogeology 'Valles Marineris - The Grand Canyon of Mars' and NASA Science: 'more than 4,000 km long, up to 7 km deep', individual canyons ~200 km wide. Answer confirmed. Position 0.696 recomputed and matches. Reveal checked: USGS attributes it to crustal extension from the Tharsis bulge, not fluvial erosion - correct. puzzles.js has Olympus Mons height but no Valles Marineris; no dupe.

verdicts.prompt: Air pressure at the surface of Mars is what percentage of Earth's at sea level?
verdicts.note: Recomputed from the cited source values: 610 Pa / 101,325 Pa = 0.602%. Position 0.360 on log 0.05..50 confirmed. Reveal checked against the water triple point (611.657 Pa, 0.01 C): Mars mean surface pressure sits just below it, so surface liquid water is unstable - correct as stated (deep basins such as Hellas can exceed it, but 'surface' average holds). No pressure-of-Mars question exists in puzzles.js; nearest is Venus surface pressure in atmospheres, a different quantity.

verdicts.prompt: Phobos, Mars's inner moon, completes one orbit in how many hours?
verdicts.note: JPL Solar System Dynamics: Phobos period 0.31891 d = 7.65 h, semi-major axis 9,376 km (about 6,000 km above the surface) - answer confirmed. Position 0.291 recomputed. Reveal verified: 24.66 h sol / 7.65 h = 3.2 laps per sol, hence west-to-east rising; tidal decay gives breakup/impact in roughly 30-50 Myr, i.e. 'tens of millions of years'. No Phobos entry in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: Sunlight takes 8 minutes to reach Earth. How many hours does it take to reach Neptune?
verdicts.note: Agree with verifier 1's call, disagree with its correction. Arithmetic independently re-verified: NASA Neptune facts gives 30 AU and ~4 hours; exact 4,514.953e6 km / 299,792.458 km/s = 15,060 s = 4.183 h (cross-check 30.07 AU x 8.317 min = 4.168 h), so 4.2 h stands and log position on 0.3..30 is 0.5731, clear of MIN_MARGIN 0.08. The spoiler is genuine: puzzles.js:917 is space17, tagged 'anchor' -- 'How many minutes does sunlight take to travel from the Sun to Earth?', answer 8.3 -- and this prompt hands a player that answer outright, with space56 (line 4798, answer 30) supplying the other factor. Not a drop: the fact is distinct, sourced and estimable once the giveaway goes. But verifier 1's fix as literally stated is broken -- deleting the first sentence leaves 'How many hours does it take to reach Neptune?' with a dangling 'it' and no antecedent, so it needed a self-contained rewrite rather than a deletion. Checked the rewrite against the near-duplicate gate at tools/assemble.js:171-178, which fires only on >=0.45 token overlap AND identical unit AND answers within 10%: unit 'hour' vs space17's 'min' clears it on the unit test. Reveal verified and left unchanged -- no existing puzzle uses New Horizons or Voyager light-lag (only Pluto width at 4841, Voyager speed at 5314), and both probes are indeed hours of light-time out (New Horizons ~8 h, Voyager 1 ~23 h). Deliberately did not move the '8 minutes to Earth' fact into the reveal, which would relocate the same anchor spoiler rather than remove it. Answer, unit and range unchanged.
verdicts.correctedPrompt: How many hours does sunlight take to cross from the Sun to Neptune?

verdicts.prompt: Mars swings close to Earth on a repeating cycle. How many days pass between one close approach and the next?
verdicts.note: Checked the Mars synodic period: 779.9 days (NASA planetary fact sheet), consistent with 1/(1/1.0000 - 1/1.8808) years = 2.135 yr = 780 d. Answer and position 0.228 confirmed. Reveal checked: Mars launch windows do recur on this synodic cadence, which is why missions cluster - correct. puzzles.js has the lunar synodic month (full moon to full moon) but no planetary synodic period; not a dupe.

verdicts.prompt: Standing on the Moon, surface gravity pulls at how many m/s squared?
verdicts.note: NASA Moon fact sheet: 1.62 m/s2 confirmed; position 0.287 recomputed. Reveal checked: the A7L suit plus PLSS is documented at 180 lb (81.6 kg) on Earth and about 30 lb (13.6 kg) on the Moon, so '82 kg ... handled like 13 kg' holds; bunny-hopping is well documented in Apollo debriefs. Dupe check: puzzles.js already has Jupiter cloud-top gravity (24.8) and solar surface gravity (274), so this is the third of that template - but the Moon's 1/6 g is the canonical instance and confusion risk between the three bodies is negligible. Keep.

verdicts.prompt: The asteroid that ended the dinosaurs is estimated at how many km across?
verdicts.note: Checked Schulte et al. 2010 (Science) Chicxulub review: impactor ~10 km diameter, crater ~180 km - both confirmed, and the 10-20x crater-to-impactor scaling in the author's reasoning is standard. Position 0.624 recomputed. Reveal verified: the Alvarez iridium anomaly in the K-Pg boundary clay, found worldwide, is the founding evidence. No Chicxulub or impactor question in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: How many grams of asteroid did OSIRIS-REx bring back from Bennu?
verdicts.note: NASA/curation final tally confirmed: 121.6 g (over twice the 60 g requirement), announced Feb 2024. Answer 122 g and position 0.385 both check out. Reveal verified in detail: exactly two of the 35 TAGSAM fasteners resisted the glovebox-approved tools, the head stayed sealed from October 2023 until custom tools freed it on 10 January 2024 - about three months. Distinct from puzzles.js's Apollo Moon-rock total (382 kg).

verdicts.prompt: NASA's Opportunity rover drove how many km across Mars over its fourteen years?
verdicts.note: Answer confirmed: NASA/JPL final odometry 45.16 km when the mission was declared complete on 13 Feb 2019, after 14 years 138 days; position 0.613 recomputed. But the reveal's design distance is wrong: the MER design requirement was 600 metres (JPL: 'the mission driving distance of 600 meters, or about one mile'), not 1,000 metres. Dust-cleaning wind events are correctly credited for the extended life. Corrected the figure only.
verdicts.correctedReveal: It was designed to drive 600 metres and to last 90 days. Wind gusts kept scouring dust off its solar panels, and that accident is what bought it fourteen years.

verdicts.prompt: The Sun outweighs all eight planets put together by roughly what factor?
verdicts.correctedReveal: Take Jupiter away and the ratio jumps to about 2,600. Mass and motion are split opposite ways, though: the planets carry more than 98% of the solar system's angular momentum, nearly all of it in Jupiter's slow orbit.
verdicts.note: Answer and range confirmed independently: NASA fact-sheet masses sum to 2.667e27 kg (Jupiter 1898, Saturn 568, Neptune 102, Uranus 86.8, terrestrials 11.8, all e24 kg); 1.9885e30 / 2.667e27 = 745.5, so 750 is correct and sits at log position 0.392 in 50..50000. The first verifier's math is right, but it checked puzzles.js only for a duplicate question and missed a duplicate-fact collision in the reveal. space60 (line 4854, 'How many Earths to match Jupiter's mass') already reveals 'Jupiter outweighs every other planet combined two and a half times over, enough to tug the Sun around a balance point that lies just above the solar surface' - which is both halves of this candidate's reveal restated (71% of the total IS 2.5x the rest), and space59 (line 4842) uses the same 'balance point outside the surface' beat for Pluto/Charon. Shipping as-is airs that fact a third time. Also space18 (line 938) already reveals the 99.86% figure, which implies ~713, so this reveal should add new information rather than recycle. Secondary point: 'barely strays outside the Sun's own surface' is looser than the first verifier allowed - the barycentre is outside the solar radius ~62% of the time and reaches ~2.2 solar radii, a full solar radius clear of the surface. Corrected reveal drops both recycled beats; its numbers check out (1.9885e30 / 7.69e26 = 2,590 without Jupiter; the Sun holds only ~0.3-2% of system angular momentum, the classic angular-momentum problem). Prompt, answer, unit and range unchanged.

verdicts.prompt: Earth's solid inner core is a ball how many km across?
verdicts.note: PREM inner-core boundary radius 1,221.5 km gives a diameter of 2,443 km; answer 2,440 confirmed, position 0.611 recomputed. Reveal checked: inner-core growth rates in the literature are ~0.5-1 mm/yr, and latent heat plus light-element release from freezing is the accepted power source for the geodynamo - both claims stand. No Earth-interior structure question in puzzles.js apart from the separate central-pressure candidate in this batch.

verdicts.prompt: Standing on the equator, how fast are you moving in km/h from Earth's spin alone?
verdicts.note: Recomputed: 40,075 km equatorial circumference / 23.934 h sidereal = 1,674 km/h (/24 h = 1,670). Answer and position 0.262 confirmed. Reveal checked: Kourou (5.2 N) and Sriharikota (13.7 N) are indeed sited near the equator to harvest that eastward velocity. Related but distinct from puzzles.js's 'Distance all the way around Earth's equator' (40,075 km) - derivable in principle, but a different quantity and the reveal gives nothing away.

verdicts.prompt: By how many degrees is Earth's axis tilted from the plane of its orbit?
verdicts.note: NASA Earth fact sheet: obliquity 23.44 degrees; answer and position 0.390 on linear 0..60 confirmed. Reveal checked: the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn lie at exactly that latitude, being the subsolar limits - correct. Dupe check: puzzles.js has 'Uranus is tipped on its side: how many degrees is its axis tilted from its orbit?' (98). Same measurand, different planet, and Earth's 23.5 is famous enough that cross-contamination is implausible - adjudicated as template reuse, not duplication.

verdicts.prompt: A sidereal day is how many seconds shorter than the 24-hour solar day?
verdicts.note: Recomputed from IERS: sidereal day 86,164.0905 s, so the gap is 235.9 s - answer 236 confirmed, position 0.326 on linear 60..600 matches. Reveal checked: 236 s is 3.93 minutes, so 'a star rises about four minutes earlier each night' and the 365-fold accumulation returning constellations to the same place after a year are both exactly right. Nothing comparable in puzzles.js (the Martian sol-vs-day question asks a different thing).

verdicts.prompt: Earth's axis wobbles like a spinning top. How many years does one full wobble take?
verdicts.note: IAU general precession gives 25,772 years; 26,000 confirmed, position 0.632 on linear 2000..40000 recomputed. Reveal checked date by date: Thuban was the pole star around 2700 BC (roughly 4,700-5,000 years ago) and Vega takes the role around AD 13,700 (about 11,700 years hence) - both statements hold. No precession question in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: Standing on a beach with your eyes 1.7 m up, how many km away is the horizon?
verdicts.note: UPHOLD the first verifier's drop, but correcting its reasoning. Independently confirmed the maths: sqrt(2Rh) = sqrt(2 x 6,371,000 x 1.7) = 4.65 km, so 4.7 km is right; the reveal's 30 m lighthouse gives sqrt(2 x 6,371,000 x 30) = 19.55 km, so 'about 20 km' is right and uses the SAME geometric convention as the headline answer, making the item internally consistent. Square-root scaling correct. The item is factually sound - this is purely a dedupe casualty. CORRECTION TO FIRST VERIFIER: it asserted the 4.7 vs 5 km gap is 'only rounding of the same calculation'. That is wrong. 4.65 km is the geometric horizon; 5.03 km is the refraction-corrected horizon using the standard 7/6-effective-Earth-radius convention (3.86*sqrt(h) km). Two different legitimate conventions, not one number rounded twice. The drop still stands because that distinction is invisible in the prompt - neither wording signals whether refraction is in scope - so a player meets the identical setup and identical asked quantity returning 4.7 and 5.0 and reads it as the game contradicting itself. Genuine duplicate. SURVIVOR CHOICE ENDORSED, with an extra reason the barrier did not give: this copy is filed under category 'space', but a beach-horizon question is geography/physics about Earth's own curvature and is a poor fit for space. The geography sibling is the better home regardless of the numbers. Noted against this: the dropped copy is the more precisely posed of the two, pinning eye height at 1.7 m rather than the sibling's vaguer 'an adult's eyes'. CORPUS CHECK: grepped data/verified.json and puzzles.js - no existing horizon-distance question ships, so this collision is in-batch only, not against published content. FLAG FOR BATCH OWNER: the surviving geography copy's 5 km answer is only correct WITH refraction. If its reveal or reasoning path derives the figure from bare sqrt(2Rh) geometry, it is internally inconsistent by about 7% and needs its own check.

verdicts.prompt: Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, lies how many light-years away?
verdicts.note: Confirms the first verifier. Answer independently re-verified: Hipparcos parallax 378.9 mas, distance 8.60 +/- 0.04 ly (Wikipedia/Hipparcos); source attribution accurate. Position on 2..200 log = log(4.3)/log(100) = 0.317, clears the 8% edge margin and is off midpoint; log scale correct for a 2-decade span; prompt 75 chars with the unit asked. Reveal clause 1 correct (Sirius A = 24.74 +/- 0.70 Lsun). Reveal clause 2 correct (Rigel 848 +/- 65 ly = 98.6x Sirius's distance). Reveal clause 3 is genuinely wrong as the first verifier said: Wikipedia's Rigel A infobox gives 120,000 (+25,000/-21,000) Lsun, so 'tens of thousands' understates the headline figure a checking player would find. The first verifier supplied no replacement text, so I supply one here. I phrased it as an estimate rather than asserting 'more than 100,000' because the infobox lower error bar (99,000) dips just under that and low published estimates reach 61,500-83,000; hedging keeps it defensible under rule 2 while preserving the contrast. Dedupe attacked and rejected: puzzles.js:852 (space12) is Proxima Centauri, 4.24 ly, range 0.5..50, a different star with a different answer, and the candidate's use of Proxima as its reasoning anchor is exactly the 'anchor' tag's intended shape rather than a collision. No other stellar-distance question exists in the bank. No change to answer, range, or prompt.
verdicts.correctedReveal: It is bright largely because it is near: Sirius puts out only about 25 times the Sun's light, while Rigel, a hundred times farther off, is estimated at around 100,000 times.

verdicts.prompt: Crush the Sun into a black hole: its event horizon would have what radius, in km?
verdicts.note: Recomputed the Schwarzschild radius myself: 2GM/c^2 = 2 x 6.674e-11 x 1.989e30 / (2.998e8)^2 = 2,953 m = 2.95 km, so 3 km is right; position 0.369 confirmed. Reveal checked by the same formula for Earth: 2 x 6.674e-11 x 5.972e24 / c^2 = 8.87 mm, i.e. 'about a large marble' - correct, and the caveat that neither body can collapse unaided is right (below the ~3 solar-mass TOV limit). Distinct from puzzles.js's neutron-star-diameter question.

verdicts.prompt: How many stars across the whole sky are bright enough to see with the naked eye?
verdicts.note: Verified against the Yale Bright Star Catalogue itself: 9,110 entries to magnitude 6.5, of which 9,095-9,096 are stars. Answer 9,100 confirmed, position 0.420 recomputed. Reveal checked: halving for the visible hemisphere gives 4,548, and Sky & Telescope's standard treatment cuts that to roughly 2,000-2,500 once horizon extinction is allowed for - 'roughly 2,500' is sound. No star-count question in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: TRAPPIST-1, with its seven Earth-sized planets, sits how many light-years from us?
verdicts.note: NASA Exoplanet Archive / NASA Science give 40-41 ly (12.47 pc = 40.7 ly); answer 41 confirmed within a couple of percent, position 0.457 recomputed. Reveal checked against the archive's orbital table: the outermost planet h orbits at 0.0619 AU, well inside Mercury's 0.387 AU, so 'the entire system would fit inside Mercury's orbit with room to spare' is correct. No exoplanet question exists in puzzles.js at all.

verdicts.prompt: The Andromeda Galaxy is falling toward the Milky Way at how many km/s?
verdicts.note: Second-pass check: the first verifier was right on both counts. ANSWER CONFIRMED independently - NASA's 2012 Hubble release (van der Marel) says Andromeda is 'hurtling toward the Milky Way at nearly 250,000 miles an hour', which is 111.8 km/s, and Wikipedia's Andromeda-Milky Way collision article gives 'about 110 km/s (68.4 mi/s)'. The frame is the one the prompt asks for: 'falling toward the Milky Way' is the galactocentric approach speed, not the -300 km/s heliocentric radial velocity, and every popular source phrases the 110 figure exactly that way. Mild residual trap - an astronomy-literate player might answer the raw heliocentric 300, which sits inside the 5..500 range - but the prompt wording is the standard one and I judged a rewrite as drift rather than repair, so the prompt is unchanged. Position 0.671 on log 5..500, confirmed by recomputation. REVEAL FIX UPHELD: Sawala et al., Nature Astronomy 2025, 'No certainty of a Milky Way-Andromeda collision' - 100,000 simulations, 22 variables, Gaia + Hubble data with the LMC included for the first time - puts the merger at roughly 50/50 within 10 Gyr and only ~2% in the classic 4-5 Gyr window. I searched for any 2026 follow-up reinstating certainty and found none; NASA and ESA/Hubble both still carry the 'casts doubt' release. So 'When the two discs meet' was a flat assertion of a now-uncertain event and had to go, while the stars-never-collide physics is solid (~160 billion km mean stellar separation; Wikipedia: 'extremely unlikely that any two stars from the merging galaxies would collide'). I kept the first verifier's hedge and polished it: house em-dash style, and credit to Gaia AND Hubble rather than Gaia alone, since the 2025 result rests on both plus the LMC term. DEDUPE CHECKED AND CLEAR: puzzles.js space84 is the Andromeda distance question, and its shipped reveal is already the corrected angular-size text, so the old 'falling towards us at about 110 km/s' line that would have leaked this answer is no longer in the pool. No other approach-speed question among the 596 prompts.
verdicts.correctedReveal: If the two discs do meet — Gaia and Hubble data have made that collision look far less certain than it once did — the stars themselves will almost certainly never touch: the gaps between them are so vast that the galaxies would pass through each other like sparse mist.

verdicts.prompt: How many watts of power does the Sun radiate in total?
verdicts.note: IAU nominal solar luminosity 3.828e26 W confirmed, and I redid the derivation: 4 x pi x (1.496e11)^2 = 2.81e23 m2 x 1361 W/m2 = 3.83e26 W. Position 0.698 on log 1e21..1e29 recomputed. Reveal checked arithmetically: Earth's cross-section 1.275e14 m2 x 1361 = 1.74e17 W, which is 4.5e-10 of the total ('less than half a billionth') and about 8,700x humanity's ~20 TW - both figures stand. Dupe considered: puzzles.js has the 1361 W/m2 solar constant, from which this is derivable, but it is a different quantity and neither reveal leaks the other's answer. Keep.

verdicts.prompt: The Large Magellanic Cloud, visible by eye from southern skies, is how many light-years away?
verdicts.note: Pietrzynski et al. 2013 (Nature) confirmed: 49.97 kpc, 2.2% accuracy = 163,000 ly; the 2019 refinement (49.59 kpc = 161,700 ly) agrees to 1%. Answer and position 0.606 confirmed. Reveal checked: SN 1987A occurred in the LMC, remains the last naked-eye supernova (peak mag +3), and its neutrino burst preceded the optical detection by about three hours - all correct. Nothing on the Magellanic Clouds in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: What percentage of the universe's ordinary matter, by mass, is helium?
verdicts.note: Checked BBN literature: Standard-Model primordial helium mass fraction Yp = 0.2467 predicted, 0.2449 +/- 0.0040 observed - so 24% is right, and the sources agree to well inside 10%. Position 0.400 on linear 0..60 recomputed. Reveal checked: the present-day solar helium fraction (~0.27) versus primordial 0.245 is exactly the 'couple of percent' that 13 Gyr of stars have added. Distinct from puzzles.js's 'What percentage of the Sun's mass is hydrogen?'

verdicts.prompt: The solar wind streams past Earth at typically how many km/s?
verdicts.note: Answer independently confirmed: NOAA SWPC gives slow solar wind ~400 km/s in the equatorial plane where Earth orbits, fast wind 500-800 km/s from coronal holes; 400 is the right 'typical' figure. Range 30..3000 log puts it at position 0.5625, mid-scale, with the common wrong guesses (fast wind 800, escape velocity 618) nearby - range is fine, keep it. On the first verifier: it was right to call fix, but its stated reason is shaky. 'Two to four days' is standard NASA/NOAA phrasing for the wind itself (800 km/s = 2.2 d, 400 km/s = 4.3 d), so it is not fabricated and not really a self-contradiction. The genuine defect is the second clause: a flare's light arrives in 8.3 minutes, and the geomagnetic storm is driven by a CME, so the ambient wind's crossing time is not the flare-to-storm warning window - three unrelated things chained together. The first verifier's replacement also overshoots: 'only a day or two of warning' sits at the extreme fast tail. NOAA's canonical CME figure is one to three days (fastest ever 15-18 hours, several sources give 3-5 days as typical). My corrected reveal keeps the wind arithmetic checkable against the stated 400 km/s (1.496e8/400 = 4.3 days) and uses NOAA's one-to-three-day CME window.
verdicts.correctedReveal: At 400 km/s the wind needs a bit over four days to cover the 150 million km to Earth. The blasts that actually drive geomagnetic storms - coronal mass ejections - plow through that wind far faster, usually landing one to three days after they launch, and that gap is the whole of the warning forecasters get.

verdicts.prompt: The Parker Solar Probe set the record for the fastest human-made object: how many km/h?
verdicts.note: Opened the Guinness record entry and NASA/JHUAPL releases: 192.22 km/s = 692,000 km/h at 11:53:48 UTC on 24 December 2024, at 6.1 million km from the Sun. Exact match; position 0.682 recomputed. Drift risk assessed and dismissed: perihelion distance is now fixed, so later passes repeat rather than beat this speed. Reveal checked: seven Venus gravity assists (the last on 6 Nov 2024) shrank the orbit, and no propulsion produced the speed - correct. Distinct from puzzles.js's Voyager 1 cruise speed (61,000 km/h).

verdicts.prompt: Armstrong and Aldrin spent how many hours on the lunar surface before lifting off?
verdicts.note: NASA Apollo 11 mission overview confirms 21 h 36 min on the surface and a single EVA of 2 h 31 min - both the answer (21.6 h) and the reveal's 'about two and a half hours' outside check out, as does the documented failed rest period on the cabin floor. Position 0.280 on linear 2..72 recomputed. puzzles.js has the Apollo 11 landing year and the Moon-rock total but nothing on surface duration.

verdicts.prompt: The International Space Station masses how many tonnes?
verdicts.note: NASA reference pages give 'over 400,000 kg', with the standard assembly-complete figure 419,725 kg; 420 t confirmed, position 0.441 recomputed. Noted that the instantaneous mass swings with visiting vehicles, but the canonical quoted value is stable, so no drift call. Reveal checked: ISS assembly took roughly 42 flights (37 Shuttle plus Russian launches), so 'more than forty launches' holds, as does the Shuttle's ~16 t station-delivery payload. puzzles.js has ISS orbital speed only.

verdicts.prompt: How many metres across is the Hubble Space Telescope's main mirror?
verdicts.note: Agree with the first verifier on both call and remedy, re-derived independently rather than assumed. Collision confirmed in the file: puzzles.js line 5302 (key space98) is 'How many metres across is the James Webb Space Telescope's main mirror?' (6.5 m, linear 1..16, same Space & Physics category). A grep for 'metres across' returns that single line, so the candidate would be the second use of an identical six-word opening differing by one proper noun. Facts all re-verified, so this is not an over-eager fix: NASA gives Hubble's primary at 2.4 m (7.8 ft, ~4.5 m2 collecting area); the reveal's spherical aberration was 2.2 micrometres, standardly described as about a fiftieth of a human hair's width (null corrector lens 1.3 mm out of place), and COSTAR plus WFPC2 flew on Servicing Mission 1 in December 1993 - reveal is sound, no correctedReveal required. Range recomputed: (2.4-1)/(8-1) = 0.200 on linear 1..8, inside the 0.10-0.90 band; the reasoning path's 4.6 m Shuttle payload bay is a real hard cap above the answer. I differ from the first verifier only in the wording of the fix: it pinned the telescope with the Shuttle-bay hint, which hands the player the reasoning path's own ladder, so I anchored the 1990 launch instead - it separates Hubble from Webb (2021) just as firmly without doing the estimating - and changed the opening, 'main' to 'primary' and 'across' to 'wide' so the two entries read as visibly different questions. Answer, range, source and reveal unchanged.
verdicts.correctedPrompt: The Hubble Space Telescope went up in 1990 - how many metres wide is its primary mirror?
verdicts.correctedReveal: It was ground to the wrong curve by about a fiftieth of the width of a human hair, and astronauts had to fly up in 1993 to fit it with corrective optics.

verdicts.prompt: Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk in 1965. How many minutes was he outside?
verdicts.note: Voskhod 2 records confirm 12 min 9 s outside the airlock on 18 March 1965 (total EVA including airlock cycling about 23 min); the prompt asks for time outside, so 12 is the right reading. Position 0.314 recomputed. Reveal checked: the suit's stiffening in vacuum, the depressurisation to re-enter the Volga airlock, and Leonov's decision not to tell ground control at the time are all documented. Distinct from puzzles.js's Gagarin flight-duration question.

verdicts.prompt: How many years did New Horizons take to fly from Earth to Pluto?
verdicts.note: Recomputed from mission dates: launch 19 Jan 2006, Pluto closest approach 14 July 2015 = 9.48 years. Answer and position 0.268 on linear 2..30 confirmed. Reveal checked: the spacecraft crossed the Moon's orbit about nine hours after launch and made its Jupiter gravity assist on 28 Feb 2007, thirteen months in, then hibernated for most of the cruise - all correct. puzzles.js mentions New Horizons only as a source string for a different question.

verdicts.prompt: Apollo 13's crew still hold the Apollo distance record: how many km from Earth at their farthest?
verdicts.note: NASA Apollo 13 mission report and the Guinness altitude record both give 400,171 km on 15 April 1970; position 0.334 on linear 200000..800000 recomputed. Reveal checked: with the SM crippled the crew flew the free-return circumlunar trajectory instead of entering lunar orbit, and the Moon being near apogee is what pushed the figure past its 384,400 km mean distance. The reveal does not state the Moon's distance, so it does not spoil the existing lunar-distance question in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: How many missions did the Space Shuttle fly across the whole programme?
verdicts.note: NASA programme record: 135 flights, STS-1 (April 1981) to STS-135 (July 2011); position 0.593 recomputed. Reveal checked arithmetically: 2 losses in 135 flights is 1 in 67.5, so 'near one flight in 68' is right, and the 1-in-100,000 figure is the management estimate Feynman contrasted with engineers' 1-in-100 in the Rogers Commission appendix - correctly characterised. No Shuttle flight-count question in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: Carbon-14 has a half-life of how many years?
verdicts.note: Cambridge half-life 5,730 +/- 40 yr confirmed as the radiocarbon standard (the Libby value 5,568 yr is still used for reporting conventional ages, but the physical half-life is 5,730). Position 0.407 recomputed. Reveal checked: the 1950s bomb pulse nearly doubled atmospheric 14C, and its decline has been used for wine-fraud detection and Frisen's cell birth-dating work - both real. Nothing on isotopes in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: Uranium-238 has a half-life of how many billion years?
verdicts.note: Second-pass verification confirms the first verifier on every point. Half-life: Wikipedia/IUPAC nuclide data now give 4.463e9 yr (older evaluations 4.468e9); either way 4.5 billion years is the right rounded answer and the range 0.01-50 log is comfortable. Position recomputed independently: (log10(4.5)+2)/log10(5000) = 2.6532/3.69897 = 0.717, matching. 'About half remains' checks out: 2^(-4.54/4.463) = 0.494. The original reveal's final clause is genuinely wrong, so the fix is not over-eager: uranium is a refractory lithophile element and the bulk-silicate-Earth model puts U and Th in crust and mantle, not the iron core; the outer core is molten from primordial accretional heat plus latent and gravitational energy of inner-core freezing, not U-238 decay. I re-verified the replacement number rather than assuming it: total radiogenic heat is about 20 TW (~8 TW U, ~8 TW Th, ~4 TW K), and 238U alone is cited as ~40% of Earth's radioactive heat, so ~8 TW is right; the crust/mantle placement matches the reference Earth model (crust 7.3 +/- 1.2 TW, mantle ~13 TW). 'A large part of what keeps the interior churning' is a fair popular framing of radiogenic heat's role in mantle convection. Dedupe: grepped puzzles.js and data/verified.json - the only other half-life question is caffeine (log 0.5-24 h, different quantity), and uranium otherwise appears only in an oganesson reveal and two Manhattan Project reveals. No duplicate, no ambiguity, no portability issue. Endorsing the first verifier's corrected reveal verbatim since it is accurate as written.
verdicts.correctedReveal: That near-match to Earth's own age means the planet still holds about half the uranium-238 it formed with, and the eight or so terawatts released by its decay in the crust and mantle are a large part of what keeps the interior churning.

verdicts.prompt: Boiling one kg of water that is already at 100 °C into steam takes how many kilojoules?
verdicts.note: CRC value for the enthalpy of vaporisation at 100 C is 2,257 kJ/kg; answer 2,260 confirmed, position 0.588 recomputed. Reveal checked by calculation: sensible heat 0-100 C is 4.186 x 100 = 419 kJ/kg, and 2,257/419 = 5.4, so 'over five times' is exact. Checked against puzzles.js's 'Heating a litre of water from 20 C to boiling takes how many kilojoules?' - different quantity (335 kJ), and the reveal's 'freezing to boiling' comparison does not hand over that answer.

verdicts.prompt: The Large Hadron Collider's ring measures how many km around?
verdicts.note: Agree with verifier 1's diagnosis and its correction, and found a second issue it missed. (1) Answer: circumference 26,659 m confirmed (CERN / LHC Design Report), so 27 km is right; position on log 1..300 recomputes to 0.578. (2) Tilt: verifier 1 is correct that the original reveal swapped units. Sources give a 1.4 PER CENT slope (14 mrad) for the LEP/LHC tunnel, chosen to maximise the run through molasse and minimise the length under Jura limestone; arctan(0.014) = 0.80 degrees, so '1.4 degrees' is wrong by ~75%. Direction also independently confirmed: about 50 m deep on the Lake Geneva side, about 175 m under the Jura. LEP tunnel excavation 1983-88, so 'dug in the 1980s' holds. I tightened verifier 1's wording to carry the two depths, which are the concrete part of the fact and are what make the slope legible. (3) ANSWER LEAK verifier 1 did not check: an already-shipped question gives this answer away verbatim. puzzles.js history65 / data/verified.json ('CERN announced the discovery of the Higgs boson in what year?') has the reveal 'Confirming it took a 27 km ring and roughly 6,000 physicists.' Any player who has seen the Higgs reveal is handed 27 outright. This is not a duplicate prompt - the two ask different quantities in different categories - so I would not drop a clean question over it; the cheap fix is on the OTHER entry: change history65's reveal to something like 'a ring tens of km around and roughly 6,000 physicists' before shipping this one. If the maintainer would rather not touch a published reveal, drop this candidate instead. (4) Reasoning path is fine; '27 km walked in a few hours' is ~5-6 hours at normal pace, loose but it does the bounding job of tens-not-hundreds.
verdicts.correctedReveal: It reuses the tunnel dug in the 1980s for an earlier machine, LEP, and the whole ring lies on a 1.4 per cent slope - about 50 m down on the Lake Geneva side, 175 m down under the Jura - which kept the boring in soft molasse instead of limestone.

verdicts.prompt: A skydiver falling flat, before the parachute opens, settles at what speed in km/h?
verdicts.note: Belly-to-earth terminal velocity is consistently documented at about 120 mph / 195-200 km/h across skydiving and physics sources - agreement well inside 10%. Position 0.429 on linear 50..400 recomputed. Reveal checked: head-down freefly speeds of 300+ km/h are standard, and the drag-area explanation is correct. No skydiving or terminal-velocity question in puzzles.js. Unit check: metric throughout, no imperial or US dependency.
