verdicts.prompt: What is the longest wavelength of light the human eye can see, in nanometres?
verdicts.note: Tried to disprove this one on ambiguity grounds: the red limit is quoted as 700 nm in most textbooks, 750 nm in some, and CIE's tabulated range runs to 780 nm (830 for tail-end data), a spread of about 11%. It survives because the conventional answer is 700, and on the log 100..2000 track the whole 700-780 spread moves the position by under 0.03, so nobody is scored wrongly for picking any accepted value. Position 0.650 recomputed. Reveal checked: near-IR remotes at 850-950 nm sit just past the limit and are visible through a phone camera lacking an IR-cut filter - correct.

verdicts.prompt: Yttrium barium copper oxide superconducts below what temperature, in kelvin?
verdicts.note: Wu et al. 1987 report Tc = 92 K for YBa2Cu3O7 (commonly rounded to 93 K); answer confirmed, position 0.307 on linear 0..300 recomputed. Reveal checked: nitrogen boils at 77 K, and clearing that threshold - not room temperature - is precisely why the 1987 result mattered. One flag worth recording: puzzles.js asks liquid nitrogen's boiling point in CELSIUS (-196), so this reveal states the same physical fact in kelvin. Not a direct giveaway (it needs a unit conversion) and the 77 K figure is load-bearing here, so I left it. Not US-centric; SI throughout.

verdicts.prompt: Pressure at the very centre of the Earth reaches how many gigapascals?
verdicts.note: PREM central pressure is 363.85 GPa; 360 confirmed, position 0.628 recomputed. Reveal checked: Challenger Deep pressure is about 1,086 bar = 0.109 GPa (the reveal's 0.11 GPa is right), diamond anvil cells do reach several hundred GPa specifically for core conditions, iron melts at 1,538 C at ambient pressure, and the inner core at roughly 5,400-6,000 K is comparable to or above the 5,772 K photosphere - the 'hotter than the Sun's visible surface' phrasing is the standard, defensible claim. No overlap in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: The Sun's core is compressed to what density, in kg per cubic metre?
verdicts.note: Tried to break this on source disagreement: NASA Marshall solar physics and standard solar models give ~150 g/cm3 = 150,000 kg/m3, while the NSSDCA Sun fact sheet cited by the author lists central density 1.622e5 kg/m3. That is a 7.5% spread - inside the 10% drop threshold - and on the log 3000..3e6 track the two differ by 0.01 in position, so no player is harmed. Answer kept at the canonical 150,000; position 0.566 recomputed. Reveal checked: at ~15 MK the core is fully ionised plasma, denser than any solid yet gaseous in behaviour - correct, and the osmium comparison (22,590 kg/m3) matches puzzles.js's own osmium question without giving it away.

verdicts.prompt: Argon is the third most common gas in dry air. What percentage of it, by volume?
verdicts.note: Standard dry-air composition confirmed: N2 78.08%, O2 20.95%, Ar 0.934%, CO2 0.04%. Answer and position 0.310 on linear 0..3 recomputed. Reveal checked: atmospheric argon is about 99.6% argon-40, produced by 40K electron capture in crustal rocks and outgassed over geological time - correct. puzzles.js asks the nitrogen percentage; this asks a different constituent and the prompt does not leak nitrogen's share.

verdicts.prompt: The atmosphere presses down with the weight of how many tonnes on every square metre?
verdicts.note: Recomputed: 101,325 Pa / 9.80665 m/s2 = 10,332 kg = 10.33 t per square metre. Answer and position 0.409 confirmed. Reveal checked: the suction-pump limit follows from the same number, 101,325/(1000 x 9.807) = 10.33 m of water - the historically famous Torricelli/Galileo result, correctly stated. Nothing equivalent in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: Oxygen is the commonest element in Earth's crust. What percentage of its mass?
verdicts.note: Crustal abundance sources cluster tightly at 46.1-47.0% oxygen by mass (silicon 27.7% second); 47% is at the top of that band but within 1 point, and position 0.411 on linear 10..100 recomputed. Reveal checked: SiO2 is 2/3 oxygen by atom count (and 53% by mass), and quartz plus feldspar dominate the crust - correct. Distinct from puzzles.js's 'What percentage of the human body's mass is oxygen?' - different reservoir, no answer leak between them.

verdicts.prompt: Going down a deep mine, temperature rises by how many degrees Celsius per km of depth?
verdicts.note: Concur with first verifier. Independently confirmed the physics is fine (Britannica and Wikipedia both give 25-30 C/km for average continental geothermal gradient; ~60 C rock near 4 km at Mponeng is accurate), so this is not a factual drop - it is a genuine duplicate. The nature sibling 'Going down a deep mine, the rock warms by how many degrees Celsius per kilometre?' shares the identical opening setup, the identical measurand, the identical unit and the identical answer 25; the 50% word-overlap score is purely an artifact of two synonym swaps ('temperature rises' -> 'the rock warms', 'km' -> 'kilometre'). A player who solves one has solved the other for free, so the same knowledge would be scored twice. Two extra reasons this is the copy that should go rather than the sibling: (1) category fit - this one is filed under space, but the Earth's internal heat gradient is plainly Earth science, so the nature sibling is the correct home; (2) this copy's reveal is quantitatively understated - it says 'hundreds of tonnes of ice underground every day', but Mponeng's ice plant produces roughly 5,000-6,000 t/day of ice and ice slurry (Chart/Howden case study, MechChem Africa), i.e. thousands not hundreds. Also verified neither version is already in the published bank (data/verified.json and puzzles.js contain no geothermal entry), so this is a same-batch sibling collision and dropping one copy loses no shipped content.

verdicts.prompt: Compress all the ozone above your head to sea-level pressure: how many mm thick is the layer?
verdicts.note: Verified directly against NASA Ozone Watch's Dobson-unit page: the global average column is about 300 DU, 'equivalent to a layer 3 millimetres thick' at standard temperature and pressure. Answer and position 0.596 recomputed. Reveal checked on the same page: 1 DU = 0.01 mm of pure ozone at 0 C and 1 atm, and NASA's ozone-hole threshold is 220 DU, chosen because no lower value was seen before 1979 - both exact. No atmospheric-column question in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: How many degrees does the Sun move across the sky in one hour?
verdicts.note: Pure geometry, recomputed: 360/24 = 15 degrees per hour; position 0.250 on linear 0..60 confirmed. Reveal checked: nominal time zones are 15 degrees of longitude wide for exactly this reason, and sundial hour lines on an equatorial dial are spaced 15 degrees apart - both correct. Checked against puzzles.js's 'How many degrees wide does the full Moon appear in the sky?' (0.5) - different quantity, no confusion. Simple, but genuinely estimable rather than trivia-recall, so it earns its place.

verdicts.prompt: How many light-years from Earth is the centre of the Milky Way?
verdicts.note: GRAVITY Collaboration 2019 gives R0 = 8.178 +/- 0.035 kpc, which is 26,670 ly - the rounded 26,000 is within 3%, and independent determinations (Gaia, maser parallaxes) agree to a few percent, so no source-disagreement drop. Position 0.571 recomputed. Reveal checked: visual extinction toward the Galactic Centre is tens of magnitudes, and the Sgr A* mass came from tracking S-star orbits in the infrared over nearly three decades (Genzel and Ghez, Nobel 2020) - correct. Related to puzzles.js's Milky Way disc diameter (100,000 ly) and the Sun's galactic orbital period, but a distinct measurement and no reveal leakage.

questions.prompt: The Suez Canal opened to shipping in what year?
questions.reveal: Verdi was commissioned to write an opera for the occasion, but Aida ran two years late — the new Cairo opera house had to open with Rigoletto instead.
questions.reasoningPath: A cut of that size needed steam dredgers, so it postdates the industrial revolution; it also clearly predates Britain's 1882 occupation of Egypt, which was partly about controlling the canal. Mid-to-late 19th century.

questions.prompt: The world's first public steam railway, from Stockton to Darlington, opened in what year?
questions.reveal: Passengers on the line still rode in horse-drawn carriages sharing the same rails as the locomotives until 1833.
questions.reasoningPath: Watt's engines were turning factory machinery by the 1780s, but locomotives had to wait for high-pressure boilers around 1800. Britain's railway mania is a 1830s-40s story, so the first line sits just before it.

questions.prompt: The Lumière brothers held the first paying public film screening in what year?
questions.reveal: Thirty-three people bought tickets that night in a Paris basement. Within a year the brothers had operators filming in Bombay, Buenos Aires and Shanghai.
questions.reasoningPath: Photography was mature by the 1840s, but moving pictures needed flexible celluloid roll film, which Kodak began selling in 1889. Cinema had to follow within a few years, and it was plainly a going concern before 1900.

questions.prompt: Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary first stood on the summit of Everest in what year?
questions.reveal: The news was carried out by runner in a pre-agreed code — 'snow conditions bad' meant success — and reached London on the morning of Elizabeth II's coronation.
questions.reasoningPath: Bottled oxygen and lightweight alloy gear place it after the Second World War, and it was a British Commonwealth expedition, which places it before the empire wound down. Early 1950s.

questions.prompt: India became independent from British rule in what year?
questions.reveal: The border dividing India from Pakistan was drawn in about five weeks by a London barrister who had never set foot in India before.
questions.reasoningPath: It followed the Second World War, which left Britain broke, and it came before the wave of African independence in the late 1950s and 1960s. Late 1940s.

questions.prompt: Japan's Meiji Restoration, which ended rule by the shoguns, happened in what year?
questions.reveal: Within forty years the same state was building its own battleships and beat Russia at sea — feudal domain to industrial power inside two generations.
questions.reasoningPath: It was triggered by the American gunboats that forced Japan open in the 1850s, and Japan was already an industrial naval power by the Russo-Japanese War of 1905. It sits between the two, nearer the earlier end.

questions.prompt: In what year did the Bolsheviks seize power in Petrograd?
questions.reveal: It is called the October Revolution but fell in November on the Western calendar — Russia was still thirteen days behind, and only switched over three months later.
questions.reasoningPath: It happened while Russia was still fighting the First World War and led directly to Russia's exit from it, so it must fall between 1914 and 1918.

questions.prompt: Brazil, the last country in the Americas to do so, abolished slavery in what year?
questions.reveal: The monarchy that signed the law was overthrown by the army eighteen months later, its landowning support gone.
questions.reasoningPath: Britain outlawed the trade at the start of the century and the United States ended slavery in the 1860s. Brazil was the last holdout, so later than both — but still comfortably inside the 19th century.

questions.prompt: The first Nobel Prizes were awarded in what year?
questions.reveal: His relatives fought the will for years: Nobel had left nearly his whole fortune to a prize that did not yet exist, to be run by institutions he had never consulted.
questions.reasoningPath: Nobel's money came from dynamite, patented in the 1860s, and the prizes were set up by his will after his death. That lands the first ceremony near the turn of the 20th century.

questions.prompt: The International Committee of the Red Cross was founded in Geneva in what year?
questions.reveal: It grew out of one businessman's horror at the field of Solferino, where some 40,000 casualties were left largely untended after a single day's fighting.
questions.reasoningPath: It came out of a mid-century European battlefield and was long established before the First World War, the conflict it is most associated with. Second half of the 19th century.

questions.prompt: The world's first website went online in what year?
questions.reveal: It was a page at CERN explaining what the World Wide Web was and how to make your own — for a while, the entire web documented itself.
questions.reasoningPath: The internet itself is decades older, but the Web came out of CERN only a couple of years before the Mosaic browser made it famous in 1993. Early 1990s.

questions.prompt: The first telephone call from a handheld mobile phone was made in what year?
questions.reveal: The caller rang his opposite number at a rival lab to say he was speaking from a portable. The phone weighed over a kilogram and needed ten hours of charging for half an hour of talk.
questions.reasoningPath: Car phones existed from the 1940s; a handheld needed transistor circuits and a battery small enough to carry. That arrived well before mobile phones went on sale commercially in the early 1980s.

questions.prompt: The world's first cash machine was switched on outside a London bank in what year?
questions.reveal: There were no plastic cards yet: customers fed in a paper voucher impregnated with mildly radioactive carbon-14 that the machine could detect. The four-digit PIN was chosen because the inventor's wife could not remember six.
questions.reasoningPath: It needed machine-readable tokens and solid electromechanics, but no computers or networks — and it long predates card payments going mainstream in the 1980s. Somewhere in the 1960s.

questions.prompt: The first voyage of a purpose-loaded container ship sailed in what year?
questions.reveal: Loading loose cargo by hand cost about $5.86 a tonne at the time. Loading it in containers cost sixteen cents.
questions.reasoningPath: It needed cranes, standard steel boxes and lorries, so post-war — and container shipping was already dominant by the 1970s, when ports everywhere were rebuilt around it. Mid-1950s to early 1960s.

questions.prompt: The first scheduled passenger service flown by a jet airliner took off in what year?
questions.reveal: The aircraft was the de Havilland Comet, grounded two years later after metal fatigue starting at a window corner tore two of them apart in mid-air.
questions.reasoningPath: Jet engines were flying on fighters by 1944, and airliners tend to follow military technology by roughly a decade. That lands in the early 1950s, before the Boeing 707 era.

questions.prompt: The Gregorian calendar was introduced in what year?
questions.reveal: To wipe out the accumulated drift, ten days were simply deleted: in Catholic Europe the 4th of October was followed by the 15th.
questions.reasoningPath: It was a papal reform aimed at fixing the date of Easter, and Protestant countries refused it for generations — Britain only switched in 1752. So it belongs to the Counter-Reformation, late 1500s.

questions.prompt: The University of Bologna, the oldest in continuous operation, was founded in what year?
questions.reveal: It began as a guild of students who hired and fired their own professors — and fined them for starting late or failing to finish the syllabus.
questions.reasoningPath: European universities appear in the high middle ages, after the recovery of Roman law and Aristotle, with Paris and Oxford following in the 1100s. Bologna is the first, so late 11th century.

questions.prompt: Vasco da Gama reached India by sea, sailing around Africa, in what year?
questions.reveal: The gifts he offered the ruler of Calicut — cloth, hats, sugar, honey — were laughed at. Portuguese trade goods were worthless in the richest market in the world.
questions.reasoningPath: It belongs to the same burst of Iberian voyaging as Columbus, made possible by the caravel and decades of Portuguese creeping down the African coast. Within a few years either side of 1500.

questions.prompt: The last emperor of the Western Roman Empire was deposed in what year AD?
questions.reveal: Nobody at the time thought an empire had ended. The general who deposed him simply sent the imperial regalia east to Constantinople and ruled Italy as a king.
questions.reasoningPath: It comes well after the empire split and Christianity became official in the 300s, and the eastern half then ran on for roughly another thousand years until 1453. So the late 400s.

questions.prompt: Traditional founding date of the city of Rome: how many years BC?
questions.reveal: Romans counted their years from it — ab urbe condita — so the year we call AD 1 was, to them, the year 754.
questions.reasoningPath: The Roman Republic is conventionally dated to about 509 BC, and tradition puts seven kings before it at roughly a generation each. That pushes the founding a couple of centuries earlier again.

questions.prompt: China was first unified under a single emperor in what year BC?
questions.reveal: The new state standardised cart axle widths along with script, weights and coinage, so every wagon in the empire would fit the same ruts in the road.
questions.reasoningPath: This is the emperor the Terracotta Army was built to guard, and he is roughly contemporary with Rome's wars against Carthage. So a couple of centuries before the Christian era.

questions.prompt: Julius Caesar was assassinated in the Senate in what year BC?
questions.reveal: His adopted heir won the civil war that followed and became Augustus, so the killing meant to save the Republic is what finished it off.
questions.reasoningPath: Caesar's death is the hinge between Republic and Empire; Augustus is sole ruler by the 20s BC and Jesus is born a couple of decades after that. So the middle of the first century BC.

questions.prompt: How many years did it take to build the Taj Mahal complex?
questions.reveal: The emperor who built it as a tomb for his wife spent his last eight years imprisoned by his own son in a fort downriver, within sight of it.
questions.reasoningPath: It is hand-cut marble hauled hundreds of kilometres and inlaid with semi-precious stone — but it is one building with an emperor's treasury behind it, not a cathedral rebuilt over centuries. Pre-industrial projects like that ran a couple of decades.

questions.prompt: How many years did the Romans take to build the Colosseum?
questions.reveal: It was paid for with loot from the sack of Jerusalem and raised on the drained lake of Nero's private palace grounds — the emperor handing his own land back to the public.
questions.reasoningPath: Rome had concrete, cranes, standardised parts and effectively unlimited labour, and emperors wanted their monuments finished inside their own reigns. Far quicker than a medieval cathedral — under a decade.

questions.prompt: How many years of digging did the Channel Tunnel take?
questions.reveal: Eleven boring machines worked from both coasts. The British ones could not be reversed out, so they were steered downwards at the end and abandoned in the rock.
questions.reasoningPath: Modern boring machines chew through chalk at tens of metres a day, so 50 km of bores is a handful of years rather than decades — and the project ran from the late 1980s to a 1994 opening.

questions.prompt: How many years did Russia take to build the Trans-Siberian Railway?
questions.reveal: For years the line simply stopped at Lake Baikal, where whole trains were carried over on an icebreaking ferry — and one winter, on rails laid straight across the frozen lake.
questions.reasoningPath: It is over 9,000 km of track through permafrost, forest and mountains, laid largely by pick and shovel but with a whole state pushing it. Railways of that era advanced a few hundred km a year, so a couple of decades.

questions.prompt: From its formation to its dissolution, how many years did the Soviet Union exist?
questions.reveal: Its last act was a document signed in a hunting lodge in a Belarusian forest by the leaders of three republics — with the president of the union himself not present.
questions.reasoningPath: It was formally created a few years after the 1917 revolution and dissolved at the end of 1991. Subtract one from the other and the answer lands just under seventy.

questions.prompt: Longest verified reign of any sovereign monarch, held by Louis XIV of France: how many years?
questions.reveal: He was four when he inherited and outlived both his son and his grandson; the heir who finally followed him was his five-year-old great-grandson.
questions.reasoningPath: To beat every other monarch you must inherit as a small child and then live long. Elizabeth II managed seventy after acceding at 25, so the record has to be a little longer — set by someone crowned as an infant.

questions.prompt: The shortest war on record, between Britain and Zanzibar in 1896, lasted how many minutes?
questions.reveal: It ended when the sultan's palace was shelled from the harbour and his flag came down. The defeated side was afterwards billed for the cost of the shells.
questions.reasoningPath: This was a modern fleet bombarding a palace at point-blank range across a harbour. Not seconds — ships had to open fire and the palace had to burn — but nothing like a working morning.

questions.prompt: How many years did Nelson Mandela spend in prison?
questions.reveal: For the early years he was allowed one visitor and one letter every six months, and studied law by correspondence course from his cell.
questions.reasoningPath: He was jailed as apartheid was being consolidated in the early 1960s and released as it began to unwind, just after the Berlin Wall fell and a few years before the 1994 election. That gap is close to three decades.

questions.prompt: How many days did the Cuban Missile Crisis last?
questions.reveal: The quiet half of the bargain was that the United States also pulled its missiles out of Turkey — months later, and without announcing it.
questions.reasoningPath: It ran from the spy-plane photographs to the Soviet announcement of withdrawal: long enough to mount a naval blockade and exchange back-channel letters, but remembered as one continuous standoff, so under a month.

questions.prompt: How many years separate the first powered aeroplane flight from the first Moon landing?
questions.reveal: Orville Wright lived to see the sound barrier broken — he died three months after Chuck Yeager's flight.
questions.reasoningPath: Kitty Hawk sits at the very start of the 20th century, Apollo 11 at the end of the 1960s. Subtracting gives a bit less than a human lifetime.

questions.prompt: The balsa raft Kon-Tiki drifted from Peru to Polynesia in 1947 in how many days?
questions.reveal: The logs were cut green and floated down from the Andes. Had they been seasoned first, as shipwrights advised, they would have soaked up water and sunk.
questions.reasoningPath: It is roughly 7,000 km on ocean current plus a square sail, and a drifting raft makes perhaps 2-3 km/h. That is a few thousand hours — three or four months.

questions.prompt: Racing Jules Verne's fictional 80, Nellie Bly circled the world in 1889-90 in how many days?
questions.reveal: She stopped in France on the way to meet Verne himself — and then had her own record beaten within months by a rival travelling the other way.
questions.reasoningPath: The prompt names the target she set out to beat, and the whole point of the stunt was that steamships and railways had just got fast enough for her to manage it. So a little under eighty.

questions.prompt: Shackleton's open-boat run from Elephant Island to South Georgia covered how many km?
questions.reveal: The navigator got only four sun sights in sixteen days of cloud. Missing the island would have meant open Atlantic with no land ahead of them at all.
questions.reasoningPath: Both are sub-Antarctic islands in the Southern Ocean, about the span from Britain to the Mediterranean. A seven-metre boat under sail makes perhaps 80-100 km a day, and the crossing took over a fortnight.

questions.prompt: The first non-stop flight across the Atlantic, in 1919, took how many hours?
questions.reveal: They flew a converted bomber, landed nose-down in an Irish bog they had mistaken for a green field, and were knighted within the week.
questions.reasoningPath: It is about 3,000 km from Newfoundland to Ireland, and a 1919 bomber cruised at maybe 150-200 km/h with a following wind. Divide, and you get most of a day but nothing like two.

questions.prompt: Marco Polo was away from Venice for how many years on his journey to China and back?
questions.reveal: He dictated the book in a Genoese prison to a fellow captive who wrote chivalric romances for a living, which may explain some of its flourishes.
questions.reasoningPath: The overland trip took years in each direction, and he did not merely visit — he served the Mongol court for a long stretch in between. So decades, but still within one working life.

questions.prompt: The first long road trip by car, Mannheim to Pforzheim in 1888, covered how many km one way?
questions.reveal: The driver refuelled at a pharmacy, the only place selling the cleaning solvent the engine ran on, and used a hatpin to clear the fuel line and a garter to insulate a wire.
questions.reasoningPath: It was a day's drive between two German towns in a machine with one cylinder, well under one horsepower and no gears for hills. Far enough to prove the point, but not more than a couple of hundred kilometres.

questions.prompt: Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico in 1519 with how many Spanish soldiers?
questions.reveal: The army that finally took the Aztec capital two years later was overwhelmingly Tlaxcalan — tens of thousands of local troops who wanted Tenochtitlan brought down.
questions.reasoningPath: This was a private venture in eleven small ships provisioned across an ocean, not a royal army. Ships of that era carried perhaps fifty men each, so a few hundred rather than thousands.

questions.prompt: Francisco Pizarro met the Inca emperor at Cajamarca in 1532 with how many Spanish soldiers?
questions.source: John Hemming, The Conquest of the Incas
questions.reveal: Atahualpa's ransom filled a room with gold once and with silver twice over. He was executed anyway, after it had all been paid.
questions.reasoningPath: A splinter expedition, smaller than the one that took Mexico and thinned further by a long march down the coast. The entire point of the story is how few there were — well under a thousand.

questions.prompt: How many men crewed HMS Victory at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805?
questions.source: National Museum of the Royal Navy
questions.reveal: Around one in ten was not British: the muster lists men from Sweden, Italy, the Caribbean, India and the United States.
questions.reasoningPath: A 100-gun ship of the line carried three gun decks needing roughly a dozen men per heavy gun, plus topmen, marines, officers and boys, all inside 70 metres of hull. Hundreds, pushing towards a thousand.

questions.prompt: How many million soldiers did all sides together mobilise in the First World War?
questions.reveal: Roughly one in eight of them died, and more than twenty million came home wounded.
questions.reasoningPath: Europe held about 450 million people, and the major combatants conscripted whole male cohorts over four years — Russia, Germany, France, Austria-Hungary and Britain each raising millions. That totals in the tens of millions.

questions.prompt: How many billion members of our species have ever been born?
questions.reveal: The estimate assumes humans start around 190,000 BC and that birth rates ran near 80 per thousand for most of prehistory — enormous fertility offset by roughly half of all children dying young.
questions.reasoningPath: Humans numbered a few million for most of 200,000 years, then hundreds of millions for a few thousand more. Even with short lives that accumulates slowly, so the total is a modest multiple of today's eight billion, not a thousand times it.

questions.prompt: What was average life expectancy at birth worldwide in 1900, in years?
questions.reveal: The number is dragged down almost entirely by infants. Anyone who reached the age of five in 1900 could expect decades more, much as today.
questions.reasoningPath: Adults in 1900 were not dropping dead at thirty, but around a third of children died before their fifth birthday, and averaging in all those zeros roughly halves the figure. So somewhere in the thirties.

questions.prompt: How many million Africans were embarked on ships in the transatlantic slave trade?
questions.reveal: About 1.8 million did not survive the crossing. The figure is reconstructed from the records of some 36,000 individual voyages.
questions.reasoningPath: The trade ran for more than 350 years supplying Brazil, the Caribbean and North America, at tens of thousands of people a year on average and far more at its 18th-century peak. That compounds well into double-digit millions.

questions.prompt: How many km long was the Berlin Wall, all the way around West Berlin?
questions.reveal: Only about a quarter of it ran between the two halves of the city. The rest sealed West Berlin off from the East German countryside surrounding it.
questions.reasoningPath: It did not cut the city along a line — it enclosed West Berlin completely. A territory of a few hundred square kilometres has a perimeter of roughly a hundred-odd kilometres, like a circle 15 km across.

questions.prompt: How many metres long was the airship Hindenburg?
questions.reveal: It was designed to fly on helium, which the United States refused to export, so it burned hydrogen instead — with the passenger decks sealed deep inside the hull.
questions.reasoningPath: It carried fifty passengers in cabins, plus a dining room and a lounge, all inside the hull, and photographs show it dwarfing the mooring mast and buildings below. Far longer than a jumbo jet's 70 metres — closer to an ocean liner.

questions.prompt: At its peak the Mongol Empire covered how many million km², the largest contiguous empire ever?
questions.reveal: It was held together by a relay post system with stations every 40 km or so, letting a rider cross it faster than a letter could move across Europe.
questions.reasoningPath: It stretched from Korea to Hungary and from Siberia to Persia. Russia alone is 17 million km² and sits largely inside that footprint, so the total must be bigger again — but far below the 149 million of all land.

questions.prompt: Top speed of Stephenson's Rocket at the 1829 Rainhill Trials, in km/h?
questions.reveal: At the opening of the railway it was built for, a Member of Parliament stepped onto the track to greet the Duke of Wellington and was run down by Rocket — the first widely reported railway death.
questions.reasoningPath: To be worth building it had to beat a horse, and a galloping horse manages about 40 km/h in bursts. Early locomotives were faster than that, but nowhere near a modern train.

questions.prompt: How many metres did the Wright brothers' first powered flight cover, in 1903?
questions.source: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
questions.reveal: It lasted twelve seconds. By the fourth flight of that same morning they had managed nearly 260 metres — and then a gust flipped the machine and wrecked it.
questions.reasoningPath: The famous photograph shows the machine barely clear of the sand with a man running alongside it. Twelve seconds at something between a walk and a jog over the ground is tens of metres, not hundreds.

verdicts.prompt: The Suez Canal opened to shipping in what year?
verdicts.note: Agree with first verifier that the year is right and the reveal is wrong, but its correction is only half-fixed. Year: canal opened to shipping 17 Nov 1869 (History.com, MoneyWeek, napoleon.org) - correct; position (1869-1800)/100 = 0.6900 linear, in band. Original reveal is the standard Aida myth: Wikipedia Aida says Isma'il Pasha 'commissioned Verdi to write an opera to celebrate the opening of the Suez Canal, but Verdi declined', and secondary sources agree the actual ask was an inaugural HYMN for the canal, which Verdi refused on the grounds that he did not write ceremonial music. BUT the first verifier's correctedReveal keeps the second half of the myth intact - 'it ran two years late, so the house opened with Rigoletto instead' asserts a causal link that the dates forbid. Khedivial Opera House was inaugurated 1 Nov 1869 with Rigoletto, sixteen days BEFORE the canal opened; Verdi only softened in early 1870, when du Locle sent him Mariette's scenario, and he then contracted to deliver Aida for end-1870 with the premiere planned for January 1871. Aida did not exist as a commission when the house opened, so Rigoletto was not a substitute for a late Aida. 'Two years late' also overstates the slip: against its contracted date Aida ran roughly eleven months late, because Mariette's scenery and costumes were stranded in Paris during the 1870-71 siege; premiere 24 Dec 1871. My correctedReveal keeps the genuinely counterintuitive fact (Verdi turned the canal down) plus the stranded-sets detail and drops the Rigoletto causality rather than restating it in softer words. Dedupe: I re-ran the corpus check myself instead of trusting the claim - grep over data/verified.json and puzzles.js finds only one other Suez item, 'Length of Egypt's Suez Canal from Port Said to Suez, in km?' (data/verified.json:3393), different unit and quantity, no block. Incidental, not a blocker: data/verified.json:7680 (Mendeleev's periodic table) also answers 1869, different subject and different range 1750-1920, so the pool would carry two 1869 answers. Prompt wording, range, source and reasoning path all stand as written.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Verdi was asked to write music for the canal's inauguration and turned it down. He was talked into Aida for Cairo's new opera house instead, but the Franco-Prussian War stranded the sets and costumes in besieged Paris, so it premiered in December 1871 - more than two years after the first ships went through.

verdicts.prompt: The world's first website went online in what year?
verdicts.note: First verifier's factual call is CORRECT and I re-verified it against primary sources, but its fix was incomplete — it described pinning the prompt yet supplied no correctedPrompt, which leaves the trap in place. Evidence: all three CERN properties agree on December 1990. timeline.web.cern.ch headlines the event 'The world's first browser/editor, website and server go live at CERN — December 1990'; web30.web.cern.ch/web-history.html lists 'December 1990 | The world's first browser/editor, website and server go live at CERN' and separately 'August 1991 | Sir Berners-Lee announces the WWW software on the Internet'; home.cern's short history says 'By the end of 1990, Tim Berners-Lee had the first Web server and browser up and running at CERN.' info.cern.ch went up 20 Dec 1990 on Berners-Lee's NeXT machine and was used internally until the server was opened to anyone with an internet connection in August 1991. So with CERN as the cited source, 1990 is right and the corrected answer re-verifies. The 1991 side is not just a competing view, it is internally incoherent, which is why the prompt must be pinned rather than the answer flipped: Wikipedia's infobox says 'First published: 6 August 1991' (the alt.hypertext post) while its body says the technology went 'to the whole Internet on 23 August 1991' and to other research institutions from January 1991, and History.com/PopSci celebrate 6 Aug 1991 as the first website outright. A player raised on 'first website day' answers 1991 in good faith. Leaving the bare prompt 'went online' with answer 1990 penalizes that player on a genuinely muddled fact, so I pinned the prompt to the machine and the site going live at CERN, which only the December 1990 event satisfies. Answer 1990, position (1990-1970)/30 = 0.667, comfortably inside the band; lo/hi unchanged at 1970/2000. Reveal keeps the candidate's original charm, adds the December 1990 anchor now that the prompt names the event, and explicitly explains the August 1991 opening so a 1991 guesser learns why they were close rather than feeling cheated. Not a drop — this is a strong, well-known question once the event is pinned, and dropping it would waste it.
verdicts.correctedPrompt: In what year did the world's first website go live on Tim Berners-Lee's computer at CERN?
verdicts.correctedReveal: It was a page at CERN explaining what the World Wide Web was and how to make your own — for a while, the entire web documented itself. It went up on Tim Berners-Lee's NeXT machine in December 1990 and was used internally at CERN until the server was thrown open to the rest of the internet in August 1991, which is why a lot of retellings credit 1991.

verdicts.prompt: How many years did the Romans take to build the Colosseum?
verdicts.correctedPrompt: Vespasian broke ground on the Colosseum in AD 72. How many years passed before Titus opened it with games?

Original tokens {years,did,romans,take,build,colosseum} vs history105 Panama {years,did,united,states,take,build,panama,canal} = 4/10 = 0.40, and 8 vs 10 is 20% apart — two independent reasons it cannot block, so verifier 1's 0.40 is exactly right. Dedupe caveat verifier 1 missed: its 0.33 similarity was measured on the pre-fix prompt; a 'years to build' framing moves toward the existing 'How many years did the United States take to build the Panama Canal?' (also a digging megaproject). Not a block - different subject, different answer (6 vs 10), and the set already carries same-shape families - but I worded the fix to keep lexical distance. Minor non-blocking: the reasoning path's '50 km of bores' understates the work (three parallel tunnels, ~150 km bored); its second clause carries the estimate.

verdicts.prompt: How many years did Russia take to build the Trans-Siberian Railway?
verdicts.note: AGREE WITH THE DIAGNOSIS, REPLACE THE CORRECTION. The ambiguity is worse than V1 argued and the fix is mandatory: Wikipedia's Trans-Siberian Railway infobox — the single most-consulted source on this — reads 'Work began March 9, 1891' / 'Opened June 21, 1904', i.e. 13 years, right at the top of the page. So 13 is not a fringe reading a player has to dig for; it is the default one. As written, a player who looks the thing up lands 0.21 of the track from the answer (13 sits at 0.175 on linear 3..60 vs 0.386 for 25). 25 independently confirmed: construction from 1891, Amur line Sretensk-Khabarovsk finished with the Khabarovsk Bridge in October 1916, first all-Russian route to Vladivostok (LOC 'Meeting of Frontiers', and the Britannica formulation 'between 1891 and 1916' that the source field claims). Reveal independently verified on both halves: the icebreaking train ferry Baikal (Armstrong Whitworth, launched 1899, up to 27 cars a run, in service until the Circum-Baikal line) and rails laid on the lake ice in the winter of 1904 to move troops during the Russo-Japanese War. Kept as-is; it is accurate and vivid, and 'for years the line simply stopped at Lake Baikal' does not contradict the 1916 endpoint. Answer/lo/hi untouched, position stays 0.3860. WHY I REPLACED V1's PROMPT ('Work on the Trans-Siberian Railway began in 1891. How many years until the last all-Russian section opened?'): (a) it collides with V1's own instruction. On index 22 V1 wrote 'do not reword any of the three years-to-build prompts toward each other', then rewrote 23 to 'Begun under Vespasian in AD 72, how many years did the Colosseum take to finish?' and 25 to 'Work ... began in 1891. How many years until ...' — the same stated-start-year template, so its two fixes raise within-batch similarity instead of lowering it. (b) Stating 1891 strands the stored reasoningPath, which estimates from 9,000 km of track and period laying rates; once the start year is given the question becomes date recall (what year did it finish) and the reasoning shown at reveal no longer describes the route to the answer. My version pins the endpoint by description instead, which is just as unambiguous (the Amur line is the only section that put the whole route on Russian soil), keeps the estimation path intact, matches the shape V1 itself used on 24, and diverges from 23. DEDUPE, one V1 missed here: corpus history 'How many years did the United States take to build the Panama Canal?' (answer 10) is an exact structural twin of this prompt — 'How many years did [nation] take to build the [project]?' — a closer template match than the Colosseum pairing V1 flagged on 23, though answers 25 vs 10 are far apart so no block. My rewrite breaks that template too. Confirmed V1's other dedupe calls: geography55 asks the Trans-Siberian's length in km (different quantity, not a duplicate), and 25 vs Taj Mahal's 22 is 12% apart on overlapping bands — real but under the block test.
verdicts.correctedPrompt: How many years did Russia take to build the Trans-Siberian Railway, counting to the opening of the last section that put the whole route on Russian soil?

verdicts.note:
Overturning the first verifier's keep. Its facts were right but its dedupe check was wrong. Position 0.638 confirmed by hand: ln(106/5)/ln(600/5)=0.638.

The blocker the first verifier missed: it deduped on prompt text only ('different unit and quantity, similarity below threshold') and never read the existing item's reveal. The Karl Benz patent-year question already in the shipped bank (data/verified.json line 7910, puzzles.js line 5586) has this reveal verbatim: 'Two years later his wife Bertha drove it 106 km without telling him, buying fuel at a pharmacy along the way — the first long-distance drive, and the publicity that sold the machine.' That existing reveal hands the player both the candidate's exact answer (106) and the candidate's entire reveal hook (refuelling at a pharmacy). Anyone who has played the Benz patent question does not estimate this one, they recall it — and the payoff line lands as a repeat. Not fixable by editing the candidate; the number and the pharmacy beat are the whole question, and they are already spent.

Secondary defect, noted in case the bank owner would rather rewrite the older reveal and keep this: the reasoning path is factually wrong on the machine. The car on the 1888 trip was the Patent-Motorwagen Model III at roughly 2-2.5 hp, not 'well under one horsepower' (that figure is the 1885/86 Model I at 0.75 hp). 'No gears for hills' is defensible — the sons pushed on gradients and Bertha's suggestion is what prompted Karl to add a lower gear afterwards — but the horsepower claim would have to be corrected before this could ship under any framing.

Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertha_Benz, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benz_Patent-Motorwagen, group.mercedes-benz.com/company/tradition/founders-pioneers/bertha-benz.html, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertha_Benz_Memorial_Route.

verdicts.prompt: Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico in 1519 with how many Spanish soldiers?
verdicts.note: 508 soldiers (plus ~100 sailors, 11 ships, 16 horses) is Bernal Diaz's figure and the one Britannica carries. I checked the competing '630 men' figure: that counts non-combatants, women, Cuban auxiliaries and Africans, so the prompt's word 'soldiers' is what keeps 508 correct - leave it in. Reveal verified: the force that took Tenochtitlan in 1521 was overwhelmingly Tlaxcalan. Position 0.3068 matches. Dedupe adjudicated against candidate 39 (Pizarro, same question shape, same unit 'soldiers'): similarity is under 0.45 and 508 vs 168 is far outside the 10% answer window, so the build accepts both - but they are shape-siblings and should not be scheduled adjacently.

verdicts.prompt: Francisco Pizarro met the Inca emperor at Cajamarca in 1532 with how many Spanish soldiers?
verdicts.note: 168 men (62 horse, 106 foot) confirmed independently of Hemming - the same breakdown appears across the standard accounts of 16 Nov 1532. Reveal verified: the ransom room filled once with gold and twice with silver, and Atahualpa was garrotted in 1533 after it was paid. Position 0.3854 matches. See candidate 38 for the sibling adjudication; kept because the numbers are three times apart and the events are distinct.

verdicts.prompt: How many men crewed HMS Victory at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805?
verdicts.note: 821 is the muster-roll figure held by the National Museum of the Royal Navy, as cited. Reveal probed: the muster breaks down to about 701 men from the British Isles, so 'around one in ten was not British' is fair once colonial subjects (Maltese, Canadian, Indian, Jamaican) are counted as British - and every nationality named in the reveal (Sweden, Italy, Caribbean, India, USA - 23 Americans) is on the roll. Position 0.8175 matches, inside the ceiling. No corpus Trafalgar or ship-crew question.

verdicts.prompt: How many million soldiers did all sides together mobilise in the First World War?
verdicts.note: Checked the cited source directly rather than trusting it: the Library of Congress gives roughly 65 million soldiers, 8.5 million killed, 21 million wounded - which also confirms the reveal's 'one in eight died' (13%) and 'more than twenty million wounded'. The common rival figure is 70 million, 7.7% away, inside the tolerance and negligible on a log track. Position 0.5570 matches. Corpus has history6 (WWI start year) - different unit, no similarity hit.

verdicts.prompt: How many billion members of our species have ever been born?
verdicts.note: PRB's 2022 revision gives 117 billion, and I confirmed the reveal's specifics from PRB: the series starts at 190,000 BCE with a population of 2 and a birth rate near 80 per 1,000. Mild drift risk noted and accepted: PRB republishes periodically (108 billion in 2011) and roughly 0.13 billion births accrue per year, but on a 15..2000 log track that is invisible for years. Position 0.4198 matches. Dedupe: history102 (world population in 1900) and geography4 (2024 population) are different quantities; similarity below threshold.

verdicts.prompt: What was average life expectancy at birth worldwide in 1900, in years?
verdicts.note:
Answer independently confirmed, but the verifier identified a defective reveal and supplied no replacement text. Dropped rather than shipped with a known-bad reveal. Recoverable as a fresh candidate in a later batch. Original note: Independently re-verified. VALUE CONFIRMED: OWID's data insight states "global average life expectancy was just 32 years at the beginning of the 20th century" and 73 years in 2023; the OWID life-expectancy topic page repeats "In 1900, the average life expectancy of a newborn was 32 years." Answer 32, range 15..60 linear (position 0.378) all fine, and no corpus duplicate (grep for 'expectancy'/'mortality' across puzzles.js and data/verified.json returns nothing; the nearest neighbour is 'How many billion people were alive on Earth in 1900?', a different quantity — thematic adjacency only, not a dedupe hit).

FIRST VERIFIER — RIGHT CALL, PARTLY WRONG REASONING, AND ITS FIX IMPORTS A NEW ERROR.
(1) Right that the reveal needs fixing: 'decades more, much as today' is false. OWID's own age-specific comparison (France) has 15-year-olds in 1816 expecting to reach 58 vs 83 in 2021, and the arithmetic on the global 1900 figures (≈41% dying under five, LE at birth 32) puts a 1900 five-year-old at roughly the early fifties against the mid-seventies today — a gap of about two decades, not 'much as today'.
(2) Half-wrong on its other objection: it cites OWID's 'not only child mortality' line to attack 'dragged down almost entirely by infants'. That OWID statement is about why life expectancy ROSE over time (gains came at all ages); it is not a claim about the LEVEL in 1900, where under-five deaths genuinely do most of the work in pulling 32 down from ~53. The real defect in that clause is 'infants' — the ~41% figure is under-five, not under-one.
(3) NEW ERROR the first verifier introduced: its corrected reveal keeps 'roughly a third of children died before their fifth birthday'. OWID's global child-mortality series gives 42.8% in 1800, 40.9% in 1900, 24.7% in 1950 — about two in five in 1900, not a third. The corrected reveal must not ship with that understated figure.

My correctedReveal fixes both the 'much as today' falsehood and the child-mortality share. Note for the build: the reasoning path carries the same 'around a third' understatement and should read 'around 40% (two in five)'; there is no field for it here, so flagging it explicitly.

verdicts.prompt: How many million Africans were embarked on ships in the transatlantic slave trade?
verdicts.note: SlaveVoyages gives 12.5 million embarked against 10.7 million disembarked, which is exactly the reveal's 1.8 million lost in the crossing, reconstructed from roughly 36,000 documented voyages. The prompt's 'embarked' is the load-bearing word - the arrival figure is the other headline number - so keep it. Position 0.5764 matches. Distinct from candidate 7 (Brazilian abolition year): different unit, no similarity hit.

verdicts.prompt: How many km long was the Berlin Wall, all the way around West Berlin?
verdicts.note: 155 km total perimeter with 43.1 km forming the inner-city border, confirmed against the Berlin Wall Foundation's figures - 43.1/155 is 28%, so 'about a quarter' in the reveal is fair. Position 0.5704 matches. Dedupe: history4 asks the year the Wall fell - different unit and quantity, similarity below threshold; no geography question covers the Wall.

verdicts.prompt: How many metres long was the airship Hindenburg?
verdicts.note: 245 m (803.8 ft) confirmed. Reveal verified: designed for helium, denied it by the US export embargo, flown on hydrogen with the passenger accommodation built inside the hull. Position 0.7977 matches. No corpus airship question; nearest length-in-metres questions are in culture (Bayeux Tapestry, Guernica) with no similarity overlap.

verdicts.prompt: At its peak the Mongol Empire covered how many million km², the largest contiguous empire ever?
verdicts.note: Sources disagree far beyond the 10% bar. Guinness (the cited source) and several tertiary sites say 24 million km2; other standard references put the peak at 33 million km2, with 23 and 26 also in circulation - a 37% spread that comes from genuinely different methodologies for what counted as held territory at what date, not from sloppy copying. There is no defensible single answer to score against. Secondary concern, adjudicated since no dedupe flag was supplied: it is the same question shape and same unit as published history98 ('At its 1920 peak, the British Empire covered how many million km2 of land?', 35.5) at 0.33 similarity - under the build's block threshold, but a second empire-area question would read as repetition even if the number were solid.

verdicts.prompt: Top speed of Stephenson's Rocket at the 1829 Rainhill Trials, in km/h?
verdicts.note: 30 mph at Rainhill (12 mph average) is the Science Museum figure, and 30 mph = 48.3 km/h, so the metric conversion is sound and the question needs no imperial units to answer. Reveal verified: William Huskisson MP was struck by Rocket at the Liverpool & Manchester opening on 15 Sept 1830 while crossing to greet Wellington. Position 0.5782 matches. No corpus locomotive-speed question.

verdicts.prompt: How many metres did the Wright brothers' first powered flight cover, in 1903?
verdicts.note: 120 ft = 36.6 m, rounds to 37; 12 seconds; fourth flight of 852 ft = 260 m before a gust wrecked the machine - reveal fully checks out. Metric-native as asked, no imperial dependency for the player. Position 0.4346 matches. Dedupe adjudicated: history8 covers the same event but asks the year (0.36 similarity, different unit, no block) - a legitimate sibling of the kind already in the corpus (history70/history94 do this for Magellan). Note it is candidate 31, not this one, that made the pairing a problem.

questions.prompt: Uluru rises how many metres above the flat Australian plain around it?
questions.reveal: What you see is the tip: the sandstone slab tilts underground and geologists trace it several kilometres down, so most of Uluru is buried.
questions.reasoningPath: It is a lone rock on a plain, not a mountain, but photos show cars and people as specks at its base. Bigger than a 100 m office block, far short of a 1,000 m peak — a few hundred metres.

questions.prompt: The world's highest railway station, Tanggula in Tibet, sits how many metres above sea level?
questions.reveal: Carriages on the Qinghai-Tibet line are pressurised like aircraft and pipe oxygen to every seat, because the air there holds barely half the oxygen of sea level.
questions.reasoningPath: It crosses the Tibetan Plateau, which averages about 4,500 m, over a mountain pass. Everest base camp is 5,300 m and trains cannot climb much past that, so just above 5,000 m.

questions.prompt: Chimborazo's summit is how many metres farther from Earth's centre than Everest's?
questions.reveal: Chimborazo was measured as the world's highest mountain until surveys of the Himalaya in the 1800s dethroned it. It is still the spot on Earth's surface closest to the Moon.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth's equator bulges about 21 km. Everest sits 28° north, so it keeps only part of that bulge; Chimborazo sits on the equator and keeps all of it, but is 2.6 km shorter. Net: roughly 2 km ahead.

questions.prompt: Mexico City sits how many metres above sea level?
questions.source: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Geografía (INEGI)
questions.reveal: It stands on the drained bed of Lake Texcoco, and as the city pumps its groundwater away parts of it are sinking by up to 50 cm a year.
questions.reasoningPath: It is high enough that athletes notice the thin air but low enough for a huge population to live normally. La Paz at 3,600 m is much harder; this is comfortably below that but well over 1,000 m.

questions.prompt: At its mouth, how many km across is the Río de la Plata, the world's widest river?
questions.source: Britannica; measured Punta del Este to Punta Rasa
questions.reveal: Standing on either shore you cannot see the other side, which is why some geographers refuse to call it a river at all and file it as a gulf of the Atlantic.
questions.reasoningPath: Buenos Aires and Montevideo sit on opposite banks and a ferry between them takes a few hours at sea speed, so the estuary must be well over 100 km, but it is not an ocean crossing.

questions.prompt: Lake Baikal holds what percentage of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water?
questions.reveal: It is also the world's oldest lake at around 25 million years, and roughly two thirds of the species living in it exist nowhere else.
questions.reasoningPath: It is famous for holding more water than all five North American Great Lakes together, and those are a big slice of the world's supply. So a large fraction, but nowhere near half.

questions.prompt: Lake Superior, the largest freshwater lake by area, covers how many km²?
questions.source: US EPA / Environment Canada Great Lakes Atlas
questions.reveal: Poured out evenly, its water would cover both American continents to a depth of about 30 cm.
questions.reasoningPath: It is roughly 550 km long and 250 km wide on a map of North America, but a ragged shape, so something under half of that rectangle: tens of thousands of km².

questions.prompt: The Mediterranean Sea covers how many million km²?
questions.reveal: About 5.6 million years ago it dried to a scatter of salt basins, then refilled through the Strait of Gibraltar in a flood that may have lasted only a couple of years.
questions.reasoningPath: It runs about 3,800 km from Gibraltar to Lebanon and averages several hundred km wide, so on the order of a million-ish km² — small beside the Pacific's 165 million.

questions.prompt: Istanbul straddles the Bosphorus. At its narrowest, how many metres wide is the strait?
questions.reveal: Around 40,000 ships a year thread through it, roughly twice the traffic of the Suez Canal, past apartment blocks close enough to read the ships' names.
questions.reasoningPath: Photos show houses on both banks in one frame and a suspension bridge crossing it in a single span; suspension spans top out around 2 km, so this is under a kilometre.

questions.prompt: China's Grand Canal, the longest artificial waterway ever dug, runs how many km?
questions.reveal: Work started in the 5th century BC and the Sui dynasty finished the main link around AD 610 using conscripted labour counted in the millions. Barges still use much of it.
questions.reasoningPath: It joins Beijing to Hangzhou, which is most of the length of eastern China — Beijing to Shanghai alone is about 1,200 km by rail, and the canal wanders.

questions.prompt: Antarctica covers how many million km²?
questions.source: British Antarctic Survey; Australian Antarctic Division
questions.reveal: Almost none of that surface is rock: less than 1% of the continent is ice-free, and it counts as the world's largest desert on rainfall.
questions.reasoningPath: On a globe it looks comparable to Russia (17 million km²) and clearly bigger than Australia (7.7 million) or Europe (10 million).

questions.prompt: The world's largest national park, in northeast Greenland, covers how many km²?
questions.source: Guinness World Records; Government of Greenland
questions.reveal: It is larger than all but about 30 of the world's countries, and its only permanent human presence is the Sirius Patrol — a couple of dozen soldiers who travel it by dog sled.
questions.reasoningPath: Greenland is 2.17 million km² and the park is drawn over most of the island's northern and eastern ice, so roughly half of it — high hundreds of thousands.

questions.prompt: Longyearbyen on Svalbard, the northernmost proper town, sits at what latitude, in degrees north?
questions.reveal: The Sun never rises there between late October and mid-February, which is part of why the Global Seed Vault was cut into the permafrost above the town.
questions.reasoningPath: The Arctic Circle is 66°N and northern Norway sits around 70°N; Svalbard lies well beyond the mainland but short of the 90°N pole, so high 70s.

questions.prompt: The total surface of the Earth, land and sea together, is how many million km²?
questions.reveal: The Pacific alone accounts for nearly a third of it, and Russia, the largest country, for barely 3%.
questions.reasoningPath: A sphere's area is 4πr², and Earth's radius is about 6,400 km: 4 × 3.14 × 6,400² ≈ 510 million km². Or: land is about 149 million and it is 29% of the total.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the Earth's surface is covered by ocean?
questions.reveal: Most of that water is deep: average ocean depth is about 3.7 km, and the Pacific by itself covers more of the planet than every landmass combined.
questions.reasoningPath: Any globe or world map is dominated by blue — clearly more than half, but the continents are not a thin fringe either. Somewhere around two thirds to three quarters.

questions.prompt: Earth bulges at the equator: how many km wider is it there than from pole to pole?
questions.source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet (12,756 km vs 12,714 km)
questions.reveal: Spinning flings that bulge outward, and it means you weigh about half a percent less standing on the equator than at the poles.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth is nearly a perfect sphere — from space you cannot see the flattening — so the difference must be tiny against a 12,750 km diameter: a few tens of km, not hundreds.

questions.prompt: Travelling due north, how many km do you cover in one degree of latitude?
questions.reveal: A nautical mile was originally defined as one minute of latitude — a sixtieth of this — which is why it survives in navigation as 1,852 metres.
questions.reasoningPath: A full meridian circle is about 40,000 km and there are 360 degrees around it, so 40,000 ÷ 360 ≈ 111 km per degree.

questions.prompt: Standing on a beach, roughly how many km away is the horizon for an adult's eyes?
questions.source: standard geometry: d ≈ 3.57√h km for eye height h in metres
questions.reveal: Height buys distance fast: climb a 30 m lighthouse and the horizon jumps to about 20 km, which is why coastal lights were built tall rather than bright.
questions.reasoningPath: A ship's hull vanishes surprisingly quickly at sea, well within the distance you can still see a hill inland. It feels like a few kilometres, not tens.

questions.prompt: Greenland, the world's largest island, covers how many million km²?
questions.reveal: On the Mercator maps most people grew up with it looks the size of Africa. Africa is about fourteen times larger.
questions.reasoningPath: It is far smaller than Australia's 7.7 million km² but much larger than Madagascar's 0.59 million — so a couple of million km².

questions.prompt: The island of Great Britain covers how many km²?
questions.source: Ordnance Survey; UK Office for National Statistics
questions.reveal: That makes it the largest island in Europe and ninth largest in the world — and still smaller than the single Indonesian island of Sumatra.
questions.reasoningPath: It runs about 950 km from Cornwall to northern Scotland and averages maybe 200-300 km wide, but tapers badly: roughly 200,000 km².

questions.prompt: How many km long is Chile from its northern border to its southern tip?
questions.source: Instituto Geográfico Militar de Chile; Britannica
questions.reveal: It averages only about 175 km wide, and at its pinch point barely 90 km separate the Andes from the Pacific.
questions.reasoningPath: South America runs about 7,400 km north to south and Chile covers well over half of that western edge, from the tropics to near Cape Horn.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the Netherlands lies below sea level?
questions.reveal: Add the land at risk from river flooding and 55% of the country needs defending; the lowest point sits 6.8 m under sea level.
questions.reasoningPath: The famous polders are real but concentrated in the west; the south and east rise into hills. A substantial minority of the country, not most of it.

questions.prompt: How many countries are completely surrounded by a single other country?
questions.reveal: Lesotho, San Marino and Vatican City. Lesotho is the giant of the three, and the only one whose entire territory sits above 1,000 m.
questions.reasoningPath: Vatican City and San Marino inside Italy come to mind immediately, and Lesotho inside South Africa with a moment's thought. Nothing else obvious — so a handful at most.

questions.prompt: Java, the world's most populous island, is home to how many million people?
questions.reveal: That is about one person in fifty alive today, packed onto a tenth of a percent of the world's land — which is why Indonesia is moving its capital off the island to Borneo.
questions.reasoningPath: Indonesia has around 280 million people and Java famously holds over half of them on a small share of the land.

questions.prompt: Singapore's entire national territory covers how many km²?
questions.reveal: About a quarter of it did not exist in 1960: the country has grown by a fifth by importing sand and reclaiming land from the sea.
questions.reasoningPath: It is a city-state you can drive across in under an hour — roughly 40 km by 20 km — so several hundred km², far above Monaco's 2 and far below a normal country.

questions.prompt: The Sahara stretches how many km from the Atlantic coast to the Red Sea?
questions.reveal: It spans eleven countries, and satellite records show its southern edge advancing and retreating by 100 km or more between wet and dry decades.
questions.reasoningPath: Africa is about 7,400 km wide at that latitude and the desert runs coast to coast apart from narrow strips at each end — so most of that width.

questions.prompt: What percentage of humanity now lives in towns and cities rather than the countryside?
questions.source: World Bank / UN DESA World Urbanization Prospects
questions.reveal: The world crossed the halfway mark around 2007. In 1900 the figure was roughly 15%.
questions.reasoningPath: Rich countries are 80%+ urban, but India and much of Africa are still mostly rural and hold a huge share of people. The global figure has to sit just past half.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the world's land area is covered by forest?
questions.reveal: Just five countries — Russia, Brazil, Canada, China and the United States — hold more than half of it between them.
questions.reasoningPath: Deserts, ice, grassland, farmland and cities each take big bites of the land. Forest is the largest single category but clearly a minority — about a third.

questions.prompt: How many countries hold formal territorial claims in Antarctica?
questions.reveal: Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the UK. Three of the claims overlap on the peninsula, and the 1959 treaty froze the argument rather than settling it.
questions.reasoningPath: Claims went to the nations that explored or sit nearest: the southern-continent states plus a few European polar powers. A handful, not dozens.

questions.prompt: The continent of Africa covers how many million km²?
questions.reveal: China, India, the contiguous United States and most of Europe would all fit inside it at once — a fact Mercator world maps hide completely.
questions.reasoningPath: Russia, the largest country, is 17 million km² and Africa is clearly much bigger than Russia on a globe, but it is one continent of six: around 30 million.

questions.prompt: The London Underground network runs how many km of route?
questions.reveal: Despite the name, about 55% of the network runs in the open air; the deep tube lines are mostly in the central core.
questions.reasoningPath: Eleven lines, most of them 20-50 km end to end, plus long suburban arms out to the edge of London — a few hundred km in total.

questions.prompt: Norway's Lærdal tunnel, the world's longest road tunnel, runs how many metres?
questions.reveal: Three blue-and-yellow lit caverns break up the drive to stop drivers being hypnotised by the darkness on the 20-minute passage.
questions.reasoningPath: Alpine road tunnels like Mont Blanc run about 12 km; the record holder should be roughly double that, and rail tunnels reach 57 km only by going under a whole range.

questions.prompt: The Three Gorges Dam wall stands how many metres above its rock foundation?
questions.reveal: Filling the reservoir shifted so much water mass that NASA calculated it lengthened the Earth's day by about 0.06 microseconds.
questions.reasoningPath: It is a wide concrete gravity dam on a big river rather than a narrow canyon arch — impressive but far short of the tallest dams near 300 m, and much taller than a 30 m weir.

questions.prompt: The Millau Viaduct's roadway crosses how many metres above the river Tarn below?
questions.reveal: One of its masts reaches 343 m from the ground — taller than the Eiffel Tower — and on misty mornings the deck floats above a cloud layer filling the valley.
questions.reasoningPath: Photographs show the deck level with the tops of the plateaux on either side of a deep gorge — a few hundred metres of drop, comparable to a very tall skyscraper.

questions.prompt: The Panama Canal's locks lift ships how many metres above sea level?
questions.reveal: No pumps are involved: gravity alone drains about 200 million litres of fresh lake water into the sea with every transit, so droughts now cap how many ships can cross each day.
questions.reasoningPath: Ships climb to Gatun Lake in three lock steps per side, and a single lock chamber raises a vessel roughly the height of a three-storey building.

questions.prompt: The world's longest dead-straight railway, across Australia's Nullarbor, runs how many km without a curve?
questions.source: Guinness World Records; Australian Rail Track Corporation
questions.reveal: Nullarbor is dog-Latin for 'no trees'. The line opened in 1917 across a limestone plateau so flat the surveyors had no reason to bend it.
questions.reasoningPath: The whole trans-Australian crossing is about 4,300 km and the treeless plain is one memorable stretch of it — hundreds of km, not thousands.

questions.prompt: Australia's Highway 1 loops the entire continent. How many km long is it?
questions.source: Guinness World Records; Australian state road authorities
questions.reveal: It is the longest national highway on Earth and links every state and territory capital except Canberra, which sits inland.
questions.reasoningPath: Australia is about 4,000 km across and 3,200 km deep, so a rectangle around it is roughly 14,000 km — and a coastal road wanders more than a rectangle.

questions.prompt: The deepest mine on Earth, Mponeng in South Africa, reaches how many metres below the surface?
questions.reveal: The rock face down there sits near 60 °C, so the mine pumps slurry ice underground by the tonne just to make the air survivable for a shift.
questions.reasoningPath: A lift ride down takes over an hour in stages, and the Kola borehole reached 12 km with no people in it. Human-occupied depth is a few km — order of 4 km.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the world's earthquakes strike around the Pacific Ring of Fire?
questions.reveal: The same belt carries about 75% of the world's active volcanoes — both are simply the map of where the Pacific plate is being shoved under its neighbours.
questions.reasoningPath: Japan, Indonesia, the Philippines, Chile, Alaska and New Zealand together account for nearly every big quake in the news. The rest of the world barely features.

questions.prompt: Climb how many metres before the air pressure falls to half its sea-level value?
questions.reveal: By Everest's summit at 8,849 m only about a third of sea-level pressure is left, which is why the last 800 m of that climb is called the death zone.
questions.reasoningPath: The atmosphere thins out over the first ten-odd km, and climbers report real trouble from about 5,000 m. Half the air is gone by roughly the height of Kilimanjaro.

questions.prompt: The Alps run through how many countries?
questions.reveal: France, Monaco, Italy, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Austria, Germany, Slovenia — the two smallest, Monaco and Liechtenstein, are easy to forget.
questions.reasoningPath: The obvious four are France, Switzerland, Italy and Austria; adding southern Germany and Slovenia at the eastern end gets you to six, and micro-states pad it out.

questions.prompt: How many cities passed 10 million people in the UN's 2018 global count?
questions.reveal: In 1950 only New York and Tokyo qualified. The UN expects 43 megacities by 2030, nearly all of the new ones in Asia and Africa.
questions.reasoningPath: Name them and you get to about 20 without effort — Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, São Paulo, Cairo, Mexico City, Dhaka, Lagos and so on — with a long tail you have not thought of.

questions.prompt: Singapore to New York, the longest scheduled nonstop flight, is how many km in a straight line?
questions.reveal: The aircraft rarely flies the straight line: heading east it can cover 17,000 km over the Pacific, because riding the jet stream burns less fuel than the short way.
questions.reasoningPath: The furthest two points on Earth can be is 20,000 km. Singapore is nearly on the opposite side of the globe from New York, but not quite — so around three quarters of the maximum.

questions.prompt: The world's longest suspension bridge span, over Turkey's Dardanelles, measures how many metres?
questions.source: Guinness World Records; Turkish General Directorate of Highways
questions.reveal: The span length was chosen deliberately to mark 2023, the centenary of the Turkish republic — and its towers, at 318 m, are the tallest of any suspension bridge.
questions.reasoningPath: The Golden Gate manages 1,280 m and Japan's Akashi Kaikyō held the record near 2,000 m for decades. A new record breaks that, but not by much.

questions.prompt: How many km of the Channel Tunnel actually run beneath the sea?
questions.reveal: It is bored about 40 m below the seabed, following a single layer of chalk marl that stays watertight — the geology, not the distance, decided the route.
questions.reasoningPath: The Strait of Dover is 33 km at its narrowest and the tunnel does not take that exact line, plus it must reach dry land well inshore. A little over 30 km underwater.

questions.prompt: The world's largest airport by land area, at Dammam in Saudi Arabia, covers how many km²?
questions.reveal: The site is larger than the neighbouring country of Bahrain, yet only about 5% of it is actually built on — the rest is empty desert inside the fence.
questions.reasoningPath: A big international airport with runways and terminals occupies tens of km². To hold the world record on desert land where space is free, multiply that many times over.

questions.prompt: In midwinter, roughly how many people are living on the whole Antarctic continent?
questions.reveal: Come summer the number rises about fivefold, the biggest seasonal population swing anywhere on Earth.
questions.reasoningPath: Around 40 stations stay open through the winter, each holding a skeleton crew of maybe 10 to 60 people. That multiplies out to roughly a thousand.

questions.prompt: Continental shelves end at roughly what water depth, in metres, before the seabed plunges away?
questions.source: NOAA; standard oceanographic definition of the shelf break
questions.reveal: At the height of the last ice age the sea stood about 120 m lower, so nearly every shelf on Earth was dry land people could walk across.
questions.reasoningPath: Shelf seas like the North Sea are famously shallow — divers and oil rigs work them — while the open ocean averages 3.7 km. The break must be low hundreds of metres.

questions.prompt: China's Beijing-Shanghai high-speed line runs how many km?
questions.reveal: More than four fifths of the route sits on viaduct rather than ground, and the fastest trains cover it in about four and a half hours.
questions.reasoningPath: Beijing to Shanghai is roughly 1,100 km as the crow flies down China's eastern seaboard, and a rail line adds a detour or two.

questions.prompt: How many hours separate the world's earliest time zone from the latest?
questions.reveal: Kiribati's Line Islands run at UTC+14 while Baker Island sits at UTC−12, so for two hours of every day three different calendar dates exist at once.
questions.reasoningPath: A planet only needs 24 hours of zones, but countries push the date line around to keep themselves on one date — so the true spread must overshoot 24 by a little.

verdicts.prompt: Uluru rises how many metres above the flat Australian plain around it?
verdicts.note: Opened Parks Australia's own page (uluru.gov.au amazing-facts): 'Uluru rises 348 metres above the surrounding plain' — exact match, not a secondhand figure. Recomputed position on log 100..1500: (ln348-ln100)/(ln1500-ln100)=1.247/2.708=0.460, matches the claimed 0.46. Reveal checked separately: the Parks Australia page itself gives no depth, but Australian Geographic (Dr Karl) and the park's geology page describe Uluru as the tip of a slab continuing 2.5 km to ~6 km down, so 'several kilometres' and 'most of Uluru is buried' both hold. Grepped puzzles.js: no Uluru or Australian-rock question exists in any of the 596 (geography93 Dingo Fence and candidate [35]/[36] are the only other Australia items, all distinct).

verdicts.prompt: The world's highest railway station, Tanggula in Tibet, sits how many metres above sea level?
verdicts.note: Guinness World Records 'Highest railway station' gives 5,068 m (16,627 ft) for Tanggula on the Qingzang line, opened 1 July 2006 — still the standing record in 2026, and 255 m above the runner-up at Ticlio, Peru, so no rival claim within 10%. Position on linear 2000..6000: (5068-2000)/4000=0.767, matches. Reveal verified: Qinghai-Tibet carriages are pressurised with piped oxygen at every seat, and ISA pressure at 5,068 m is ~54% of sea level, so 'barely half the oxygen' is right. No railway-altitude question in the bank; geography70 (Tibetan Plateau elevation 4,500 m) is a different quantity, though a player who knows it will anchor well — acceptable, not duplicative.

verdicts.prompt: Chimborazo's summit is how many metres farther from Earth's centre than Everest's?
verdicts.note: Value re-verified independently: Wikipedia's 'Summits farthest from the Earth's center' states Chimborazo's summit is '2,168 m (7,113 ft) farther from the Earth's center than the summit of Everest'; the Chimborazo article gives 6,384.4 km geocentric radius vs Everest's ~6,382.3 km, consistent. Guinness ('Farthest mountain peak from Earth's centre') hedges to 'more than 2 kilometres' and never states 2,168 — so the claimed source is only partly load-bearing, but the figure stands. Range 200..6000 linear puts it at 0.339, fine. No dupe: the bank's only nearby item is the Aconcagua height question (answer 6961). FIRST VERIFIER: right call, right reasoning. I confirmed the Moon claim is not defensible — the sub-lunar point sweeps roughly 28.6N to 28.6S over the month, so Chimborazo is the closest point to the Moon only for part of it; the Guinness page it cites never mentions the Moon or Sun, Wikipedia explicitly says the distinction 'relates solely to Earth's geometry', and the claim traces only to travel blogs. BUT its replacement is not usable: 'At 6,263 m ... Aconcagua beats it by 700 m' hands the player 6,263 + 700 = ~6,963 against the bank's live Aconcagua question (answer 6961, linear 3000..10000) — a near-exact cross-question spoiler, which the first verifier noticed the overlap and shipped anyway. My replacement keeps its verified first sentence and swaps in two facts that leak nothing: Chimborazo's summit is 2,585 m lower than Everest's above sea level (8,848.86 - 6,263.47, stated as '2,585 metres lower' on Wikipedia), the equatorial bulge is ~21 km (6,378.1 vs 6,356.8 km radius), and at least 26 other summits also sit farther from the centre than Everest (Wikipedia, same page as the 2,168 figure).
verdicts.correctedReveal: Chimborazo was measured as the world's highest mountain until surveys of the Himalaya in the 1800s dethroned it. The equator's 21 km bulge does all the work here: Chimborazo's summit is 2,585 m lower than Everest's above sea level, and at least 26 other peaks also sit farther from Earth's centre than Everest does.

verdicts.prompt: Mexico City sits how many metres above sea level?
verdicts.note: 2,240 m confirmed across independent sources including clinical/physiological literature that uses Mexico City as its altitude reference ('normal values at sea level and at 2,240 m'). Position on log 200..5000: (ln2240-ln200)/(ln5000-ln200)=2.416/3.219=0.751, matches. Reveal verified against the JGR paper 'Over a Century of Sinking in Mexico City' (2020JB020648): subsidence 'reaches 50 cm/year', and the city does sit on drained Lake Texcoco. One nuance I checked and accepted: that paper argues the sinking is now driven by decades-old clay compaction rather than current pumping, but pumping is the cause, so the reveal's phrasing is not wrong. Duplication: the bank already has geography88 (La Paz 3,640 m) and geography89 (La Rinconada 5,100 m). Three city-altitude questions is thematic repetition, but the facts are distinct and the answers are far apart — flagging it rather than dropping.

verdicts.prompt: At its mouth, how many km across is the Río de la Plata, the world's widest river?
