verdicts.note: Tried to break this on source disagreement and couldn't: cited maximum widths cluster at 220 km, 227 km (Springer/CONICET, measured to the Atlantic boundary) and 230 km — a 4.5% spread, well inside the 10% bar. Position on log 10..500: (ln220-ln10)/(ln500-ln10)=3.091/3.912=0.790, matches. The real objection is the prompt's 'world's widest river' when geographers file it variously as an estuary, gulf or marginal sea — but the reveal itself surfaces exactly that dispute, which defuses it rather than hiding it. No Plata/estuary question in the bank.

verdicts.prompt: Lake Baikal holds what percentage of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water?
verdicts.note: UNESCO World Heritage Centre's own listing (whc.unesco.org/en/list/754) states Baikal 'contains 20% of the world's total unfrozen freshwater reserve' — the claimed source checks out verbatim. Position on linear 0..60: 20/60=0.333, matches. Reveal: 25 million years is UNESCO's figure ✓. The endemism claim I probed separately and it is the soft spot — sources give 60%, two-thirds, and 80% depending on species count and whether the whole lake or only the open water is counted; 'roughly two thirds' sits inside that documented range and matches the Britannica-style framing, so it survives, but it is the weakest sentence in the batch of keeps. Bank check: nature91 asks what share of fresh water is locked in glaciers/ice (69%) — a different quantity, and the 'unfrozen' qualifier here keeps them from colliding. geography58 (Baikal max depth) is a second Baikal item but a distinct fact.

verdicts.prompt: Lake Superior, the largest freshwater lake by area, covers how many km²?
verdicts.note: 82,100 km² confirmed by Michigan EGLE citing the Great Lakes Atlas, and the superlative holds because the larger Caspian is saline. Position on log 20000..2000000: (ln82100-ln20000)/(ln2000000-ln20000)=1.413/4.606=0.3068, matches 0.307. I recomputed the reveal rather than trusting it: Superior holds 12,100 km³; North plus South America is ~42.5M km²; 12,100/42.5e6 = 0.285 km = 28.5 cm, so 'about 30 cm' is arithmetically sound. Considered a US-centric objection and rejected it — this is a world superlative, not a domestic one. No Great Lakes question in the bank; geography50 (Caspian area) is the nearest and is a different water body.

verdicts.prompt: The Mediterranean Sea covers how many million km²?
verdicts.note: 2.5M km² agreed by WWF's Mediterranean programme and multiple encyclopaedic sources (~965,000 sq mi); no source I found dissents by more than a rounding step. Position on log 0.1..10: (ln2.5-ln0.1)/(ln10-ln0.1)=3.219/4.605=0.699, matches. Reveal checked against the Messinian salinity crisis literature: the basin desiccated between 5.96 and 5.33 Mya (so '5.6 million years ago' falls inside the event, not outside it) and the Zanclean refill through Gibraltar is estimated at months to about two years (Garcia-Castellanos 2009), so 'may have lasted only a couple of years' is properly hedged. Bank: geography74 gives the Mediterranean's deepest point (Calypso Deep) — different quantity, no collision.

verdicts.prompt: Istanbul straddles the Bosphorus. At its narrowest, how many metres wide is the strait?
verdicts.note: Second verifier, independent. AGREE with first verifier's fix. Answer 700 m confirmed: Wikipedia and Turkish Straits pilotage sources give a 700 m minimum between Kandilli Point and Asiyan. Note the first verifier missed a source variant: Britannica itself gives 750 m (2,450 ft, between Rumelihisari and Anadoluhisari), not 700 m, so the 'Britannica' source line is loose — but on log 100..10000 that is 0.423 vs 0.433, scoring-identical, so no answer or range change. Reveal ratio independently re-checked: Bosphorus 41,363 transits in 2024 and 29,710 in Jan-Sep 2025 (~39.6k annualized), so 'around 40,000 a year' is sound. Suez transits: 26,434 in 2023 (SCA all-time record), 13,213 in 2024, 12,758 in 2025. 'Roughly twice' is therefore ~1.6x in Suez's best year and ~3.1x today; it was accurate only around 2019-2021 (18,880 Suez vs ~41,000 Bosphorus), i.e. a stale figure rather than a fabricated one. Fix re-verified at both extremes: 39-41k vs Suez's record 26.4k is still comfortably more, and Suez has never exceeded ~26.5k while the Bosphorus has held 38-46k for decades, so the replacement is true in every recent year and drift-proof. Adopting the first verifier's corrected reveal verbatim; no further change warranted.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Around 40,000 ships a year thread through it — comfortably more than pass through the Suez Canal — past apartment blocks close enough to read the ships' names.

verdicts.prompt: China's Grand Canal, the longest artificial waterway ever dug, runs how many km?
verdicts.note: 1,776 km is the standard Beijing-Hangzhou figure and is consistent across Wikipedia and UNESCO's listing (whc.unesco.org/en/list/1443). I checked the one ambiguity that could sink this: UNESCO also says the network exceeded 2,000 km of artificial waterway by the 13th century, so a pedant could argue for a larger number — but 1,776 km is what every source gives for the canal itself, and the 100..5000 band absorbs the difference. Position on log 100..5000: (ln1776-ln100)/(ln5000-ln100)=2.877/3.912=0.7354, matches 0.735. Reveal verified: UNESCO dates construction from the 5th century BC with Sui-dynasty unification c. AD 609-610, the conscripted workforce is documented in the millions, and southern reaches remain in commercial barge use. No canal-length duplication risk — geography41 (Panama, 82 km) and geography47 (Suez, 193 km) are an order of magnitude away.

verdicts.prompt: Antarctica covers how many million km²?
verdicts.note: 14M km² confirmed (Wikipedia/BAS give 14.0-14.2M). Position on linear 2..30: (14-2)/28=0.4286, matches 0.429. The reveal's '<1% ice-free' looked like the weak point so I chased it specifically: BAS states only 0.4% of Antarctica's surface is free of snow and ice, and a 2016 BAS mapping study refined exposed rock to 0.18% — both under 1%, so the reveal is right and is right for the cited source. (Wikipedia's '2% ice-free' counts a different denominator; I checked and it does not contradict BAS.) Largest-desert-by-rainfall claim is standard and correct. Bank: geography66 (sea-level rise if Antarctic ice melts) plus candidates [28] and [46] make five Antarctica items in circulation — worth the author knowing, but all five ask genuinely different things.

verdicts.prompt: The world's largest national park, in northeast Greenland, covers how many km²?
verdicts.note: Answer independently confirmed, but the verifier identified a defective reveal and supplied no replacement text. Dropped rather than shipped with a known-bad reveal. Recoverable as a fresh candidate in a later batch. Original note: Area confirmed independently: Guinness ('Largest national park') and Wikipedia both give 972,000 km² (375,291 sq mi), established 1974, enlarged 1988. Log position (ln972000-ln10000)/(ln3000000-ln10000) = 0.802, comfortably inside the range. 'Larger than all but about 30 countries' verified: bigger than 166 of 195 = all but 29. First verifier was right to flag the reveal and right about why — the park's recorded census population is zero, at least five stations are manned through the winter, and Sirius over-winters 12 at Daneborg, so 'only permanent human presence... a couple of dozen soldiers' is false twice over. But its correction introduces two numbers that do not match the sources: Wikipedia's park article lists FIVE year-round-staffed stations (Daneborg 12, Danmarkshavn 8 — Danmarkshavn's own article says 6 — Station Nord 5, Mestersvig 2, Summit Camp 4), not six; and those sum to ~29-31, so 'fewer than fifty' is true but badly loose, and it throws away the better hook. Summit Camp's inclusion (on the ice sheet at 72°N) also makes any hard station count fragile, so my correction drops the count and keeps the figure the sources actually support. Everything else in the candidate stands: unambiguous single-value answer, sourced to Guinness, no portability issue, no dedupe concern found.

verdicts.prompt: Longyearbyen on Svalbard, the northernmost proper town, sits at what latitude, in degrees north?
verdicts.note: 78.13°N confirmed; answer 78 is correct to the degree the question asks for. Position on linear 50..90: (78-50)/40=0.70, matches. The superlative is correctly hedged — 'proper town' is exactly the qualifier needed, since Ny-Ålesund and Alert lie further north but are research/military settlements, and sources make that same distinction. Reveal verified: Longyearbyen's polar night runs roughly 26 October to 15 February, so 'late October to mid-February' is accurate rather than approximate, and the Global Seed Vault is indeed cut into permafrost above the town. No latitude or Svalbard question anywhere in the 596.

verdicts.prompt: The total surface of the Earth, land and sea together, is how many million km²?
verdicts.note: 510M km² per the NASA Earth Fact Sheet (510.1M). Position on log 20..1000: (ln510-ln20)/(ln1000-ln20)=3.239/3.912=0.828, matches. I recomputed both reveal claims rather than accepting them: Pacific 165.25M/510.1M = 32.4%, so 'nearly a third' ✓; Russia 17.1M/510.1M = 3.35%, so 'barely 3%' is a slightly loose phrasing for a number just over 3, but not false. Bank check: geography20 (equatorial circumference 40,075 km) and space6 (Earth's diameter 12,756 km) are the neighbours — both linear measures, neither an area, so no duplication.

verdicts.prompt: What percentage of the Earth's surface is covered by ocean?
verdicts.note: 71% is NOAA's standard figure and I found no source dissenting outside 70-71%. Position on linear 20..100: (71-20)/80=0.6375, matches 0.637. Reveal: average ocean depth 3.7 km ✓ (the bank's own nature85 gives 3,682 m, consistent); Pacific 165.25M km² genuinely exceeds total land area 148.9M km², so 'covers more of the planet than every landmass combined' is literally true, not rhetorical. Grepped every 'what percentage' question in the bank — there are eleven, none about ocean coverage; the nearest is geography78 (87% of humanity in the Northern Hemisphere), which is a different subject.

verdicts.prompt: Earth bulges at the equator: how many km wider is it there than from pole to pole?
verdicts.note: Recomputed straight from the NASA Earth Fact Sheet values the source cites: 12,756.2 − 12,713.6 = 42.6 km, rounds to 43 ✓. Position on log 1..300: (ln43-ln1)/(ln300-ln1)=3.761/5.704=0.6594, matches 0.659. Reveal arithmetic also checks: g is 9.780 m/s² at the equator versus 9.832 at the poles, a 0.53% difference, so 'about half a percent less' is right. Adjacency to space6 (Earth's equatorial diameter) noted — this asks for the difference between the two axes, which that question does not supply.

verdicts.prompt: Travelling due north, how many km do you cover in one degree of latitude?
verdicts.note: 111 km is the WGS-84 mean (110.574 km at the equator rising to 111.694 km at the poles), so the answer is correct and the variation is under 1%. Position on linear 20..300: (111-20)/280=0.325, matches. Reveal verified: the nautical mile was defined as one minute of latitude and is fixed at 1,852 m ✓ — and note 1,852 × 60 = 111.1 km, which independently confirms the answer. Nothing comparable in the bank.

verdicts.prompt: Standing on a beach, roughly how many km away is the horizon for an adult's eyes?
verdicts.note: UPHOLD the drop, on partly different grounds. (1) Dedupe confirmed independently: the sibling ('eyes 1.7 m up', 4.7 km) and this one ask for the same physical quantity under the same setup, differing only in whether the eye height is stated. Not a shared template — one fact, one number. A player who sees either scores the other from memory. (2) I confirmed the bank premise myself: grepping data/verified.json (596 entries) and puzzles.js for 'horizon' returns only incidental uses in other reveals/reasoning paths (Olympus Mons, rainbow, star counts, salt flat) plus a 'New Horizons' source string. No horizon-distance question is shipped, so exactly one of the twins should ship and one should go. (3) I DISAGREE with one of the first verifier's three tiebreaks: its category argument is backwards. Horizon distance from a beach is Earth-curvature — geography is the better home for it than the sibling's space batch. That reason should not have been used to condemn this one. (4) But I found a stronger reason this is nevertheless the twin to cut, which the first verifier missed. Web-verified: d = 3.57*sqrt(h) is the geometric (no-refraction) formula and 3.86*sqrt(h) is the standard refraction-corrected one; at h=1.7 m these give 4.65 km and 5.03 km. This candidate CITES the geometric formula as its source but states the refracted answer (5), so its number does not follow from the source it names — 3.57*sqrt(1.7)=4.65, which rounds to the sibling's 4.7. To reach 5 geometrically you need ~1.96 m eye height, taller than 'an adult'. The sibling states its height and its answer follows from the formula; this one fails rule 2 ('one defensible number') at the source level. That, not vagueness or category, is why this is the copy to drop. (5) Reveal checked and sound, so it should be carried to the survivor: 3.57*sqrt(30)=19.6 km (21.1 km refracted), both ~20 km; and the 'tall rather than bright' claim is genuine lighthouse doctrine — geographic range is set by height and curvature, luminous range by intensity, and for principal lights the luminous range exceeds the geographic one, so extra brightness buys nothing past the horizon (Britannica, USCG CG-232). (6) CAVEAT for the assembler: this drop is only free if the sibling actually ships. If the sibling is cut for an unrelated reason, the bank loses the horizon fact entirely — in that case reinstate this one with the answer corrected to 4.7 and the source left as 3.57*sqrt(h), or keep 5 and change the source to the refraction-corrected 3.86*sqrt(h).

verdicts.prompt: Greenland, the world's largest island, covers how many million km²?
verdicts.note: 2,166,086 km² confirmed; 2.17M ✓. Position on log 0.2..20: (ln2.17-ln0.2)/(ln20-ln0.2)=2.384/4.605=0.5177, matches 0.518. I recomputed the reveal's ratio instead of trusting 'fourteen times': Africa 30.37M / Greenland 2.17M = 14.0 ✓ — genuinely exact, which is unusual for a Mercator factoid. Duplication check is the real issue here and it comes out clean but crowded: the bank has geography73 (% of Greenland under ice) and geography81 (Greenland's population), and candidate [11] is the Greenland national park. Four Greenland items, all distinct facts, but [11]'s own reasoning leans on this exact 2.17M figure — so if both ship, keep them far apart in the schedule.

verdicts.prompt: The island of Great Britain covers how many km²?
verdicts.note: 209,331 km² per Wikipedia/Ordnance Survey-derived figures; 209,000 ✓. Position on log 20000..2000000: (ln209000-ln20000)/(ln2000000-ln20000)=2.347/4.606=0.5096, matches 0.51. Both reveal claims verified: largest island in Europe and ninth-largest in the world ✓, and Sumatra at 473,481 km² is indeed more than twice its size ✓. UK-centric portability was worth weighing — but Great Britain is a top-ten world island and the bank already carries geography29/30/46 on British subjects, so this is in keeping rather than an outlier.

verdicts.prompt: How many km long is Chile from its northern border to its southern tip?
verdicts.note: Britannica gives 4,300 km (2,700 mi) from the Peru boundary to Cape Horn, and Wikipedia's Geography of Chile independently states 4,300 km long and 175 km average width — two sources agreeing on both the answer and the reveal. Position on linear 1000..8000: (4300-1000)/7000=0.4714, matches 0.471. The pinch-point figure I checked separately: ~90 km is the commonly cited minimum (some sources quote a narrower 64 km at one point), so 'barely 90 km' is the conservative reading and safe. No country-length question in the bank.

verdicts.prompt: What percentage of the Netherlands lies below sea level?
verdicts.note: This one has a trap I checked for specifically, and the candidate is on the right side of it: the 2007 IPCC report wrongly said 55% of the Netherlands is below sea level, and PBL — the cited source — issued a formal correction stating 26% is below sea level while 55% is flood-prone (26% below sea level plus 29% at risk from river flooding). The candidate uses 26% for the answer and 55% for the flood figure, i.e. it reproduces the correction rather than the error. Lowest point −6.76 m ✓ matches 'sits 6.8 m under'. Position on linear 0..60: 26/60=0.4333, matches 0.433. Stable figure, no drift. Nothing similar in the bank.

verdicts.prompt: How many countries are completely surrounded by a single other country?
verdicts.note: Three is unambiguous and I could not find a fourth candidate: Lesotho (South Africa), San Marino and Vatican City (both Italy). The near-misses that could have made this contestable all fail cleanly — Monaco borders the sea, Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan touch two neighbours each, so there is no defensible alternative count. Position on linear 0..15: 3/15=0.20, matches. Reveal verified: Lesotho is the only sovereign state whose entire territory lies above 1,000 m (its lowest point is ~1,400 m), which is a well-documented superlative and not a throwaway. Bank: geography87 counts landlocked countries (44) — related framing, entirely different set.

verdicts.prompt: Java, the world's most populous island, is home to how many million people?
verdicts.note: ~156M confirmed (156.9M for 2024 in independent compilations; BPS mid-2023 lands in the same place), and Java is unarguably the most populous island. Position on log 10..400: (ln156-ln10)/(ln400-ln10)=2.747/3.688=0.7448, matches 0.745. I recomputed both reveal claims: 156M/8.1B = 1.9%, so 'one person in fifty' ✓; Java's 128,297 km² against 148.9M km² of land = 0.086%, so 'a tenth of a percent' ✓; Nusantara/Borneo capital move ✓. I considered failing this on drift since the prompt carries no date, unlike the bank's convention (geography25, geography80 etc. are year-stamped) — but the growth is ~1.7M/year against a log band spanning a factor of forty, which moves the track position by well under a percent per year. Immaterial, so keep rather than churn the prompt.

verdicts.prompt: Singapore's entire national territory covers how many km²?
verdicts.note: Agree with the first verifier, confirmed independently rather than assumed. Answer stands: SingStat's 'Land Area as at June' series gives 734.4 km² (2023), 735.6 (2024), 736.3 (2025), so 735 is within 0.1%; alternate definitions (World Bank land-only 718, CIA total ~728, Wikipedia ~744) span only ~3.5%, invisible on this scale. Log position re-derived from scratch: (ln735-ln50)/(ln20000-ln50) = 2.6879/5.9915 = 0.449, nicely centered. The reveal inversion is real and I re-did the arithmetic against the 581.5 km² 1960 baseline: growth is 152.9 km² = +26.3% of the 1960 area (a quarter), while new land is 152.9/734.4 = 20.8% of today's area (a fifth). The candidate attaches each fraction to the wrong quantity, and '+26% = a fifth' is flatly wrong, so this is not an over-eager fix. Likely origin of the muddle: the Guinness page still cites the stale '+100 km², 17%, with 150 km²/25% as a 2030 target' — a target Singapore already passed. First verifier's corrected reveal checks out on both halves, so I adopt it verbatim rather than churn it. Dedupe re-checked in data/verified.json: only Singapore entry is a population question (6 million, 2024); nearest area items are Monaco 2 km², Vatican 44 ha, metropolitan France 552000 km². No collision. Two minor points I deliberately did not act on: 'entire national territory' doesn't literally say land area, but every reading lands in 718-745 km² so it cannot move an estimate; and the claimed source year 2023 actually maps to 734.4 (735 is the 2024 value), with no schema field available to correct the source string.
verdicts.correctedReveal: About a fifth of it is land that did not exist in 1960: importing sand and reclaiming from the sea has grown the country by roughly a quarter, up from about 580 km².

verdicts.prompt: The Sahara stretches how many km from the Atlantic coast to the Red Sea?
verdicts.note: 4,800 km (3,000 mi) Atlantic to Red Sea, given consistently by Britannica and WorldAtlas. Position on log 1000..30000: (ln4800-ln1000)/(ln30000-ln1000)=1.569/3.401=0.4612, matches 0.461. Reveal: the eleven-country span is the standard count but rests on treating Western Sahara as one of the eleven, which is a disputed territory rather than a country — a pedant could argue ten; the 0..? band makes this harmless since it isn't the answer. The Sahel boundary oscillation is real and documented from satellite records (the southern edge shifted on the order of 100+ km between the early-80s drought and wetter years). Two notes for the author: the hi bound of 30,000 km is slack for a desert width, and this is the bank's second Sahara item after geography57 (area, 9.2M km²) — different measure, so not a duplicate, but schedule them apart.

verdicts.prompt: What percentage of humanity now lives in towns and cities rather than the countryside?
verdicts.note: World Bank reports 57.7% urban for 2024, so 58 ✓. Position on linear 10..90: (58-10)/80=0.60, matches. Reveal both parts verified: the UN puts the 50% crossover at 2007, and Our World in Data puts 1900 at roughly 15-16%, so 'roughly 15%' ✓. I weighed dropping this on drift given the prompt says 'now' with no date — but urbanisation advances ~0.5 percentage points a year against an 80-point band, i.e. 0.6% of the band annually, which will not move a score for years. Keeping, with the drift measured rather than assumed. No urbanisation question in the bank.

verdicts.prompt: What percentage of the world's land area is covered by forest?
verdicts.note: DEDUPE BARRIER ADJUDICATION — this is not a template collision, it is the same question twice. The nature-batch sibling is character-for-character identical (100% word overlap is literal here, not approximate) and carries the identical answer, 31%. There is no reading under which these are two different questions, so one must go, and forest cover is more natural in nature than in geography — the geography copy is the one to drop. Separately, and relevant to whichever copy survives: I opened the FAO source and the figure has moved. FRA 2020 gives 4.06 billion ha = 31%, but FRA 2025 gives 4.14 billion ha and describes it as 'close to one-third (32 percent)' of global land area. 31% is now the superseded number; the surviving sibling should be revised to 32% against FRA 2025 or explicitly anchored to FRA 2020. Bank check: no forest-cover question exists among the 596, so dropping this loses nothing.

verdicts.prompt: How many countries hold formal territorial claims in Antarctica?
verdicts.note: Seven is firm and the set is closed: Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the UK, exactly as the reveal lists. I checked the two ways this could be wrong — the US and Russia reserve a right to claim but have filed none (so they do not raise the count), and Brazil's 'zone of interest' is not a formal claim. Position on linear 0..25: 7/25=0.28, matches. Reveal verified: the Argentine, Chilean and British claims do overlap on the Antarctic Peninsula, and the 1959 treaty's Article IV froze rather than resolved them. Bank: history73 asks the treaty's signing year (1959) — a date, not a count, so no overlap.

verdicts.prompt: The continent of Africa covers how many million km²?
verdicts.note: 30.3-30.37M km² including adjacent islands, consistent across Wikipedia and Britannica; 30 ✓ to within 1%. Position on linear 5..60: (30-5)/55=0.4545, matches 0.455. I checked the reveal's fit claim by arithmetic rather than trusting the familiar graphic: contiguous US 8.1M + China 9.6M + India 3.3M = 21.0M, leaving ~9M km² inside Africa's 30.3M for 'most of Europe' (Europe is 10.2M) — so the claim holds with room to spare. Bank: geography7 (54 African countries) and geography79 (Africa's population) exist; the continent's area is a new fact, and geography3/10/31/38 establish that 'area of X in millions of km²' is already an accepted house pattern.

verdicts.prompt: The London Underground network runs how many km of route?
verdicts.note: 402 km (250 miles) is TfL's own figure and the 55% above-ground share comes from the same statistics page — the reveal and the answer share one authoritative source, which I confirmed rather than assumed. Position on linear 100..1000: (402-100)/900=0.3356, matches 0.336. Eleven lines ✓ as the reasoning states. Portability considered: this is UK-specific, but the Underground is a globally known system and the bank already carries geography30/46 (Thames, Elizabeth Tower) and history76 (world's first underground railway, 1863) — that last one is a date, not a length, so no duplication.

verdicts.prompt: Norway's Lærdal tunnel, the world's longest road tunnel, runs how many metres?
verdicts.note: 24,510 m confirmed by Guinness ('Longest road tunnel') and Statens vegvesen-derived sources; still the record in 2026 — I checked the runner-up, China's Zhongnanshan at ~18 km, so the superlative is not close to falling. Position on log 2000..100000: (ln24500-ln2000)/(ln100000-ln2000)=2.505/3.912=0.640, matches 0.64. Reveal verified: three lit rock caverns spaced roughly every 6 km, specifically to break the monotony, and 24.5 km at tunnel speeds is ~18-20 minutes ✓. Bank: geography90 is the Gotthard Base Tunnel (57 km, rail) — the reasoning here even uses it as an anchor; road versus rail keeps them distinct, but they are close enough that I would not run them in the same week.

verdicts.prompt: The Three Gorges Dam wall stands how many metres above its rock foundation?
verdicts.note: 181 m above the rock foundation, with a crest elevation of 185 m — the prompt asks for exactly the right one of those two numbers, which is the failure mode I was looking for here and it avoids it. Position on linear 50..350: (181-50)/300=0.4367, matches 0.437. Reveal verified: the 0.06-microsecond day-lengthening is NASA's (Benjamin Fong Chao's) calculation and is quoted at that value, not rounded up into something splashier. No dam question in the bank.

verdicts.prompt: The Millau Viaduct's roadway crosses how many metres above the river Tarn below?
verdicts.note: 270 m deck height above the Tarn confirmed by ICE and Wikipedia. Position on linear 50..500: (270-50)/450=0.4889, matches 0.489. Reveal checked against the bank's own data for internal consistency: the highest mast reaches 343 m, and geography12 puts the Eiffel Tower at 330 m, so 'taller than the Eiffel Tower' is true by the game's own numbers — a rare case where the reveal can be validated against an existing question rather than only externally. Bank: geography91 is the longest bridge by total length (Danyang-Kunshan) and candidate [43] is the longest suspension span — three bridge questions, three different superlatives, no duplication.

verdicts.prompt: The Panama Canal's locks lift ships how many metres above sea level?
verdicts.note: 26 m (85 ft) to Gatun Lake, stated by the Panama Canal Authority and matching Wikipedia's lock articles. Position on linear 0..80: 26/80=0.325, matches. Reveal verified: the ~200 million litres per transit is the standard 52-million-gallon figure converted correctly (197M L), it is gravity-fed with no pumps, and the 2023-24 drought restrictions on daily transits are documented. Reasoning's 'three lock steps per side' also checks (Gatun's three, versus Pedro Miguel's one plus Miraflores' two). Bank crowding is the only concern: geography41 (canal length) and history105 (years to build) already exist, making this the third Panama Canal item — distinct fact, but flagging the concentration.

verdicts.prompt: The world's longest dead-straight railway, across Australia's Nullarbor, runs how many km without a curve?
verdicts.note: 478 km confirmed by Guinness ('Longest railroad straight') with the endpoints specified — Mile 496 near Nurina/Loongana WA to Mile 793 near Ooldea/Watson SA — which is the kind of corroboration that makes a superlative safe. Position on log 100..3000: (ln478-ln100)/(ln3000-ln100)=1.564/3.401=0.4599, matches 0.46. Reveal verified: 'nullarbor' is coined from Latin for 'no trees' ✓, the line was completed in 1917 ✓, limestone plateau ✓. No straight-line or Australian rail question in the bank; geography55 (Trans-Siberian) and geography92 (Indian rail network) are different measures entirely.

verdicts.prompt: Australia's Highway 1 loops the entire continent. How many km long is it?
verdicts.note: 14,500 km (9,000 mi), confirmed as the world's longest national highway ahead of the Trans-Siberian Highway (~11,000 km) and Trans-Canada (8,030 km) — I checked the runners-up so the superlative isn't taken on faith. Position on log 2000..50000: (ln14500-ln2000)/(ln50000-ln2000)=1.981/3.219=0.6154, matches 0.615. Reveal verified: Highway 1 reaches every state and territory capital — Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Perth, Adelaide, Hobart, Darwin — except inland Canberra ✓. No highway-length question in the bank.

verdicts.prompt: The deepest mine on Earth, Mponeng in South Africa, reaches how many metres below the surface?
verdicts.note: I opened the Guinness record page itself rather than trusting the citation: it states the depth as '4 kilometre(s)' and notes operations had reached 3.9 km by 2012 with later expansion below the 4-km mark. So 4,000 m is the cited source's own headline number. Position on linear 500..5000: (4000-500)/4500=0.7778, matches 0.778. I looked hard for a >10% source disagreement, since depth measures differ (3,891 m below datum for the deepest shaft, workings past 4 km, 2,062 m below sea level) — the shaft-versus-workings spread is under 3%, and the sea-level figure is a different quantity the prompt does not ask for. Reveal verified: virgin rock temperature is quoted near 60-66 °C and the mine runs a slurry-ice cooling system by the tonne. Bank: geography95 (Arsenalna metro station, 105.5 m) is the nearest depth question and is two orders of magnitude away.

verdicts.prompt: What percentage of the world's earthquakes strike around the Pacific Ring of Fire?
verdicts.note: I concur with the first verifier, having re-checked each leg rather than assuming it. (1) The graded value survives: 90% is USGS's own published figure (USGS posted 'Approximately 90% of the world's earthquakes...' verbatim), and it is the standard number across NatGeo, Britannica and Wikipedia, usually paired with '81% of the world's largest earthquakes'. Source attribution 'US Geological Survey' is accurate. (2) The companion 75%-of-active-volcanoes figure is the standard co-citation and survives, though with a wobble worth noting: USGS's own 'Volcanoes of the United States' text says only 'more than half of the world's active volcanoes above sea level', and Wikipedia's Ring of Fire article counts ~750-915 active-or-dormant, 'around two-thirds of the world total'. The reveal's 'about 75%' is the most widely cited version and is hedged, so it stands - but it is not as ironclad as the 90%. (3) The reveal's mechanism is genuinely wrong and the fix is warranted. Wikipedia's plate-by-plate breakdown confirms the belt is not the Pacific plate alone: Nazca, Cocos and Antarctic subduct beneath South America, Cocos beneath the Caribbean in Central America, Juan de Fuca beneath North America, and the Philippine Sea plate beneath Eurasia at Japan/Taiwan/the Philippines. The Pacific plate proper drives only the Aleutian-Kamchatka-Kuril and southwest-Pacific arcs. (4) I re-verified the first verifier's replacement wording and it is correct: 'the ocean plates ringing the Pacific are being shoved under their neighbours' covers every listed subducting plate without naming the wrong one. Minor residual imprecision - the belt also contains transform segments (San Andreas, Queen Charlotte) that are not subduction - but those are non-volcanic and a small share of the arc, so the 'simply the map of' framing remains a fair simplification and I would not add hedging noise for it. I adopt the correction verbatim rather than churn it. (5) Independent checks the first verifier did not raise, all passing: range position 0.875 on linear 20..100 is inside band, though the first verifier is right that the top end is doing little work; the reasoning path (Japan, Indonesia, Philippines, Chile, Alaska, New Zealand dominate the quake news) is a legitimate route to a high estimate and does not leak the exact number; no ambiguity in the prompt's wording ('earthquakes' unqualified reads as count, which is what the 90% measures); no portability problem since the figure is a stable textbook constant, not a drifting statistic. No grounds for a drop - this is a good question with one false clause in the reveal.
verdicts.correctedReveal: The same belt carries about 75% of the world's active volcanoes — both are simply the map of where the ocean plates ringing the Pacific are being shoved under their neighbours.

verdicts.prompt: Climb how many metres before the air pressure falls to half its sea-level value?
verdicts.note: Checked against the International Standard Atmosphere rather than a secondary source: the 500 hPa level sits at ~5,570 m, and the widely used teaching figure is that pressure halves roughly every 5,500 m — so 5,500 is correct and conservatively rounded. Position on linear 1000..15000: (5500-1000)/14000=0.3214, matches 0.321. Reveal verified by computation: ISA pressure at 8,849 m is ~314 hPa, about 31% of sea level, so 'about a third' ✓; and the death zone begins at 8,000 m, leaving 849 m of Everest above it, so 'the last 800 m' ✓. More physics than geography, but the bank already mixes (space44, everyday93), and there is no atmospheric-pressure-versus-altitude question among the 596.

verdicts.prompt: The Alps run through how many countries?
verdicts.note: Eight, and I checked the definitional risk that could have sunk this: the count depends on including Monaco, which has no genuine alpine terrain. It survives because both the cited source and the general reference agree — the Alpine Convention is a treaty between exactly those eight states (Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Liechtenstein, Monaco, Slovenia, Switzerland), and Wikipedia's Alps article lists the same eight. A player reasoning to six or seven still scores well on a 0..20 linear band, so the definitional wobble cannot produce an angry email. Position: 8/20=0.40, matches. Reveal names all eight and flags the two easy-to-forget micro-states ✓. Bank: geography76 counts Danube countries (10) — same shape of question, different feature; acceptable, but not the same week.

verdicts.prompt: How many cities passed 10 million people in the UN's 2018 global count?
verdicts.note: 33 megacities confirmed from UN DESA World Urbanization Prospects 2018, with the 'one in eight people' framing from the same release. Position on linear 0..100: 33/100=0.33, matches. Reveal verified against the same source: New York and Tokyo were the only two in 1950 ✓, and the 2030 projection is 43 ✓. Notably this is the one candidate in the batch that is fully drift-proof by construction — the prompt anchors to a named, dated count, so a later revision cannot invalidate it. Bank: geography25 gives Greater Tokyo's population; a count of cities is a different quantity.

verdicts.prompt: Singapore to New York, the longest scheduled nonstop flight, is how many km in a straight line?
verdicts.note: The number is exact and safe: 15,349 km great-circle (9,537 mi; 8,288 nmi) for SQ23/24, confirmed on the route's own reference page. Position on log 2000..30000: (ln15349-ln2000)/(ln30000-ln2000)=2.038/2.708=0.7526, matches 0.753. Reveal verified too — SQ24 routinely flies ~17,250 km over the Pacific to ride the jet stream, so 'can cover 17,000 km' ✓. What fails is the superlative in the prompt. Searching current coverage, SQ23 holds the title today but Singapore's A350-900ULRs are due to be superseded in 2026 by the longer-ranged A350-1000ULRs built for Qantas, whose Sydney-London Project Sunrise service would take the record. For a daily game with a long shelf life, a superlative with a known expiry date is a complaint waiting to happen — and it is free to remove, because the distance itself never changes. Bank note: geography6, geography13 and geography34 are already great-circle distance questions, making this the fourth; distinct city pair, but the category is getting formulaic.
verdicts.correctedPrompt: Singapore to New York, one of the world's longest nonstop flights, is how many km in a straight line?

verdicts.prompt: The world's longest suspension bridge span, over Turkey's Dardanelles, measures how many metres?
verdicts.note: 2,023 m main span for the 1915 Çanakkale Bridge, opened 18 March 2022, confirmed across Dezeen, ENR and the contractor's own project page. Position on linear 800..2500: (2023-800)/1700=0.7194, matches 0.719. Reveal verified and slightly richer than claimed: the 2,023 m span marks the 2023 republic centenary ✓, and the 318 m towers are the tallest of any suspension bridge ✓ (they also encode 18 March, the Gallipoli commemoration and opening date — a bonus the reveal doesn't need). The reasoning's anchors check out too: Golden Gate 1,280 m, Akashi Kaikyō 1,991 m. Bank: geography91 is the longest bridge by total length — different superlative, no collision.

verdicts.prompt: How many km of the Channel Tunnel actually run beneath the sea?
verdicts.note: Getlink/Eurotunnel's own material gives the undersea section as 38 km (25 miles) out of 50.5 km total, with 37 km appearing in some phrasings — a 2.6% spread. Position on linear 5..80: (38-5)/75=0.44, matches. Reveal verified from the same operator source: bored at an average 40 m below the seabed, following the chalk marl layer, and the geology genuinely drove the alignment. One adjacency worth naming: the bank's geography27 asks the narrowest England-France sea gap (33 km), and this candidate's own reasoning uses that number as its anchor — a player who has seen geography27 will answer near 33 and score well here. The questions are genuinely different (strait width versus tunnel length under water), so not a duplicate, but they should not run close together.

verdicts.prompt: The world's largest airport by land area, at Dammam in Saudi Arabia, covers how many km²?
verdicts.note: Answer and range verified independently and stand: Guinness 'Largest airport (area)' gives King Fahd International, Saudi Arabia, 780 km², record set 12 Dec 2011 (first verifier's '2013' is a harmless slip). Log position (ln78/ln500)=0.701, off both rails; some sources cite 776 km², which lands at the same place on the scale. No airport question in the 685-entry bank (only an incidental El Alto mention inside a La Paz reveal). BUT the first verifier accepted the reveal's Bahrain comparison by leaning on Guinness's own wording instead of checking Bahrain today, and that comparison is now false. Guinness wrote 'bigger than the nearby country of Bahrain' in 2011, when Bahrain was ~765 km²; continuous land reclamation has since pushed Bahrain to 786.8 km² (Wikipedia infobox) and 787.79 km² (Survey and Land Registration Bureau's latest official survey). So the 780 km² airport is now SMALLER than Bahrain — the reveal asserts the reverse as present fact, and one lookup breaks it. The first verifier said it was 'close enough that I checked it rather than assuming', but close fell on the wrong side. Second half of the reveal is fine: 36.75 km² utilized (airport's own figure, echoed by Wikipedia) / 780 = 4.7%, so 'about 5%' ✓. Corrected reveal keeps the country-scale flavour, states parity rather than a false inequality, and turns the reclamation fact into the hook.
verdicts.correctedReveal: The site is about the size of the whole neighbouring country of Bahrain — which has only just edged past it by reclaiming land from the sea — yet barely 5% of the airport is actually built on; the rest is empty desert inside the fence.

verdicts.prompt: In midwinter, roughly how many people are living on the whole Antarctic continent?
verdicts.note: ~1,000 in winter rising to ~5,000 in summer is the consistent figure across Wikipedia's Demographics of Antarctica and expedition/COMNAP-derived sources. Position on log 100..50000: (ln1000-ln100)/(ln50000-ln100)=2.303/6.215=0.3705, matches 0.371. Reveal verified: the fivefold swing is right, and Guinness carries it as a formal record ('Highest seasonal population difference'), so 'the biggest seasonal population swing anywhere on Earth' is a documented claim rather than a flourish. Reasoning's ~40 year-round stations also checks against COMNAP's station count. Year-to-year variation of a hundred or so people is nothing against a log band spanning 500×. Fifth Antarctica item in circulation counting the bank's geography66/history73 and candidate [28] — all distinct.

verdicts.prompt: Continental shelves end at roughly what water depth, in metres, before the seabed plunges away?
verdicts.note: 140 m is the standard global average for the shelf break, with 133 m and 135 m appearing in other references — a ~5% spread, inside tolerance, and the individual shelf break ranges from 20 to 550 m which the word 'roughly' correctly signals. Position on linear 20..500: (140-20)/480=0.25, matches. Reveal verified: Last Glacial Maximum sea level stood ~120-125 m lower, which is precisely why the break sits at a 'remarkably uniform' depth — the reveal's causal link is the one the literature actually makes. 'Nearly every shelf was dry land' is slightly strong given the break averages 140 m against a 120 m drop, but 'nearly' carries it. Bank: geography56/nature24 (Challenger Deep) and nature85 (mean ocean depth) are the neighbours, both far deeper and distinct.

verdicts.prompt: China's Beijing-Shanghai high-speed line runs how many km?
verdicts.note: 1,318 km confirmed via the line's own reference page and the builder CREC. Position on linear 300..3000: (1318-300)/2700=0.377, matches. Reveal verified by computation: 1,140 km of the 1,318 km is bridge/viaduct = 86.5%, so 'more than four fifths' ✓ (a related source gives 88% for bridges plus tunnels, consistent); fastest scheduled runs are ~4h18m-4h30m, so 'about four and a half hours' ✓. Bank: geography92 (India's rail network, 68,000 km) and geography55 (Trans-Siberian, 9,289 km) are the other rail-length questions and are an order of magnitude away.

verdicts.prompt: How many hours separate the world's earliest time zone from the latest?
verdicts.note: 26 hours, from UTC+14 (Kiribati's Line Islands) to UTC−12, confirmed against the IANA-derived zone listings. Position on linear 12..30: (26-12)/18=0.7778, matches 0.778. I verified the reveal's three-dates claim by working the clock rather than trusting it: at 10:00 UTC, UTC−12 reads 22:00 the previous day, UTC reads today, and UTC+14 reads 00:00 tomorrow — three calendar dates coexisting, and the window runs from 10:00 to 12:00 UTC, exactly the two hours claimed. Baker Island is correctly placed at UTC−12 (Howland shares it); both are uninhabited US territories, which is why the reveal's phrasing 'sits at' rather than 'lives at' is right. Bank: geography77 counts Russia's time zones (11) — a per-country count, not the global spread.

questions.prompt: How many litres of blood are in the body of an average adult?
questions.reveal: Blood is about 7% of body weight, and roughly a fifth of it can be lost before blood pressure collapses — which is why a donation of under half a litre barely registers.
questions.reasoningPath: A person is ~70 kg and mostly water. Blood is clearly a small fraction of that — not 50 litres, not half a litre. A bucket of blood is the horror-film image; the real figure is a few large drink bottles, so around 5 litres.

questions.prompt: What percentage of an adult human body is water?
questions.reveal: Newborns run closer to 75%, and fat tissue holds far less water than muscle — so the figure falls with age and with body fat.
questions.reasoningPath: Cells are mostly water, and blood, lymph and the fluid between cells add more. But bone, fat and protein are not water, so it cannot be 90%. Somewhere well above half and well below three-quarters — about 60%.

questions.prompt: An adult human brain weighs about how many grams?
questions.reveal: Floating in cerebrospinal fluid it effectively weighs only about 25 grams — without that buoyancy it would crush its own lower blood vessels.
questions.reasoningPath: The brain fills most of a skull you can cup in two hands, so its volume is roughly 1.3-1.5 litres. Brain tissue is about as dense as water, so the mass is close to that in kilograms: about 1.4 kg.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many hairs grow on an average human scalp?
questions.reveal: About a hundred are shed every day, and each follicle runs on its own independent clock — which is why hair thins gradually rather than falling out in synchronised waves.
questions.reasoningPath: A scalp is roughly 600 cm² of skin. Look closely at a patch of scalp: hairs sit maybe a millimetre or two apart, so on the order of 100-200 per square centimetre. Multiply and you get around 100,000.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the air you breathe out is carbon dioxide?
questions.reveal: Exhaled air still contains around 16% oxygen — barely a fifth less than the air going in — which is exactly why mouth-to-mouth resuscitation works at all.
questions.reasoningPath: Incoming air is 0.04% CO2, and one pass through the lungs raises it a lot but not to anything like pure CO2 — you would suffocate instantly. It has to be a low single-digit percentage: about 4%.

questions.prompt: Averaged over every adult on Earth, how many kilograms does a person weigh?
questions.source: Walpole et al., BMC Public Health 2012
questions.reveal: North America holds 6% of the world's adults but a third of the world's human biomass; the average adult there is close to 81 kg.
questions.reasoningPath: A European or North American adult averages roughly 75-80 kg, but Asia holds most of the world's people and averages closer to 58 kg. Weight the two and the global figure lands in the low 60s.

questions.prompt: Filled to capacity, how many litres of air do an adult's lungs hold?
questions.reveal: About 1.2 litres can never be pushed out — the residual volume that stops the lungs from collapsing flat and sticking shut.
questions.reasoningPath: A quiet breath moves about half a litre, and a full deep breath feels like maybe eight or ten times that. The chest cavity is a few litres of space shared with the heart. That points to around 6 litres.

questions.prompt: How many millimetres across is an adult human eyeball?
questions.reveal: It reaches nearly adult size by age three, which is why children's eyes look so oversized for their faces.
questions.reasoningPath: The visible white of the eye is about a centimetre wide, and most of the ball is hidden in the socket. A grape is a fair model. So roughly 2 to 3 centimetres — call it 24 mm.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many light-sensitive cells are packed into one human retina?
questions.reveal: Only about 6 million are cones. They crowd into a patch the size of a pinhead, and everything you see outside that patch is effectively colour-blind and blurry.
questions.reasoningPath: A digital camera sensor of similar physical size holds tens of millions of pixels, and the eye out-resolves a phone camera. Cells are a few micrometres across on a retina of a few square centimetres. That lands around 100 million.

questions.prompt: How many litres of fluid do the kidneys filter out of the blood in a day?
questions.reveal: Over 99% of it is reabsorbed before it leaves; the body's entire plasma volume passes through the filter roughly sixty times a day.
questions.reasoningPath: A quarter of the heart's 5 litres a minute goes to the kidneys, and about a fifth of that plasma gets filtered — around 0.12 L/min. Over 1,440 minutes that is well over a hundred litres.

questions.prompt: Human vision is most sensitive to light of what wavelength, in nanometres?
questions.reveal: That is yellow-green, which is why high-visibility jackets are that colour rather than red. In darkness the peak shifts about 50 nm towards blue.
questions.reasoningPath: Visible light runs roughly 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). The eye evolved under sunlight, whose peak output is in the middle of that band, and green is the colour that looks brightest at equal power — so around 550 nm.

questions.prompt: What is the average birth weight of a human baby, in kilograms?
questions.reveal: Babies typically shed up to a tenth of it in the first days after birth and take about a fortnight to win it back.
questions.reasoningPath: A newborn is the length of a forearm and roughly the heft of a large bag of flour or a full 3-litre bottle. Under 2.5 kg is officially low birth weight and over 4 kg is called large — so the middle sits near 3.3 kg.

questions.prompt: A landmark 2007 recording study found the average person speaks how many words a day?
questions.reveal: The study set out to test the claim that women talk three times as much as men. Men averaged 15,669 words a day; women 16,215 — a difference too small to matter.
questions.reasoningPath: People speak at roughly 130 words a minute. Nobody talks continuously, but a couple of hours of actual speaking across a whole day is plausible: 120 minutes times 130 is about 16,000 words.

questions.prompt: Non-vintage Champagne must rest on its yeast lees for a legal minimum of how many months?
questions.reveal: Vintage Champagne must wait three years. The dead yeast cells slowly break down and release the compounds behind that brioche-and-toast smell.
questions.reasoningPath: The rule has to be long enough to separate Champagne from cheap sparkling wine, but short enough that a house can sell most of its production yearly. That rules out weeks and rules out a decade — a bit over a year fits.

questions.prompt: To be labelled extra virgin, olive oil's free acidity must stay below what percentage?
questions.source: International Olive Council trade standard; EU Reg. 2568/91
questions.reveal: Free acidity is tasteless. It is a forensic marker of bruised fruit or a slow trip to the mill, not a flavour you could pick out of a spoonful.
questions.reasoningPath: The limit has to be a small fraction — oil that was several percent acid would be rancid and inedible. Ordinary virgin oil is allowed up to 2%, so the top grade must be well under that: under 1%.

questions.prompt: EU law says a bar can only be called chocolate above what percentage of dry cocoa solids?
questions.reveal: Milk chocolate needs only 25%, and the directive also sets floors for cocoa butter and non-fat solids separately, so a maker cannot hit the total with cheap fat alone.
questions.reasoningPath: Bars marketed as 'dark 70%' are clearly above the bar, and sweet everyday chocolate is well below 70% yet still legally chocolate. The threshold must sit in between, closer to the low end: around a third.

questions.prompt: Household vinegar is what percentage acetic acid?
questions.reveal: Cleaning vinegar is roughly double that, and above about 20% acetic acid the liquid burns skin on contact.
questions.reasoningPath: Vinegar is drinkable and mostly water — you can swallow a spoonful without harm — so the acid is a small fraction. But it is sharp enough to pickle and preserve, so not a trace either. A few percent.

questions.prompt: What percentage of whole cow's milk is fat?
questions.reveal: Semi-skimmed sits near 1.7% and skimmed under 0.3%. Human milk is fattier than whole cow's milk, at roughly 4%.
questions.reasoningPath: Milk looks and pours like water, so fat cannot be a large share. Cream separates out as a thin layer on top of a whole bottle — a few percent at most. Around 3 to 4%.

questions.prompt: The shell accounts for what percentage of a chicken egg's total weight?
questions.reveal: It is nearly pure calcium carbonate, and a laying hen has to move about 2 g of calcium a day to build one — far more than is circulating in her entire bloodstream at any moment.
questions.reasoningPath: A large egg is about 57 g and the shell is thin and brittle — you can crush it in a fist. Cracked shells feel like a few grams in the hand, so roughly a tenth of the whole egg.

questions.prompt: How many grams of tea are in a standard teabag?
questions.reveal: Loose-leaf brewing uses two to three times as much per cup, because whole leaves need room to unfurl and give up less flavour per gram than the dust in a bag.
questions.reasoningPath: A teabag is flat, small and almost weightless in the hand — noticeably less than a teaspoon of sugar, which is about 4 g. A pinch or two of dry leaf: around 2 g.

questions.prompt: The Italian standard for a single espresso specifies how many grams of ground coffee?
questions.reveal: The same standard fixes 25 mL in the cup and 25 seconds of extraction. Despite its reputation, one shot carries less caffeine than a mug of filter coffee.
questions.reasoningPath: The puck that knocks out of a portafilter is a thin disc a few centimetres across — visibly less than a tablespoon of grounds. A tablespoon of coffee is around 5-7 g, so a single dose is about 7 g.

questions.prompt: An espresso machine forces water through the grounds at what pressure, in bar?
questions.reveal: That is roughly four times a car tyre. Before pump machines arrived in 1961, baristas generated it by hand, compressing a heavy spring with a lever.
questions.reasoningPath: Mains water is around 3 bar and will not push through packed grounds. A car tyre is about 2 bar, a bicycle tyre 8. Espresso needs more than plumbing but is contained by a hand-clamped handle, so single digits: about 9 bar.

questions.prompt: What percentage of an arabica coffee bean's weight is caffeine?
questions.reveal: Robusta beans carry roughly double, part of why they taste harsher — caffeine itself is bitter, and the plant makes it as an insecticide.
questions.reasoningPath: A mug of coffee uses about 10 g of grounds and delivers roughly 100 mg of caffeine, and not all of it extracts. So caffeine is on the order of 1% of the bean, not 10%.

questions.prompt: EFSA puts the safe daily caffeine intake for a healthy adult at how many milligrams?
questions.source: EFSA Scientific Opinion on the safety of caffeine, 2015
questions.reveal: The same opinion caps a single dose at 200 mg and halves the daily figure during pregnancy. A lethal dose is roughly twenty-five times the daily limit.
questions.reasoningPath: A mug of coffee is about 95 mg. Regulators would not declare one cup a day the ceiling, nor ten. Three or four cups is the familiar 'moderate' advice, so roughly 400 mg.

questions.prompt: A 330 mL beer at 5% ABV contains how many grams of pure alcohol?
questions.reveal: Alcohol is lighter than water at 0.79 g per mL, so the grams always come out below the millilitres. The liver clears roughly this much in an hour.
questions.reasoningPath: 5% of 330 mL is 16.5 mL of ethanol. Alcohol is a bit lighter than water, so multiply by about 0.8: roughly 13 g.

questions.prompt: Egg white begins to set at what temperature, in Celsius?
questions.source: Harold McGee, On Food and Cooking
questions.reveal: Yolk needs about 70 °C. Hold an egg between the two and you get the Japanese onsen egg: liquid white around a set, custardy yolk — the reverse of a soft boil.
questions.reasoningPath: Egg cooks well below boiling — a custard sets long before 100 °C, and body temperature obviously does nothing. Hot tap water at 55 °C leaves it raw. So somewhere in the low 60s.

questions.prompt: Inside a pressure cooker at one bar above atmospheric, water boils at what temperature in Celsius?
questions.reveal: That same 121 °C is the standard for autoclave sterilisation: fifteen minutes at that temperature kills botulism spores, which survive ordinary boiling indefinitely.
questions.reasoningPath: Doubling the pressure raises the boiling point, but not dramatically — a pressure cooker cuts cooking times to about a third, not to nothing. Twenty degrees or so above 100 °C, so about 120 °C.

questions.prompt: How many litres of seawater must you evaporate to get one kilogram of sea salt?
questions.source: computed from average ocean salinity, 35 g/L
questions.reveal: Solar salt pans take months and never run dry: the last liquor is drained off and discarded, because the bitter magnesium salts crystallise only at the very end.
questions.reasoningPath: Seawater is about 3.5% salt by weight, or 35 grams per litre. To reach 1,000 grams you need 1,000 divided by 35, which is a bit under 30 litres.

questions.prompt: How many days does a chicken egg take to hatch?
questions.reveal: The chick punctures an internal air pocket and starts breathing about a day before it breaks the shell — you can hear it cheeping from inside.
questions.reasoningPath: Birds develop far faster than mammals but a chick emerges fully feathered and walking, so it is not days. Farmers talk about it in weeks, and a hen cannot sit for months without starving. Three weeks.

questions.prompt: A modern commercial laying hen produces how many eggs in a year?
questions.reveal: Her wild ancestor, the red junglefowl, lays 10 to 15 eggs a year in a couple of clutches. Continuous laying is entirely a product of breeding and controlled lighting.
questions.reasoningPath: An egg takes about 25 hours to build, so the physical ceiling is roughly one a day, or 365. Hens take breaks and moult, so a bit under that: around 300.

questions.prompt: How many litres of water go into producing one kilogram of beef, on the global average?
questions.reveal: Almost all of it is rain falling on pasture and feed crops rather than water drawn from taps or rivers. Chicken comes in at about 4,300 litres by the same accounting.
questions.reasoningPath: A beef animal eats several tonnes of grain and grass over years, and growing a kilogram of grain takes on the order of 1,500 litres. With roughly ten kilograms of feed per kilogram of meat, the total lands in the tens of thousands.

questions.prompt: Finland drinks more coffee than anywhere else: how many kilograms per person per year?
questions.reveal: That works out at roughly four cups a day for every man, woman and child. Finnish collective labour agreements have written coffee breaks into working conditions for decades.
questions.reasoningPath: A cup uses about 7 grams of coffee. Four cups a day is 28 g, times 365 is around 10 kg. Finns are famous for drinking far more than most, so the low teens fits.

questions.prompt: How many kilograms of food does the average person throw away at home each year?
questions.reveal: Households account for 60% of all food waste worldwide, and the per-person figure differs by only about 7 kg between rich and middle-income countries.
questions.reasoningPath: A person eats roughly 1.5 kg of food a day, about 550 kg a year. Household waste is a meaningful slice but not most of it — call it 10-15%, which lands near 70-80 kg.

questions.prompt: How many kilograms of meat does the average person on Earth eat in a year?
questions.reveal: Poultry overtook pork as the world's most-produced meat in the late 2010s, and the global average has roughly doubled since 1960.
questions.reasoningPath: A daily portion of meat is around 150 g, which is 55 kg a year — but a large share of the world eats meat only occasionally. Weighting for that pulls the global average to the low 40s.

questions.prompt: How thick is ordinary kitchen aluminium foil, in micrometres?
questions.reveal: The dull side is not a coating. Foil is rolled two sheets at a time, so the faces pressed together come out matte and the faces touching the rollers come out shiny.
questions.reasoningPath: Printer paper is about 0.1 mm and foil is obviously several times thinner than that — thin enough to tear on a fingernail and to let light through when stretched. So a few hundredths of a millimetre: around 15 µm.

questions.prompt: How thick is a single sheet of ordinary 80 gsm printer paper, in micrometres?
questions.reveal: It is why the folding problem gets impossible so fast: seven folds already stack 128 sheets into a 1.3 cm slab you are trying to bend in half.
questions.reasoningPath: A 500-sheet ream is about 5 cm tall. Divide 50 mm by 500 and each sheet is a tenth of a millimetre — 100 micrometres.

questions.prompt: One cubic metre of ordinary concrete weighs how many kilograms?
questions.reveal: The stone and sand do most of the work: cement is only about a seventh of the mix by weight, and water another tenth.
questions.reasoningPath: Concrete is mostly rock, and rock sinks in water — it is denser than 1,000 kg per cubic metre but nothing like steel at 7,850. Common stone is about 2.5 times water, so roughly 2,400 kg.

questions.prompt: One litre of olive oil weighs how many grams?
questions.source: IOC physical-chemical characteristics of olive oil
questions.reveal: Every edible oil lands within a few percent of this figure, which is precisely why oil floats on water and a vinaigrette separates the moment you stop shaking it.
questions.reasoningPath: Oil floats on water, so a litre must weigh less than 1,000 g. But it floats only just — it sits as a thin layer rather than beading high — so it is close: about 900 g.

questions.prompt: An LED bulb sold as a '60-watt equivalent' emits how many lumens?
questions.reveal: The incandescent it replaces turned about 95% of its 60 watts into heat. The LED makes the same light from roughly 8 watts.
questions.reasoningPath: An old filament bulb produced roughly 13 lumens per watt. Multiply by 60 and you get about 800 lumens — the number now printed on every replacement bulb box.

questions.prompt: A British kettle on a 13-amp, 230-volt socket draws close to how many watts?
questions.reveal: North American sockets deliver half the voltage, so kettles there cap out near 1,500 W and take twice as long — one reason the electric kettle never took hold.
questions.reasoningPath: Power is volts times amps. 230 multiplied by 13 is just under 3,000, and a kettle is designed to use the whole circuit — it is the hungriest thing in most kitchens.

questions.prompt: European standards call for how many lux of light on an office desk?
questions.reveal: An overcast day outdoors delivers around 1,000 lux and direct sun over 50,000. Indoor lighting is far dimmer than it feels, because the eye adapts.
questions.reasoningPath: A living room feels comfortable at a hundred-odd lux and an operating theatre needs tens of thousands. Desk work is closer to the domestic end but brighter than a lounge — a few hundred lux.

questions.prompt: EU law says a car tyre is worn out below how many millimetres of tread depth?
questions.reveal: Tyres are moulded with wear bars standing exactly that proud of the groove floor, so the tyre tells you itself when it is finished. Wet braking distance at the limit can be half again as long as on new tread.
questions.reasoningPath: A new tyre's grooves are about 8 mm deep and a bald tyre is flat. The legal cut-off has to leave some channel for water but be shallow enough that most drivers reach it — a millimetre or two.

questions.prompt: How many millimetres across is a compact disc?
questions.reveal: The story told for decades is that the size was set so a disc would hold Beethoven's Ninth without a break; Philips had originally wanted 115 mm.
questions.reasoningPath: A CD sits comfortably in a spread palm and slots into a jewel case a hand's width across. That is around 12 cm — noticeably smaller than a vinyl single at 17 cm.

questions.prompt: A classic black-and-white football is stitched from how many panels?
questions.reveal: Twelve black pentagons and twenty white hexagons — a truncated icosahedron, the same shape as the carbon molecule that won the 1996 Nobel Prize in chemistry.
questions.reasoningPath: Picture the ball: the black patches are pentagons and there are twelve of them, one at each corner of a hidden dodecahedron. The white hexagons fill the gaps between, about twenty. Together, 32.

questions.prompt: Paper supposedly cannot be folded in half more than seven times. How many folds did a US student manage in 2002?
questions.reveal: Britney Gallivan first derived the formula for how much paper a given number of folds requires, then laid out a single 1.2 km roll of toilet paper down a shopping-mall corridor to prove it.
questions.reasoningPath: Each fold doubles the thickness and halves the length, so the difficulty compounds brutally. Beating seven is a real achievement but the doubling means twenty is physically absurd — the record has to be low double figures.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many litres of helium does it take to lift one kilogram off the ground?
questions.source: computed from air (1.225 g/L) and helium (0.179 g/L) densities
questions.reveal: A litre of helium lifts only about a gram, because the lift is the difference between air and helium, not the helium's own lightness. Hydrogen improves on it by just 8%.
questions.reasoningPath: A cubic metre of air weighs about 1.2 kg; the same volume of helium weighs about 0.18 kg. The difference, roughly 1 kg, is the lift. So you need close to a full cubic metre — around 1,000 litres.

questions.prompt: One cubic metre of air at 20 °C can hold at most how many grams of water vapour?
questions.reveal: The capacity roughly doubles for every 10 °C of warming, which is why a cold window pane pulls water straight out of warm room air.
questions.reasoningPath: A room of 30 cubic metres at full saturation would not yield a bucket of water — dehumidifiers pull out well under a litre a day from a damp room. That means grams, not kilograms, per cubic metre: roughly a tablespoon's worth.

questions.prompt: A tap dripping once a second wastes how many litres of water in a day?
questions.reveal: Over a year that is more than 1,500 litres. A leak you can actually hear from another room is usually running several times faster than one drop a second.
questions.reasoningPath: About 20 drops make a millilitre, so one drop is 0.05 mL. A day holds 86,400 seconds, so 86,400 drops times 0.05 mL is about 4,300 mL — a bit over four litres.

questions.prompt: European workplace rules require hearing protection above what noise level, in decibels?
questions.reveal: Decibels are logarithmic, so safe exposure halves with every 3 dB: eight hours at 85 dB becomes about fifteen minutes at 100 dB.
questions.reasoningPath: Conversation runs about 60 dB and is obviously harmless. A rock concert at 110 dB clearly is not. The regulatory line sits nearer the loud-machinery end — a busy factory floor, around 85 dB.

questions.prompt: Climbing a 10-metre staircase, a 70 kg person does how many kilojoules of work against gravity?
questions.reveal: That is under two kilocalories — roughly a third of a single peanut. Muscle is only about a quarter efficient, so the body spends four times as much, nearly all of it lost as heat.
questions.reasoningPath: Work against gravity is mass times gravity times height: 70 × 9.8 × 10. That is about 6,900 joules, or roughly 7 kilojoules.

verdicts.prompt: How many litres of blood are in the body of an average adult?
verdicts.note: CONFIRM first verifier's drop, with stronger grounds than it gave. Verified at source: puzzles.js line 1332 space49 = "How many litres of blood does a resting adult heart pump every minute?", answer 5 L/min, shipped reveal reads verbatim "Your whole blood supply is about 5 litres, so the entire lot completes a lap roughly every minute." That reveal states this candidate's exact answer. Two additions the first verifier missed: (1) space49 sits in PUBLISHED day index 52 of 119 in tests/published-schedule.json, and PUZZLE-STANDARD.md's inviolable rule freezes published days, so the spoiler cannot be edited out; any new question schedules after day 119, guaranteeing the spoiler reaches the player BEFORE this question. (2) assemble.js's near-duplicate check (line ~172) would not have flagged this, since it requires matching units and this is L vs L/min. One part of the first verifier's reasoning I discount: "both answers are 5" is weak, as nine shipped questions already use answer 5 (lines 450, 554, 1334, 3050, 3336, 4811, 5099, 6743, 6767); the verbatim reveal text is what is decisive. Facts are sound, so this is not a factual drop: web-verified adult blood volume 4.5-6 L at ~7-8% of body weight (StatPearls, Britannica); "a fifth lost before BP collapses" is conservative but correct per ATLS (Class II 15-30% shows minimal systolic change, hypotension at Class III 30-40%); donation 470 mL is under half a litre; answer sits at 62% of a 0.5-20 log track, inside the 8% margin. I considered rescuing it by reframing to "What percentage of an adult's body weight is blood?" (answer 7) but rejected that: it authors a new question rather than correcting this one, changes the qid identity the pipeline uses to bind corrections to the reviewed question, and the value remains one trivial step from the frozen spoiler plus a 70 kg body. Not an over-eager drop.

verdicts.prompt: What percentage of an adult human body is water?
verdicts.note: Checked USGS Water Science School and standard physiology: adult ~60% (men ~60%, women ~55%), newborn ~75-78% — reveal's "closer to 75%" and the fat-vs-muscle claim both hold. Position recomputed: (60-20)/(85-20)=0.615, matches author. No duplicate in puzzles.js — the only nearby water question is `everyday` "What percentage of a watermelon's weight is water?" (line 3231), a different subject.

verdicts.prompt: An adult human brain weighs about how many grams?
verdicts.note: Answer verified: standard anatomy gives 1300-1400 g; 1.4 kg is the canonical teaching figure. Position recomputed: ln(1400/200)/ln(3000/200)=0.719, matches. Checked the reveal's 25 g claim directly against StatPearls (NCBI NBK459286), which states verbatim: "The CSF supports the weight of the brain, estimated at 1500 g, and suspends it in neutral buoyancy to a net weight of approximately 25 g." Flagging honestly: a straight buoyancy calculation (brain 1.04 g/mL, CSF 1.007) gives ~45 g, and many texts say 50 g, so the 25-50 g range is genuinely split. I left it because the reveal's number is quoted from a mainstream clinical reference. No duplicate: puzzles.js has "How many billion neurons are in the average adult human brain?" (line 1385) and the sperm whale brain (line 189), neither of which is brain mass in grams.

verdicts.prompt: Roughly how many hairs grow on an average human scalp?
verdicts.note: Answer and range confirmed independently: dermatology sources put the average scalp at ~100,000 hairs (typical 80,000-150,000; ~150 hairs/cm2 over ~600 cm2 of scalp reproduces the figure), so 100000 on a 5000..1000000 log track at position 0.565 is sound, and the automated near-duplicate check cannot fire (units 'hair' vs 'cm' vs 'hair/cm2', answers orders apart). Where the first verifier stopped short: it compared PROMPTS only and cleared line 6826 as a different quantity. It is a different quantity, but that question's shipped reveal already reads 'Each follicle grows for only two to six years, then rests and lets that hair go ... around 100 hairs leave your head daily. At any moment, 85-95% of scalp follicles are in that growing phase.' The candidate's reveal delivers exactly those two facts again (~100 shed daily + independent follicle clocks) in the same category, so a player who has seen everyday90 gets no new payoff from this one. Both facts are also correct, so this is repetition, not error. Replacement reveal uses verified, non-overlapping facts: follicles are all formed in utero (~week 22, ~5 million body-wide, ~100k scalp) with no new ones after birth, and the hair-colour gradient (blonde ~150,000 fine hairs, red ~90,000 thicker ones). Prompt, answer, unit, scale and bounds all stand unchanged.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Every one of them was formed before you were born — about five million follicles across the body, roughly a hundred thousand of them on the scalp — and no new ones ever appear afterwards. Colour shifts the count: blondes average around 150,000 fine hairs, redheads about 90,000 thicker ones.

verdicts.prompt: What percentage of the air you breathe out is carbon dioxide?
verdicts.note: Answer independently confirmed: exhaled air is ~78% N2, ~16% O2 (16-17%), ~4% CO2, against ~0.04% CO2 inhaled. Multiple sources agree; CPR literature measures mouth-to-mouth delivered gas at 3.5-4.0% CO2 and 16.4-17.8% O2 (PubMed 7988205 / Chest). Range 0.5..12 linear puts 4 at (4-0.5)/11.5 = 0.304 - a fair, non-central position, and the band covers the 4-5% spread that some textbooks quote. Prompt is unambiguous (percent by volume of exhaled air) and does not duplicate anything in data/verified.json - the nearest neighbours are the tidal-volume question (line 9669, 500 mL) and the dry-atmosphere nitrogen question (line 1468), both different quantities. No reveal leak: the reveal talks about oxygen, not CO2. First verifier's drop-free call was right, and its reveal complaint holds: with its own stated 16%, the drop from 21% is 5/21 = 23.8% relative, which is MORE than a fifth, so 'barely a fifth less' understates it and is internally inconsistent with the 16% figure it just gave ('barely a fifth less' would land at ~17%). Re-checked the correction: 16/21 = 0.762, so 'about three-quarters of what went in' is accurate, and the mouth-to-mouth rationale is standard (rescue breaths deliver 16-17% O2, enough to sustain life). Adopting the supplied corrected reveal verbatim. Answer 4, range 0.5..12 linear, and prompt all unchanged.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Exhaled air still contains around 16% oxygen — about three-quarters of what went in — which is exactly why mouth-to-mouth resuscitation works at all.

verdicts.prompt: Averaged over every adult on Earth, how many kilograms does a person weigh?
verdicts.note: Opened Walpole et al., BMC Public Health 2012 ("The weight of nations"). Confirmed all three figures: global average adult body mass 62 kg; North America highest at 80.7 kg; North America 6% of world population but 34% of world biomass — so the reveal's "a third" and "close to 81 kg" are both accurate. Position: (62-35)/(75-35)=0.675, matches. Residual drift risk noted: the underlying data is 2005-vintage and global mean weight has crept up since, but not by anywhere near 10%, and no newer equivalent global estimate exists.

verdicts.prompt: Filled to capacity, how many litres of air do an adult's lungs hold?
verdicts.note: Verified against StatPearls Physiology, Lung Capacity and Physiology, Residual Volume: TLC ≈6 L average; residual volume reference 1-1.2 L, so the reveal's 1.2 L and its function (keeping alveoli from collapsing) are correct. Position: (6-2)/(12-2)=0.4, matches. Checked against puzzles.js `everyday` line 6502 "How many millilitres of air move in and out with one relaxed breath?" (tidal volume) and line 6682 (alveoli count) — related organ, different quantity, and neither reveal gives away 6 L.

verdicts.prompt: How many millimetres across is an adult human eyeball?
verdicts.note: Verified adult eyeball dimensions: ~24.2 mm transverse, 23.7 mm sagittal, axial 22.0-24.8 mm — 24 mm "across" is right. Position: (24-8)/(30-8)=0.727, matches. Reveal checked: newborn axial length ~16.8 mm, ~22.5-23 mm (about 90-95% of adult) by age three, with full size reached in the teens — so "nearly adult size by age three" is defensible as written; I would have dropped it had the reveal claimed "full" adult size. No duplicate in puzzles.js (only the colossal squid eye, line 137, and the dragonfly compound eye, line 4366).

verdicts.prompt: Roughly how many light-sensitive cells are packed into one human retina?
verdicts.note: First verifier was RIGHT to say fix, and right about both defects. Independently confirmed. (1) Answer holds: Webvision 'Facts and Figures Concerning the Human Retina' (NCBI NBK11556) gives ~6.4 million cones and 110-125 million rods; the standard textbook pairing is ~120M rods + 6-7M cones = ~126M photoreceptors. (Curcio 1990's more conservative counts, ~92M rods + 4.6M cones, land near 96M — a negligible shift on a log axis spanning 5e5..2e9.) Position ln(126e6/5e5)/ln(2e9/5e5) = 5.529/8.294 = 0.667, comfortably off both rails. Range, category, and reasoning path all fine; no dedupe concern. (2) The candidate reveal is decisively false as verifier 1 said. Curcio: the rod-free zone averages 0.350 mm (1.25 deg) horizontally and holds only ~17,500 cones; the whole fovea (~1.5 mm) holds only ~200,000. So 6 million cones do NOT 'crowd into a patch the size of a pinhead' — they are spread across the entire retina, thinning outward. And peripheral vision is not 'effectively colour-blind': cone-mediated colour vision persists well into the periphery, just degraded, especially for small stimuli. (3) Verifier 1's correction is substantively correct but has one loose seam worth closing: it calls the pinhead-sized pit 'rod-free'. The pit (fovea, ~1.5 mm, roughly pinhead-sized) is not rod-free; only its central 0.35 mm foveola is. Webvision's own Facts and Figures page muddies this by calling the fovea centralis a '0.3 mm diameter rod-free area', so the phrasing is defensible but conflates two different structures. I supply a tightened reveal that keeps verifier 1's punch, quantifies the foveal cone count, and puts 'rod-free' where it belongs (at the centre).
verdicts.correctedReveal: Only about 6 million of them are cones, and they thin out fast toward the edges. Barely 200,000 sit in the fovea — a pinhead-sized pit, rod-free at its very centre — yet that speck carries all your sharp detail; step outside it and vision turns blurry and much poorer at colour.

verdicts.prompt: How many litres of fluid do the kidneys filter out of the blood in a day?
verdicts.note: Recomputed from standard renal physiology: GFR 125 mL/min × 1440 min = 180 L/day. Reveal checked: urine output ~1.5-2 L means >99% reabsorption (correct), and plasma volume ~3 L means 180/3 = 60 passes a day (correct). Position: ln(180/10)/ln(300/10)=0.850 — inside the 0.10-0.90 band, but it sits right at the top edge, so if the range is ever retuned this is the first candidate to widen. No duplicate found in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: Human vision is most sensitive to light of what wavelength, in nanometres?
verdicts.note: Checked the CIE photopic luminosity function V(λ): peak 555 nm; scotopic V'(λ) peak 507 nm, a 48 nm shift toward blue — reveal's "about 50 nm" is right, and the hi-vis yellow-green rationale is standard. Position: (555-300)/(700-300)=0.6375, matches author's 0.637. No wavelength question exists in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: What is the average birth weight of a human baby, in kilograms?
verdicts.note: WHO/standard obstetrics: term average 3.2-3.4 kg, low birth weight defined <2.5 kg, macrosomia >4 kg — reveal's up-to-10% postnatal loss regained in roughly two weeks is the standard paediatric figure. Position: (3.3-1)/(4.5-1)=0.657, matches. Caveat I checked and accepted: the global mean is lower than the Western mean (South Asian averages run ~2.8-3.0 kg), so 3.3 kg is a rich-world-leaning figure — but the spread is under 15% on a 1-4.5 linear track, so no player is meaningfully penalised. No duplicate in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: A landmark 2007 recording study found the average person speaks how many words a day?
