verdicts.note: Verified Mehl, Vazire & Pennebaker, Science 2007 ("Are Women Really More Talkative Than Men?"): 396 participants, EAR recorders; women 16,215 words/day, men 15,669 — a 546-word gap. Both reveal figures are exact and the stated motivation (testing the three-times-as-talkative claim) is the paper's own framing. Prompt is correctly anchored to "a 2007 recording study", which insulates it from the 2024-25 registered-report replication that found a larger midlife gender gap. Position: ln(16000/2000)/ln(300000/2000)=0.415, matches.

verdicts.prompt: Non-vintage Champagne must rest on its yeast lees for a legal minimum of how many months?
verdicts.note: First verifier's diagnosis CONFIRMED against the primary source. The AOC Champagne cahier des charges (section IX) states: 'Le degorgement ne peut etre effectue avant une periode de douze mois a compter de la date de tirage' (12 months on lees) and 'Les vins ne sont mis en marche a destination du consommateur qu'a l'issue d'une periode d'elevage de quinze mois minimum a compter de la date du tirage' (15 months total), with 'trente-six mois' for millesimes. So as originally asked, the answer is 12, not 15. I agree with re-framing the prompt to total ageing rather than setting the answer to 12: the vintage 36-month rule is also a total-ageing rule (so a 12-vs-36 reveal comparison would be apples-to-oranges), and 'NV must spend 15 months on lees' is a very widely repeated popular misstatement, which makes the lees framing a contested-answer trap. BUT the first verifier's correction is incomplete and partly wrong on two counts. (1) It never supplied a correctedPrompt despite saying it re-framed the prompt, so the item would have shipped with the original lees wording against answer 15 - the exact defect it diagnosed. I supply the prompt here. (2) Its reveal claims 'the last three after disgorgement', which the regulation does not say: the text only bars disgorgement before month 12: a producer may disgorge at month 14 or long after month 15. I rewrote the reveal to say only that at least the first twelve months are on lees. Answer stays 15; range 1..60 log unchanged, position ln(15)/ln(60)=0.661, and the 36-month vintage figure sits comfortably inside the range.
verdicts.correctedPrompt: Non-vintage Champagne must age in the bottle for a legal minimum of how many months before it can be sold?
verdicts.correctedReveal: The rules also bar disgorging the bottle before month twelve, so at least the first twelve of those months are spent on the dead yeast lees - the cells slowly break down and release the compounds behind that brioche-and-toast smell. Vintage Champagne must wait thirty-six months.

verdicts.prompt: To be labelled extra virgin, olive oil's free acidity must stay below what percentage?
verdicts.note: Checked the IOC trade standard COI/T.15/NC and EU Reg. 2568/91: extra virgin ≤0.8 g oleic acid per 100 g, virgin ≤2.0, lampante >2.0 — both the answer and the reveal's virgin comparison hold. Free acidity being organoleptically undetectable and serving as a proxy for fruit damage/lag to the mill is the standard IOC explanation. Position: 0.8/4=0.2, matches; low but inside the band. Existing olive oil questions in puzzles.js are calories per tablespoon (line 2932) — no overlap.

verdicts.prompt: EU law says a bar can only be called chocolate above what percentage of dry cocoa solids?
verdicts.note: Opened Directive 2000/36/EC Annex I. "Chocolate": not less than 35% total dry cocoa solids, including not less than 18% cocoa butter and not less than 14% dry non-fat cocoa solids — so both the answer and the reveal's claim about separate floors for fat and non-fat solids are exactly right. Also verified the reveal's milk-chocolate figure: milk chocolate is 25% total dry cocoa solids (family milk chocolate 20%). An early search hit claiming 30% was a member-state derogation, not the base definition. Position: (35-5)/(50-5)=0.667, matches.

verdicts.prompt: Household vinegar is what percentage acetic acid?
verdicts.note: Codex Alimentarius / food-grade vinegar standards: table vinegar 4-6%, 5% is the standard distilled white figure; cleaning vinegar 6-10%, i.e. roughly double. Reveal's skin-burn threshold checked against GHS classification: acetic acid solutions are classed skin-corrosive at ≥25% and irritant from ~10-25%, so "above about 20%" is a fair statement of where it starts burning on contact. Position: 5/25=0.2, matches. No vinegar question in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: What percentage of whole cow's milk is fat?
verdicts.note: Dairy composition standards: whole milk 3.5-4.0% fat (UK whole milk minimum 3.5%). Reveal verified item by item: UK semi-skimmed 1.7%, skimmed ≤0.3%, human milk ~3.5-4.5% — all correct, including the counterintuitive claim that human milk is fattier. Position: (3.5-0.5)/(12-0.5)=0.261, matches. Checked puzzles.js milk entries: "A full US gallon of milk weighs about how many kilograms?" (line 3023) and "litres of milk per kg of Parmigiano-Reggiano" (line 6550) — neither touches fat content.

verdicts.prompt: The shell accounts for what percentage of a chicken egg's total weight?
verdicts.note: Poultry science sources: shell is 9-12% of total egg weight, 10-11% typical. Reveal verified: shell is ~95% calcium carbonate and contains 1.7-2.5 g of calcium, so "about 2 g of calcium a day" is right for a daily layer (dietary requirement runs 4-4.5 g/day because absorption is partial). I checked the bloodstream comparison numerically: a hen carries roughly 100 mL of blood at ~20-30 mg/dL plasma calcium, so ~25-35 mg circulating — the shell demand really is dozens of times that. Position: (10-2)/(25-2)=0.348, matches. Existing egg question in puzzles.js is total egg mass in grams (line 2880), a different quantity.

verdicts.prompt: How many grams of tea are in a standard teabag?
verdicts.note:
Second-pass check: I agree with the first verifier's call, and its corrected reveal is factually sound, but I tightened one broken causal link in it.

ANSWER — CONFIRMED, no change. Multiple independent sources put a standard single-serve teabag at ~2 g, with a 1.5-3 g spread by brand/type (black ~2 g, green ~1.8 g). 2 g is the right central figure. Position in range (2-0.5)/(10-0.5) = 0.158 — low in the band but comfortably inside, and a 0.5..10 g linear range is a fair guessing spread for a kitchen-scale quantity, so no range change needed. Reasoning path also checks out: a teaspoon of granulated sugar is ~4.2 g, so 'noticeably less than a teaspoon of sugar' correctly lands a guesser near 2 g. Everyday portability is fine — teabags are the same object in UK/US/AU.

ORIGINAL REVEAL — CONFIRMED WRONG. It claims loose-leaf uses 'two to three times as much per cup'. Standard loose-leaf dosing is 2-3 g per 200 ml / 6-8 oz cup — essentially the same dose as a bag, not 2-3x. Only outlier styles (oolong, pu-erh at ~5 g, white at ~4 g) run higher, and those are not 'loose-leaf brewing' generally. The second half of the original reveal is wrong too: whole leaves are not dosed heavier to compensate for lower flavour-per-gram; per-gram extraction differs in RATE, not in ultimate yield.

FIRST VERIFIER'S CORRECTION — facts verified, prose flawed. Its two load-bearing claims both hold: (a) loose leaf is the same 2-3 g/cup, difference is grind not dose; (b) pyramid bags run heavier, roughly 2-3 g with fruit/black blends at 3 g and up to ~50% more capacity than flat bags. But the sentence has a logic break: it says bagged tea is milled to dust, then writes 'which is why a big pyramid bag holds nearer 3 grams' — a non sequitur, since pyramid bags are the whole-leaf EXCEPTION to dust, not a consequence of it. I supplied a rewrite that keeps every verified fact and fixes the causal chain (dust extracts fast in a cramped flat bag / whole leaf needs room, hence the roomier 3 g pyramid).

No dedupe concern: this is the only mass-of-a-common-object tea item in play.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Loose leaf calls for much the same 2 to 3 grams per cup — the difference is grind, not dose. Bagged tea is milled to fannings and dust, whose huge surface area colours the water in under a minute inside a cramped flat bag, while whole leaves need minutes and room to open, which is why premium pyramid bags are built bigger and hold nearer 3 grams.

verdicts.prompt: The Italian standard for a single espresso specifies how many grams of ground coffee?
verdicts.note: Opened the Istituto Nazionale Espresso Italiano certification spec: 7 g ± 0.5 ground coffee, 25 mL ± 2.5 in the cup, 25 s ± 5 extraction, 88 °C ± 2 water, 9 bar ± 1 — the answer and both reveal figures come straight from the same five-value certification. Caffeine claim also holds: a single espresso is ~63 mg against ~95-165 mg for a mug of filter. Position: (7-2)/(25-2)=0.217, matches. No espresso question exists in puzzles.js (the nearest is caffeine per 240 mL brewed cup, line 2984).

verdicts.prompt: An espresso machine forces water through the grounds at what pressure, in bar?
verdicts.note: Same INEI spec confirms 9 bar ± 1. Reveal checked: a car tyre runs ~2.2-2.4 bar, so 9 bar is roughly four times that (correct); and the Faema E61, the first pump-driven machine, launched in 1961, before which lever machines generated pressure via a hand-compressed spring (correct). Position: (9-1)/(30-1)=0.276, matches. Sibling risk noted but cleared: this and candidate 20 share a source but ask for different quantities on different scales; puzzles.js line 3192 asks for champagne bottle pressure in psi, a different subject.

verdicts.prompt: What percentage of an arabica coffee bean's weight is caffeine?
verdicts.note: Coffee chemistry sources: arabica 1.2-1.5% caffeine by dry weight (green bean range 0.8-1.9%), robusta 2.2-2.7% — the reveal's "roughly double" is right, as is caffeine being a bitter natural insecticide. Position: (1.2-0.1)/(6-0.1)=0.186, low but inside the band. Verified the reasoning's arithmetic too: 10 g grounds yielding ~100 mg with incomplete extraction is consistent with ~1.2%.

verdicts.prompt: EFSA puts the safe daily caffeine intake for a healthy adult at how many milligrams?
verdicts.note: Opened the EFSA Scientific Opinion on the safety of caffeine (EFSA Journal 2015;13(5):4102): single doses up to 200 mg and habitual daily intake up to 400 mg are safe for healthy adults; 200 mg/day for pregnant women — all three reveal figures verified against the opinion itself. Lethal dose commonly cited at ~10 g, i.e. 25× the daily limit, so that clause holds too. Position: ln(400/25)/ln(2000/25)=0.633, matches. Distinct from puzzles.js line 2984 (caffeine per cup) and 6742 (caffeine half-life).

verdicts.prompt: A 330 mL beer at 5% ABV contains how many grams of pure alcohol?
verdicts.note: Recomputed: 330 × 0.05 = 16.5 mL ethanol × 0.789 g/mL = 13.0 g. Position: (13-2)/(40-2)=0.289, matches. I probed the reveal's "liver clears roughly this much in an hour" hardest, since published rates span 7-14 g/h; the standard public-health formulation ("about one standard drink per hour", US standard drink = 14 g) supports it and the reveal hedges with "roughly", so it survives — but it is the softest claim in this candidate. The ethanol-density-below-water point is exact.

verdicts.prompt: Egg white begins to set at what temperature, in Celsius?
verdicts.note: Fact confirmed independently, so the first verifier's 'keep' was right on substance: McGee gives white begins to thicken at 63 C / tender solid at 65 C, yolk thickens 65 C and sets 70 C, and the reveal's onsen tamago description is accurate (it correctly says hold BETWEEN 63 and 70, i.e. the 65-68 C window where ovalbumin, needing ~80 C, leaves the white a loose custard while the yolk sets custardy - genuinely the inverse of a soft boil). Where the first verifier erred is the position check: it cited pos=0.46 as 'matches', but tools/check-batch.js:96 counts 0.45<pos<0.55 toward the 'midpoint must not be a tell' gate (warn >12%, fail >18%). 0.46 is inside the tell band, not merely inside the 0.08-0.92 edge margin. Bank-wide midpoint share is 33/596 = 5.5%, so this is not fatal, but the fix is free. Widening hi to 100 puts pos at 0.383, out of the band, and 100 C (boiling) is a more natural ceiling for an egg question than an arbitrary 90 - the point of the question is that egg sets far below boiling. Span 60 still snaps to 1 C steps, so play is unchanged. Dedupe verified clean: nearest shipped neighbours are everyday62 (hot-water tank 60 C, token sim ~0.17, well under the 0.45 threshold) and everyday5 (chicken 74 C, 15% away so outside near()); no egg- or cooking-protein-temperature question exists in the bank. Minor residual noted and deliberately not changed: 'begins to set' could be read as McGee's 65 C 'tender solid' rather than 63 C 'begins to thicken', but with bracket scoring any sane 60-68 interval captures 63, so re-wording is churn.

verdicts.prompt: Inside a pressure cooker at one bar above atmospheric, water boils at what temperature in Celsius?
verdicts.note: Checked steam tables: 2 bar absolute (1 bar gauge) gives 120.2 °C, and the autoclave standard of 121 °C corresponds to 15 psi ≈ 1.03 bar gauge — so 121 is within a degree of the literal reading and is the number the reveal's sterilisation fact hangs on. On a linear 100-180 track a one-degree offset is invisible. Reveal verified: 121 °C for 15 minutes is the standard moist-heat sterilisation cycle and does kill C. botulinum spores, which survive 100 °C indefinitely. Position: (121-100)/(180-100)=0.263, matches. Sibling in puzzles.js is "On Everest's summit, water boils at what temperature?" (line 2867) — same physics, opposite direction, different answer; not a duplicate but I would not schedule them in the same week.

verdicts.prompt: How many litres of seawater must you evaporate to get one kilogram of sea salt?
verdicts.note: First verifier's drop is CORRECT, and I found a second independent reason to drop. (1) Dedupe confirmed at source: puzzles.js line 4630 is question id `nature86` inside window.BALLPARK_DATA — the shipped generated pack (header: '596 verified questions | 119 days of puzzles'), not a draft. Its prompt is 'How many grams of salt are dissolved in one litre of average seawater?', answer 35, unit g/L, source NOAA. The candidate's 29 L is exactly 1000/35. One division, one underlying fact, and with a 3..1000 log range a player who has seen nature86 lands it dead-on for free. (2) Web search independently reproduces only that same one-step derivation — there is no separate empirical figure that would make this a distinct question. (3) NEW, missed by the first verifier: the reveal contradicts the arithmetic. NaCl is only ~85% of seawater's 35 g/L total dissolved solids, and the reveal itself states the bittern liquor is drained off and discarded — so you cannot recover 35 g of harvestable sea salt per litre. Real solar-pan yield per kg of marketable salt is nearer 35-45 L. The candidate is self-inconsistent: read as total dissolved solids it is the shipped fact inverted and the reveal is off-topic; read as harvested sea salt the answer 29 L is simply wrong. Neither reading rescues it. Drop confirmed; no correction offered because a corrected numeric value would still be the algebraic inverse of nature86.

verdicts.prompt: How many days does a chicken egg take to hatch?
verdicts.note: Poultry husbandry: 21 days is the standard incubation period for Gallus gallus domesticus, uncontested across sources. Reveal verified: internal pipping into the air cell occurs around day 19, roughly a day before external pipping, and chicks do vocalise audibly from inside the shell at that stage. Position: (21-5)/(60-5)=0.291, matches. No incubation question in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: A modern commercial laying hen produces how many eggs in a year?
verdicts.note:
CONFIRMS first verifier's drop, but on a stronger evidentiary basis — and I record that the item itself is factually excellent, so the drop is purely a dedupe casualty, not a quality one.

FACT CHECK (independent, and the first verifier never did this): the answer is not merely defensible, it is exact against the claimed source. United Egg Producers' own Facts & Stats page (unitedegg.com/facts-stats) states each laying hen produced 300 eggs in 2025, with the laying rate 'peaking at 301 eggs in 2024' and a historical series of 266 (2004) and 286 (2014). USDA NASS gives 290 eggs per layer on hand for 2024. So answer=300, unit=egg, source='United Egg Producers' all check out precisely — an unusually clean attribution. The reveal also holds: 10-15 eggs/year across a couple of clutches is the standard figure for wild red junglefowl (clutches of 4-8), and the wild-ancestor framing is correct. Reasoning path (25h per egg, ~365 ceiling, moult/pause discount) is sound. Nothing here was wrong.

DEDUPE RE-ADJUDICATION: I agree the barrier flag is a genuine duplicate, not a shared sentence template. The distinction the first verifier drew is the right one — a template collision is two different subjects in one sentence frame; here subject, quantity, unit and answer (300 egg/year, laying hen) are all identical and only the adverb 'roughly' differs. Critically, a prompt rewrite cannot cure this: the duplication lives in the answer and the subject, not the wording, so 'fix' is not an available path. One of the two must go.

CORPUS CHECK (verified independently, not taken on trust): grep over puzzles.js (596 shipped questions) and data/verified.json for 'laying hen', 'junglefowl', 'eggs in a year' returns nothing, so the first verifier's claim that neither version has shipped is correct and the collision is internal to this generation run.

WHERE I PUSHED BACK ON THE TIEBREAK: the first verifier's 'the hen belongs in nature' was asserted, not argued, so I tested it. Nature already carries nature70 — 'How many billion chickens are alive on Earth at any one moment?' (FAO, 26 billion), whose reveal already works the industrial-poultry seam ('a modern broiler reaches slaughter weight in about six weeks'). Everyday, meanwhile, holds the chicken-egg-mass question (line 2880, USDA egg grading) and the chicken cooking-temp question — an adjacent but genuinely distinct fact. So nature is arguably the more crowded home for the industrial-chicken theme, which is a real argument the first verifier missed for keeping the everyday copy instead. On balance I still land on its side: this candidate's reveal is built entirely on the red junglefowl wild-ancestor contrast, which is a nature payload, and the sibling's 'roughly' is the better hedge for a figure that ranges 290-301 across sources. The tiebreak survives scrutiny.

DECISION DISCIPLINE: even where I found the tiebreak arguable, reversing it from my seat would be actively harmful — I can only rule on this candidate and cannot drop the sibling, so a 'keep' here would ship both and produce a true duplicate pair, the exact outcome the barrier exists to prevent. Drop confirmed.

Minor note for the surviving sibling, if it is still editable: range 50..400 linear puts the answer at 0.71 of the track (a little high), and the 400 ceiling sits above the ~365 physical maximum implied by one-egg-per-25-hours, so guesses in 365-400 are biologically impossible. Tightening to roughly 50..365 would both center the answer better and stop leaking dead space. This does not affect the drop verdict here.

verdicts.prompt: How many litres of water go into producing one kilogram of beef, on the global average?
verdicts.note: Opened Mekonnen & Hoekstra (Water Footprint Network): beef 15,400 m³/tonne = 15,400 L/kg; chicken 4,325 L/kg — both the answer and the reveal's chicken comparison are the study's own numbers. The green-water point is also the study's central caveat (the great majority is rainfall on pasture and feed, not blue water). Position: ln(15400/1000)/ln(30000/1000)=0.804, matches. Sibling in puzzles.js is "litres of water per pair of jeans, per the UN" (line 3439) — same genre, different product and different source; acceptable, though the two should not land on the same day.

verdicts.prompt: Finland drinks more coffee than anywhere else: how many kilograms per person per year?
verdicts.note: Drop upheld, on stronger grounds than the first verifier gave. Confirmed independently: sources span 9.0-12.0 kg. ICO/thisisFINLAND 12 kg; FAOSTAT 10.8 kg (2023); Finnpartnership market report ~9 kg roasted (2025); several current datasets 9.6 kg. That is well past rule 2's 10% bar. Root cause the first verifier missed: ICO reports per-capita consumption in Green Bean Equivalent (roasted x 1.19), so 12 kg GBE and ~10 kg roasted are partly the same consumption on two unstated bases. This is decisive because the candidate's OWN reasoning path computes on the roasted basis (7 g/cup x 4 cups x 365 = 10.2 kg) and the reveal reinforces it ('four cups a day'), while the answer 12 is the green-bean basis. A player following the intended reasoning perfectly lands on 10 and is scored against 12 - rule 1 failing from the inside. It also kills any fix: rule 2's Note exception (bamboo, 91 cm/day = 4 cm/hour) does not apply, because that dispute resolves by arithmetic anyone can do, whereas GBE requires knowing an industry conversion factor. Pinning 'roasted' and answering 10 is worse, since the first figure a checking player Googles is 12. Rule 8 independently bites: 12 (2015 ICO) -> 10.8 (2023) -> 9.6 (2025) is a measurable downward drift and the candidate sets no asOf. Correction to the first verifier: its second leg is overstated. Luxembourg's ~12.5 kg is a well-documented cross-border-commuter artifact and most sources do crown Finland, so the stem is contested rather than false - though notably thisisFINLAND, the same page carrying the 12 kg figure, calls Finland second. That leg is weak; leg (1) plus the basis ambiguity is sufficient on its own.

verdicts.prompt: How many kilograms of food does the average person throw away at home each year?
verdicts.note: Verified against the UNEP Food Waste Index Report 2024: 79 kg of household food waste per capita per year; households responsible for 631 Mt of the 1.05 bn tonnes total, i.e. 60%; and the report's own headline point that household waste per capita differs by only about 7 kg across high-, upper-middle- and lower-middle-income countries. All three reveal claims are the report's. Position: ln(79/5)/ln(400/5)=0.630, matches. Drift risk is real but slow (the 2021 edition said 74 kg) — worth carrying an asOf date if the schema supports it, but not enough to drop.

verdicts.prompt: How many kilograms of meat does the average person on Earth eat in a year?
verdicts.note: FAO food balance sheets / OECD-FAO Outlook: global per-capita meat consumption 41.5 kg (2013) rising to 45.3 kg (2023), carcass-weight equivalent — 44 kg sits squarely in the current band. Reveal verified: poultry passed pork as the world's most-produced meat in the late 2010s, and the global average has roughly doubled since 1960 (~23 kg then). Position: (44-15)/(60-15)=0.644, matches. Drift is ~0.4 kg/year, so the answer stays inside 10% for the better part of a decade. One caveat I checked and accepted: FAO reports carcass weight, so a player thinking in edible boneless terms (~34 kg) lands low — but the linear 15-60 range keeps the penalty small.

verdicts.prompt: How thick is ordinary kitchen aluminium foil, in micrometres?
verdicts.note: 16 µm (0.016 mm) is the dominant published spec for standard-duty household foil; heavy-duty runs 18-24 µm and economy grades 10-12 µm. I nearly dropped this on the brand-dependency rule, since the real product spread is about 10-25 µm, but checked the scoring consequence: on a log 2..1000 track, an answer anywhere in 10-25 µm scores within a hair of 16, so the spread cannot actually hurt a player. Position: ln(16/2)/ln(1000/2)=0.335, matches. Reveal verified: the dull/shiny asymmetry really is a product of double-sheet (pack) rolling, not a coating — that one is worth keeping because it kills a popular myth.

verdicts.prompt: How thick is a single sheet of ordinary 80 gsm printer paper, in micrometres?
verdicts.note: Paper caliper specs put 80 gsm office paper at ~100-110 µm, and the ream check is self-consistent (500 sheets ≈ 5 cm). Position: ln(100/10)/ln(2000/10)=0.435, matches. Reveal arithmetic recomputed: 2^7 = 128 sheets × 0.1 mm = 12.8 mm ≈ 1.3 cm — correct. Sibling check in puzzles.js: line 3335 asks the WEIGHT of one 80 gsm A4 sheet (grams) and line 6670 asks A4 sheets per A0. Same paper, different quantities, and neither reveal leaks thickness — but note candidate 44 in this same batch is the paper-folding record, which leans on this exact doubling argument, so the two should not be scheduled adjacently.

verdicts.prompt: One cubic metre of ordinary concrete weighs how many kilograms?
verdicts.note: Agree with first verifier on both the keep-the-question call and the specific reveal defect. Answer independently confirmed: EN 1991-1-1 Annex A Table A.1 gives plain normal-weight concrete 24 kN/m3 (reinforced 25), i.e. ~2,400 kg/m3; range 800..3200 linear puts it at 0.667, prompt is portable and undated, reasoning path (denser than water, far lighter than steel, stone ~2.5x water) is sound. Reveal's cement clause checks out: typical structural mixes carry ~320-350 kg cement per m3 and 2400/7 = 343, so 'about a seventh' is right. Water clause does not: free-water content in normal mix design runs ~150-205 kg/m3 (ACI ~168-175 for 50-75 mm slump; BRE/BS method 180-205 depending on aggregate), which is 6-8.5% of 2,400 kg. 'A tenth' would require 240 kg/m3, above the normal envelope. The first verifier's correction to 'less than a tenth' is true across the entire typical range and preserves the aggregate-does-the-heavy-lifting point, so I adopt it verbatim rather than churning the wording. No dedupe or portability concerns found.
verdicts.correctedReveal: The stone and sand do most of the work: cement is only about a seventh of the mix by weight, and water less than a tenth.

verdicts.prompt: One litre of olive oil weighs how many grams?
verdicts.note: Verified 0.916 g/mL at 20 °C against IOC physical-chemical characteristics (published range 0.910-0.916, with 0.911-0.918 across authenticity testing); ISO 662 / AOAC 943.04 govern the temperature dependence. Position: (916-600)/(1500-600)=0.351, matches. Reveal verified: all edible oils sit within a few percent of this, which is exactly why oil floats and vinaigrettes separate. Sibling in puzzles.js is calories per tablespoon of olive oil (line 2932) and grams of honey per litre (line 6454) — different quantities, no leak.

verdicts.prompt: An LED bulb sold as a '60-watt equivalent' emits how many lumens?
verdicts.note: Confirmed the 60 W ≈ 800 lm equivalence across lighting conversion tables (and the corresponding 75 W ≈ 1,100 lm, 100 W ≈ 1,600 lm rungs). Reveal verified: the LED replacement draws 8-12 W, so "roughly 8 watts" is at the efficient end but accurate for current bulbs, and incandescents do radiate ~95% of their input as heat. Position: ln(800/100)/ln(20000/100)=0.392, matches. Portability is fine — 800 lm on the box is the same number in every market, and the 60 W reference is universally understood. The cited source ("EU energy labelling equivalence tables") is vaguer than the fact warrants but the fact itself is not in doubt.

verdicts.prompt: A British kettle on a 13-amp, 230-volt socket draws close to how many watts?
verdicts.note: Recomputed: 230 V × 13 A = 2,990 W, and 3 kW is the standard UK kettle rating. Position: ln(3000/200)/ln(10000/200)=0.692, matches. Reveal verified: a US 15 A/120 V circuit at the usual 80% continuous derating gives ~1,440-1,500 W, so North American kettles do cap near 1,500 W and take about twice as long. Portability considered and cleared: the prompt names Britain and states both the voltage and the amperage, so a non-UK player has everything needed to compute it — the region-specificity is in the stem, not hidden.

verdicts.prompt: European standards call for how many lux of light on an office desk?
verdicts.note: Verified against EN 12464-1 (lighting of indoor workplaces): 500 lux maintained for writing, typing, reading and data processing, with U₀ 0.60 and Ra 80; 750 lux for technical drawing, 300 for filing/copying. Position: ln(500/50)/ln(10000/50)=0.435, matches. Reveal verified: overcast daylight ~1,000-2,000 lux, direct sun >50,000 — the point that indoor light is far dimmer than it feels because of eye adaptation is sound.

verdicts.prompt: EU law says a car tyre is worn out below how many millimetres of tread depth?
verdicts.note: Confirmed 1.6 mm as the EU minimum legal tread depth for passenger cars, introduced by Directive 89/459/EEC. Reveal verified: tread wear indicators (wear bars) are moulded into the grooves at exactly 1.6 mm, and wet braking distances at the legal limit are substantially longer than on new tread. Position: (1.6-0.2)/(6-0.2)=0.241, matches. Metric throughout, no imperial dependency, no duplicate in puzzles.js.

verdicts.prompt: How many millimetres across is a compact disc?
verdicts.note: 120 mm is fixed by the IEC 60908 Red Book standard. Reveal verified and, importantly, correctly hedged: Philips proposed 100 mm (Sony) / 115 mm (Philips) for a 60-minute disc, and the extension to 74 minutes and 120 mm is attributed to Norio Ohga wanting Furtwängler's 1951 Bayreuth Ninth to fit — but Snopes and others rate the Beethoven story undetermined, with competing versions naming Ohga's favourite piece, Morita's wife, or Karajan. The reveal's phrasing "The story told for decades is that..." is exactly the right register; had it asserted the legend as fact I would have required a fix. Position: (120-50)/(180-50)=0.538, matches.

verdicts.prompt: A classic black-and-white football is stitched from how many panels?
verdicts.note: 32 panels = 12 black pentagons + 20 white hexagons, the truncated icosahedron (Adidas Telstar pattern). Reveal verified: buckminsterfullerene C60 has that same geometry, and Curl, Kroto and Smalley took the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its discovery. Position: (32-10)/(40-10)=0.733, matches. Checked puzzles.js for football overlap — line 7354 is the height of a football crossbar, unrelated. Note that modern match balls (Brazuca, Telstar 18) use fewer, differently shaped panels, but the prompt says "classic black-and-white", which pins it correctly.

verdicts.prompt: Paper supposedly cannot be folded in half more than seven times. How many folds did a US student manage in 2002?
verdicts.note: Verified every element: on 27 January 2002 Britney Gallivan, a high school student in Pomona, California, folded a single sheet in half 12 times, using 4,000 ft (1,219 m ≈ 1.2 km) of tissue/toilet paper laid out along a shopping mall corridor over about eight hours; she derived the folding-limit equations first and published them through the Historical Society of Pomona Valley. Reveal is accurate on all counts including the order of operations (formula first, then the demonstration). Position: (12-5)/(30-5)=0.28, matches. Date-anchoring in the prompt is load-bearing and correct: later records exist (13 folds, MIT 2012), but "a US student in 2002" pins the answer unambiguously.

verdicts.prompt: Roughly how many litres of helium does it take to lift one kilogram off the ground?
verdicts.note: Recomputed from scratch: air 1.225 g/L minus helium 0.179 g/L = 1.046 g/L of lift, so 1000/1.046 = 956 L — 950 is right. Position: ln(950/100)/ln(2000/100)=0.751, matches. Reveal verified by calculation: hydrogen gives 1.225-0.0899=1.135 g/L, which is 8.5% better than helium — the "just 8%" figure is correct and is the genuinely counterintuitive part, since hydrogen is half helium's density. The framing that lift is the density difference, not the gas's own lightness, is the key physics and is stated correctly.

verdicts.prompt: One cubic metre of air at 20 °C can hold at most how many grams of water vapour?
verdicts.note: Verified saturation vapour density at 20 °C = 17.3 g/m³ (17.2 in some tables, corresponding to a partial pressure of 2.33 kPa). Position: (17-3)/(40-3)=0.378, matches. Reveal verified: SVD roughly doubles per 10 °C (9.4 g/m³ at 10 °C, 17.3 at 20, 30.4 at 30 — a 1.76× step, fairly called 'roughly doubles'), and condensation on cold glass follows directly. Checked against puzzles.js line 4546 (tonnes of water in a cumulus cloud) — same theme, entirely different scale and quantity.

verdicts.prompt: A tap dripping once a second wastes how many litres of water in a day?
verdicts.note: Agree with the drop, but the first verifier's primary reason was the secondary problem. The load-bearing defect is factual: the candidate applies the pharmacist's 20-drops-per-millilitre dropper convention to a faucet, and a tap drop is several times larger than a dropper drop. Independently checked against the two most authoritative sources for this exact scenario. EPA WaterSense (Fix a Leak Week) states a faucet dripping at one drip per second wastes more than 3,000 gallons per year = ~11,400 L/yr = ~31 L/day. USGS's drip calculator uses 15,140 drips per gallon = ~0.25 mL per drop, giving 86,400 x 0.25 mL = ~21.6 L/day (~2,080 gal/yr). Commonly cited UK water-industry figure for a dripping tap is ~15 L/day (~5,500 L/yr, WaterSafe). So the defensible answer band for the question as literally asked is ~15-31 L/day; the candidate's 4.3 L is 3.5x to 7x low. The physics agrees: by Tate's law drop volume scales with the detachment diameter, ~3 mm at a calibrated dropper tip (~0.05 mL) versus the much wider rim of a spout or aerator (~0.25 mL). The reveal's '1,500 litres a year' is arithmetically consistent with 4.3 L/day but understates the authoritative figure by the same 5-7x. I confirmed the first verifier's dedupe citation: puzzles.js line 6478 everyday61, 'How many drops of water add up to one millilitre?', answer 20, same Everyday Scale category, and its reveal does concede the 20-drop figure is 'a pharmacist's agreement, not a law of nature'. That citation is accurate, but on its own it would only argue for rewording. The two defects together are what make this unsalvageable rather than fixable. A fix to ~20-25 L/day is arithmetically available, but it would turn shipped everyday61 into an active trap: a player who correctly remembers the 20-drops/mL fact and applies it gets 4.3 and is scored badly wrong, so the question would punish retention of a fact the game itself taught. Combined with a genuine 2x spread among EPA, USGS and UK utilities on the corrected value, there is no answer that is both defensible and fair to prior players. Drop stands.

verdicts.prompt: European workplace rules require hearing protection above what noise level, in decibels?
verdicts.note: Opened Directive 2003/10/EC: lower exposure action value 80 dB(A) (protection must be made available), upper exposure action value 85 dB(A) (use is mandatory), exposure limit value 87 dB(A). The prompt asks where protection is REQUIRED, which is precisely the 85 dB upper action value — the wording lands on the right one of the three thresholds, which is the trap here. Reveal verified by calculation: the EU uses a 3 dB exchange rate, so 85 dB for 8 h becomes 100 dB for 8h/2^5 = 15 minutes. Position: (85-60)/(120-60)=0.417, matches. Distinct from puzzles.js line 6910 (conversation dB) and 4378 (blue whale call).

verdicts.prompt: Climbing a 10-metre staircase, a 70 kg person does how many kilojoules of work against gravity?
verdicts.note: Recomputed: 70 × 9.81 × 10 = 6,867 J = 6.9 kJ. Position: ln(6.9/0.5)/ln(200/0.5)=0.438, matches. Reveal checked numerically: 6.9 kJ = 1.64 kcal, so "under two kilocalories" is right; a peanut is ~5.5-6 kcal, so "roughly a third of a single peanut" is right; and skeletal muscle efficiency of ~20-25% means the body spends about four times the mechanical work, the rest as heat — right. Sibling in puzzles.js is line 6418, kilojoules to heat a litre of water, which is a different calculation with a different answer (~335 kJ); no leak in either direction.

questions.prompt: The Academy Award statuette stands how many centimetres tall?
questions.source: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences
questions.reveal: Wartime metal rationing meant winners from 1942 to 1944 were handed painted plaster versions, swapped for the real thing once the war ended.
questions.reasoningPath: It is carried in one hand and held up over the head, so it is trophy-sized rather than furniture-sized: bigger than a wine bottle's label but shorter than a bottle of wine is tall. That lands you in the 30-40 cm band.

questions.prompt: Guinness's largest cast of extras: how many people appeared in the funeral scene of Gandhi (1982)?
questions.reveal: Eleven camera crews shot it in a single morning, on the anniversary of the real funeral, and 6,000 metres of film was cut down to 125 seconds of screen time.
questions.reasoningPath: A big stadium holds 50,000-80,000. The scene fills Delhi streets and is famous precisely for dwarfing any stadium crowd, so think several stadiums' worth: a few hundred thousand, not tens of thousands and not millions.

questions.prompt: What is the most Academy Awards ever won by a single film?
questions.source: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences
questions.reveal: Three films share the record — Ben-Hur, Titanic and The Return of the King — and only the last of them swept every single category it was nominated in.
questions.reasoningPath: There are only a couple of dozen categories, and a film can win at most one each. A dominant film takes the big ones plus the craft awards, but never the acting categories it isn't in, so a total sweep tops out around ten or so.

questions.prompt: Standard cinema projection runs at how many frames per second?
questions.reveal: Silent films ran nearer 16-18 frames a second; the higher rate was adopted around 1929 because it was the slowest speed that let an optical soundtrack sound decent.
questions.reasoningPath: Motion looks smooth to us somewhere above about 15 flashes a second, and film was expensive, so the standard would sit just above the threshold rather than far beyond it — a couple of dozen, not hundreds.

questions.prompt: How many James Bond films had Eon Productions made when it handed the series over in 2025?
questions.reveal: Six actors carried the role across that run, and Daniel Craig alone took fifteen years to deliver five of them.
questions.reasoningPath: The series ran from 1962 to 2021, roughly 60 years. Early on a film appeared almost every other year; later gaps stretched to four or five. Average one every two and a half years and you get around 25.

questions.prompt: How many strings are stretched inside a modern grand piano?
questions.reveal: Together they pull with roughly 20 tonnes of tension, which is why the frame under the soundboard is cast iron rather than wood.
questions.reasoningPath: There are 88 keys. The treble notes use three strings each for volume, the middle two, and the deepest bass notes just one. Most of the keyboard is treble, so the total sits well above 88 but below 3 x 88 = 264.

questions.prompt: Orchestras tune to the A above middle C. What is its frequency in hertz?
questions.reveal: The pitch drifted for centuries — Handel's own tuning fork sat nearer 415 Hz, about a semitone flat — before an international standard fixed it in 1955.
questions.reasoningPath: Human hearing runs roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, and a singing voice sits in the low hundreds. This note is a little above the middle of the keyboard and comfortably inside the soprano range, so a few hundred hertz.

questions.prompt: Eurovision Song Contest rules cap each entry at how many minutes?
questions.reveal: The same rulebook bans any song released before September of the previous year, and forbids more than six people on stage.
questions.reasoningPath: Around forty countries perform in one live evening broadcast. Multiply the song length by forty, add voting and interval acts, and anything over about three minutes a song makes the show unbroadcastably long.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many of Antonio Stradivari's instruments still survive today?
questions.reveal: He worked into his nineties, and the instruments from his final decade are noticeably smaller and easier to handle than the famous middle-period ones.
questions.reasoningPath: He made well over a thousand instruments in a long career. Violins are valuable and carefully kept, so survival over three centuries should be good but not total — expect roughly half to two thirds still accounted for.

questions.prompt: Wagner's complete Ring cycle contains roughly how many hours of music?
questions.reveal: He spent 26 years writing it, and had a whole theatre built at Bayreuth because no existing opera house could stage the thing.
questions.reasoningPath: It is four operas performed on four evenings. A normal full-length opera runs two to three hours; these are famously long ones, so three to five hours each across four nights gets you to the mid-teens.

questions.prompt: Mozart's works are numbered in the Köchel catalogue. How many entries did it reach?
questions.reveal: He died at 35 while writing the very last entry in it, the Requiem, which one of his pupils had to finish for the widow to collect the fee.
questions.reasoningPath: He composed from age five to 35, so about thirty working years. He was famously fast, but symphonies, operas and concertos take weeks each — averaging roughly twenty finished works a year gives several hundred.

questions.prompt: How many minutes of audio does the original compact disc standard hold?
questions.reveal: The story goes that a Sony executive insisted Beethoven's Ninth fit on one disc; the 12 cm diameter was then chosen to make that capacity possible.
questions.reasoningPath: A CD had to comfortably beat a vinyl LP, which held about 45 minutes across two sides, and it was pitched as holding a whole long classical work without a break. That points to somewhere over an hour.

questions.prompt: How many words are in Tolstoy's War and Peace?
questions.reveal: Tolstoy's wife Sofia is said to have copied the whole manuscript out by hand several times over as he kept revising it.
questions.reasoningPath: A typical novel runs 80,000-100,000 words in roughly 300 pages. War and Peace is about 1,200 pages of dense text, so multiply the ordinary novel by five or six.

questions.prompt: How many words does the Oxford English Dictionary define?
questions.reveal: The first edition took seventy years to finish, and one of its most prolific volunteer contributors was writing in from an asylum for the criminally insane.
questions.reasoningPath: An educated speaker knows perhaps 30,000 words. A desk dictionary holds around 100,000. The OED is the full historical record including obsolete and regional words, so several times a desk dictionary.

questions.prompt: The complete Bible has been translated into how many languages?
questions.reveal: Parts of it exist in more than 3,700 further languages, and roughly 500 languages still have no translation work of any kind under way.
questions.reasoningPath: There are about 7,000 living languages, but most have tiny speaker numbers and no writing tradition. Translating an entire Bible takes a team years, so only a modest slice of languages — around a tenth — will have the whole thing.

questions.prompt: How many different words did Shakespeare use across his complete works?
questions.reveal: Around 1,700 of them turn up in print for the first time in his plays — he was as much a coiner of words as a user of them.
questions.reasoningPath: An educated adult's working vocabulary is roughly 20,000-30,000 words. A writer of nearly forty plays and a book of poems will stretch beyond ordinary usage but not by an order of magnitude, so expect thirty-odd thousand.

questions.prompt: The last printed Encyclopaedia Britannica (2010) ran to how many volumes?
questions.reveal: It closed a 244-year run in print; the set weighed nearly 60 kg, and of 12,000 printed only about 8,000 were ever sold.
questions.reasoningPath: Picture the shelf: a full encyclopedia occupies about a metre of shelving, and each volume is a few centimetres thick. That gives a few dozen books, and the alphabet needs splitting many times over for the big letters.

questions.prompt: The world's longest alphabet, Cambodia's Khmer script, has how many letters?
questions.reveal: It breaks down into 33 consonants, 23 vowels and 12 independent vowels — and several of the letters are no longer used in modern Cambodian at all.
questions.reasoningPath: Ordinary alphabets run 24 to 33 letters: Greek 24, Latin 26, Cyrillic 33. A record-holder writes vowels out as full letters too, so roughly double or triple a normal alphabet rather than ten times it.

questions.prompt: How many characters fit in a single original SMS text message?
questions.reveal: The limit was fixed in 1985 by an engineer who typed out random questions and postcard messages on his typewriter, decided that length covered nearly all of them, and rounded.
questions.reasoningPath: A text is about one or two sentences. An English sentence averages 15-20 words, and words average five letters plus a space, so one sentence is roughly 100 characters — the cap must be a small multiple of that.

questions.prompt: How many characters does the Unicode standard encode?
questions.reveal: Chinese, Japanese and Korean ideographs make up around 60% of the total; all the emoji together account for fewer than 4,000.
questions.reasoningPath: Chinese alone contributes tens of thousands of characters, and dictionaries list up to about 90,000. Add every alphabet, syllabary, historic script, symbol set and emoji and you roughly double that — but nowhere near a million.

questions.prompt: How many intersections does a standard Go board have?
questions.reveal: That yields about 10^170 legal positions, which is why Go was the last of the classic board games computers learned to beat humans at.
questions.reasoningPath: Stones sit on the crossings of a 19-by-19 grid, and 19 squared is a bit under 400. Even without recalling the grid size, a board visibly denser than chess's 8x8 but still hand-sized implies a few hundred points.

questions.prompt: How many oil paintings did Vincent van Gogh produce in his lifetime?
questions.reveal: He painted for barely a decade, and turned out roughly a third of that output in his final two years alone.
questions.reasoningPath: He took up painting at 27 and died at 37, so about ten years of work. He was famously prolific, finishing canvases in a day or two but not every day — call it under two a week, which comes to several hundred.

questions.prompt: How many strings does a full-size concert harp have?
questions.reveal: Seven pedals, each with three positions, retune whole classes of string at once — which is how an instrument strung like a white-keys-only piano manages to play in every key.
questions.reasoningPath: Its range is roughly six and a half octaves, close to a piano's seven. But the strings are laid out like the white keys only — seven per octave rather than twelve — so multiply 6.5 by 7.

questions.prompt: How many objects are in the British Museum's collection?
questions.reveal: Only about 80,000 are on show at any one time, and a 2023 audit found that more than two million had never been properly catalogued at all.
questions.reasoningPath: Great museums count coins, potsherds and flint tools individually, and those run to hundreds of thousands each. A 270-year-old imperial collection accumulating whole excavation archives lands in the millions, not the tens of thousands on display.

questions.prompt: How many people visited the Louvre in 2024, the world's most-visited museum?
questions.reveal: Three-quarters of them came from outside France, and the museum is being rebuilt to handle 12 million a year by 2031.
questions.reasoningPath: Paris receives roughly 30-40 million tourists a year, and a large share of first-time visitors do the Louvre. Divide the year's opening days into it: 25,000-30,000 people a day is already crowded, giving under 10 million.

questions.prompt: How many billion active mobile-phone subscriptions are there worldwide?
questions.reveal: That is more subscriptions than there are people, largely from second SIMs and work phones — yet roughly a third of humanity has still never used the internet.
questions.reasoningPath: World population is about 8 billion. Phone ownership is near-universal among adults in rich countries and very high elsewhere, and many people hold two SIMs, so the count should sit slightly above the population.

questions.prompt: How many steps lead from the ground to the top of the Eiffel Tower?
questions.source: Société d'Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel
questions.reveal: The public may only climb as far as the second floor, 674 steps up; above that the staircase is closed and the lift takes over.
questions.reasoningPath: The tower is about 300 m tall. A stair step rises roughly 18 cm, so a straight climb needs about 1,700 steps — and the tower's spiral staircases add little to that count.

questions.prompt: How many rooms does the Palace of Versailles contain?
questions.reveal: They spread across 63,000 m² of floor space, and at its height the palace housed something like 3,000 courtiers and servants inside it.
questions.reasoningPath: The floor area is around 60,000 m². Rooms in a palace average perhaps 25-30 m² once you include the servants' quarters and closets alongside the state halls, so a couple of thousand rooms.

questions.prompt: How many metres above the ground does the spire of Notre-Dame de Paris reach?
questions.reveal: The spire is not medieval at all: Viollet-le-Duc added it in 1859, and the 2024 reconstruction copied his design oak beam for oak beam.
questions.reasoningPath: The cathedral's west towers are the familiar reference at about 69 m, roughly a twenty-storey building. The spire rises from the roof ridge behind them and clearly overtops the towers, but not by a huge amount.

questions.prompt: How many columns hold up the prayer hall of the Great Mosque of Córdoba?
questions.reveal: Many were salvaged from Roman and Visigothic buildings, which is why they differ from one another in stone, height and capital.
questions.reasoningPath: The hall covers roughly 20,000 m² and the columns stand in a grid spaced only a few metres apart, giving perhaps one every 20-25 m². That arithmetic points to high hundreds, not dozens.

questions.prompt: How many arched entrances ring the ground floor of the Colosseum?
questions.reveal: Seventy-six of them were numbered in Roman numerals so ticket-holders could find their own staircase, letting the whole crowd clear the building in minutes.
questions.reasoningPath: The outer wall runs about 530 m around. Each arch with its pier takes up something like six or seven metres of that facade, so divide 530 by 6.5.

questions.prompt: How many hectares does Beijing's Forbidden City cover?
questions.reveal: Around 980 buildings still stand inside the walls, and the whole complex was raised in fourteen years, finishing in 1420.
questions.reasoningPath: The walled rectangle is roughly 960 m by 750 m — a ten-minute walk end to end. That is about 720,000 m², and a hectare is 10,000 m².

questions.prompt: How many matches were played at the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar?
questions.reveal: The 2026 edition jumps to 48 teams and 104 matches, adding more games in one step than the tournament played in total before 1982.
questions.reasoningPath: Thirty-two teams in eight groups of four means six matches per group, so 48 group games. Then sixteen teams knock out: 8 + 4 + 2 + the final, plus a third-place match — sixteen more.

questions.prompt: How many medal events were contested at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games?
questions.reveal: Paris was the first Games with equal numbers of male and female athletes — about 10,500 competitors across 32 sports.
questions.reasoningPath: There are around 32 sports. Athletics and swimming carry 40-50 events each, but most sports have only a handful. Average ten events per sport and you land in the low hundreds.

questions.prompt: How many kilometres did the 2024 Tour de France cover over its 21 stages?
questions.reveal: The riders also climbed 52,000 vertical metres along the way — close to six times the height of Everest from sea level.
questions.reasoningPath: Twenty-one racing days, most of them four to five hours long at an average of about 40 km/h. That is roughly 170 km a stage, and 21 x 170 is around 3,500.

questions.prompt: The fastest Formula 1 pit stop ever recorded took how many seconds?
questions.reveal: About twenty mechanics touch the car at once. In the 1950s the same job, refuelling included, took closer to a minute.
questions.reasoningPath: Four wheels come off and four go on simultaneously, each by its own three-person crew. A single practised movement — gun off, wheel off, wheel on, gun on — takes a second or two, and the car must stop and go on top of that.

questions.prompt: How many grams does a regulation table tennis ball weigh?
questions.reveal: The ball was enlarged from 38 mm to 40 mm in 2000 for the express purpose of slowing rallies down enough to follow on television.
questions.reasoningPath: It is a hollow plastic sphere 40 mm across with walls under half a millimetre thick. A large chicken egg is 60 g, a golf ball 45 g; this is far lighter than either, floating on air currents — a couple of grams.

questions.prompt: How many overs must be bowled in a full day of Test cricket?
questions.reveal: That works out at 540 legal deliveries, and a fielding side can be fined a share of its match fee for failing to get through them in time.
questions.reasoningPath: Play runs about six hours excluding intervals. An over of six balls, with the field changing ends, takes roughly four minutes. Six hours of four-minute overs is ninety.

questions.prompt: The first sub-2-hour marathon record (London 2026) averaged what speed in km/h?
questions.reveal: Kenya's Sabastian Sawe took the mark under two hours; the previous record, 2:00:35, had stood since Chicago in 2023.
questions.reasoningPath: The distance is 42.195 km and the time is just under two hours, so divide 42 by 2. A brisk cycle is 20 km/h — that is the pace, held for two hours, on foot.

questions.prompt: How many different opening moves can White play in chess?
questions.reveal: Only two of them — pushing the king's or the queen's pawn two squares — account for the large majority of games at top level.
questions.reasoningPath: Only pawns and knights can move at all on move one. Each of the eight pawns can go one or two squares, giving 16, and each of the two knights has two legal squares, giving four more.

questions.prompt: How many transistors were on the Intel 4004, the first microprocessor (1971)?
questions.reveal: It was designed for a Japanese desk calculator, and Intel had to buy the rights back from that customer before it could sell the chip to anyone else.
questions.reasoningPath: It was a complete 4-bit processor drawn by hand at ten-micron features on a chip a few millimetres across. A handful of registers and an adder need hundreds of gates, and each gate a few transistors — thousands, not millions.

questions.prompt: How many billion transistors are packed into Apple's M2 chip?
questions.reveal: They sit on a die about the size of a postage stamp, drawn at features around 5 nm across — a few dozen silicon atoms wide.
questions.reasoningPath: Moore's law doubled counts roughly every two years from the 1971 microprocessor's few thousand. Fifty years of that is enormous; by the 2010s desktop chips were in the low billions, and a modern laptop system-on-chip is a further step up.

questions.prompt: How many kilometres of submarine cable carry the world's internet traffic?
questions.reveal: Around 200 faults a year, mostly from anchors and fishing gear, are patched up by a global fleet of fewer than sixty cable-repair ships.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth's circumference is 40,000 km. There are roughly 500 cable systems; a transatlantic link is about 6,000 km, though many are short regional hops, so average perhaps 3,000 km each.

questions.prompt: Chip factories process silicon wafers of what diameter, in millimetres?
questions.reveal: One wafer yields hundreds of finished chips, and the industry's long-promised move to 450 mm was quietly abandoned as too expensive to tool up for.
questions.reasoningPath: A wafer must hold many chips at once to be economic, and processors are a couple of centimetres square. A dinner-plate-sized disc holds a few hundred of those, and anything much bigger is hard to keep flat and uniform.

questions.prompt: How many terawatt-hours of electricity did the world's data centres use in 2024?
questions.reveal: That is about 1.5% of global electricity, and the agency expects it to more than double by 2030 — with the United States accounting for nearly half of today's total.
questions.reasoningPath: World electricity use is around 28,000 TWh. Data centres are much discussed but still a small slice — one or two percent — which puts them in the hundreds of terawatt-hours, comparable to a mid-sized country.

questions.prompt: How many articles does the English-language Wikipedia contain?
questions.reveal: Printed at encyclopedia page density it would run past 3,000 bound volumes, and it still grows by several hundred articles a day.
questions.reasoningPath: A printed encyclopedia holds tens of thousands of articles. Wikipedia covers every settlement, species, footballer and album, so it should be two to three orders of magnitude larger — millions, and it passed one million back in 2006.

questions.prompt: How many tonnes did ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic computer, weigh?
questions.reveal: Its 18,000 vacuum tubes failed so often that engineers built a dedicated tester to hunt the dead ones down; the machine filled a room of about 170 m².
questions.reasoningPath: It filled a large room with steel cabinets of wiring and glass tubes. A single tall equipment rack runs a few hundred kilograms, and there were dozens of them — so tens of tonnes, roughly a couple of loaded lorries.

questions.prompt: The record fee for a footballer: how many million euros did PSG pay for Neymar in 2017?
questions.reveal: It more than doubled the previous record, and was paid by triggering a release clause — so Barcelona had no say in whether the sale happened.
questions.reasoningPath: Big-club transfer records climbed steadily: around 35 million at the turn of the century, 94 for Ronaldo in 2009, 105 for Pogba in 2016. This one shocked the sport by roughly doubling that last figure.

questions.prompt: Budgeted at 7 million Australian dollars, the Sydney Opera House finally cost how many million?
questions.reveal: A state lottery paid for it, it opened ten years late, and its architect left the country in 1966 and never came back to see it finished.
questions.reasoningPath: It is the standard textbook case of cost overrun, so the multiple has to be large enough to be notorious — not 50% over but something like ten to fifteen times the estimate.

questions.prompt: The Mona Lisa was insured for how many million dollars for its 1962 trip abroad?
questions.reveal: France then decided the premium was so steep that it was cheaper to spend the money on guards and transport, and sent the painting uninsured.
questions.reasoningPath: The priciest paintings changing hands in the early 1960s went for a few million dollars. Valuing the single most famous painting alive means a round number many times that — and it stayed the record valuation for decades.

verdicts.prompt: The Academy Award statuette stands how many centimetres tall?
verdicts.correctedReveal: Wartime metal rationing meant the statuettes handed out at the 1943, 1944 and 1945 ceremonies were painted plaster; once the war ended the Academy invited winners to swap them for gold-plated metal.
verdicts.note: Answer re-verified independently: oscars.org/oscars/statuette gives 13.5 in and 8.5 lb; 13.5 in = 34.29 cm, so 34 cm is right. Range 5..60 log puts 34 at ln(6.8)/ln(12) = 0.771 — top third but within tolerance and no repo rule covers it (tools/assemble.js:209 only prints the spread), so not a drop. Dedupe re-run myself over data/verified.json and puzzles.js for oscar/statuette/academy award: only three unrelated film-trivia reveals (LOTR sweep, Shrek, RRR), no height collision. First verifier's reveal fix: I accept it, but its reasoning overstates the case. 'Winners from 1942 to 1944' is defensible under the award-year convention (plaster covered the films of 1942, 1943 and 1944, i.e. the 15th-17th ceremonies held in 1943, 1944 and 1945), so the original is ambiguous rather than false. The correction is still the better line because it is unambiguous, and I confirmed it independently: oscars.org states three years of painted plaster plus a post-war exchange, and the Heritage Auctions listing for a wartime plaster Oscar reproduces the base sticker reading 'Temporary Trophy ... will be replaced by the gold and bronze trophies as soon as metals are available'. Adopting correctedReveal as supplied. THE FIRST VERIFIER MISSED A SECOND DEFECT: the reasoning path is backwards and must be replaced before ship. It tells the player the statuette is 'shorter than a bottle of wine is tall', but a standard 750 ml bottle is about 30 cm (11.8 in; 29-33 cm across Bordeaux/Burgundy/Champagne shapes) while the Oscar is 34.3 cm — taller, not shorter. The path therefore argues the player down below 30 cm while simultaneously claiming to land them in the 30-40 cm band, so it undercuts its own answer. There is no correctedReasoningPath field in this schema, so applying it by hand; suggested replacement: 'It is carried in one hand and hoisted overhead, so it is trophy-sized rather than furniture-sized: a shade taller than a 30 cm school ruler, and taller than a standard wine bottle rather than shorter. That lands you in the 30-40 cm band.' Ship only with both the reveal and the reasoning path corrected.

verdicts.prompt: Guinness's largest cast of extras: how many people appeared in the funeral scene of Gandhi (1982)?
verdicts.note: Checked Guinness 'most film extras' plus secondary coverage: 200,000 volunteers plus 94,560 contracted = ~294,560, universally rounded to 300,000. Reveal verified: shot in a single morning on 31 Jan 1981, the 33rd anniversary of the real funeral; 20,000 ft (=6,096 m) cut to 125 seconds; eleven camera crews is the standard account. Position log 5000..2000000: ln(60)/ln(400)=0.683, matches. No dedupe flag supplied; no extras/crowd question exists in the pack (culture73 is a Rod Stewart concert crowd, a real-world audience, not a film cast) — adjudicated as distinct.

verdicts.prompt: What is the most Academy Awards ever won by a single film?
verdicts.note: Verified against Guinness 'most Oscars won by a film' and Wikipedia's Academy Award records: Ben-Hur 11 of 12, Titanic 11 of 14, Return of the King 11 of 11. Reveal's claim that only the last swept every nomination is correct. Position linear 2..15: (11-2)/13=0.692, matches. No dedupe flag supplied; nearest shipped items are culture4 (ROTK runtime) and culture9 (Titanic box office) — different quantities, and the reveal leaks no numeric answer to either. Tried to break it on 'a film can win at most one per category' and found no counterexample above 11.

verdicts.prompt: Standard cinema projection runs at how many frames per second?
verdicts.note: Verified 24 fps as the SMPTE/industry sound-film standard, adopted around 1927-29 with optical sound because it was the slowest rate giving acceptable soundtrack quality; silent films ran 16-20 fps hand-cranked. Reveal matches sources. Position linear 10..90: (24-10)/80=0.175, matches. No dedupe flag supplied; no frame-rate or projection question anywhere in the 596 (checked all categories).

verdicts.prompt: How many James Bond films had Eon Productions made when it handed the series over in 2025?
verdicts.note: Confirmed via Variety/Deadline/The Conversation coverage: Amazon MGM took creative control in February 2025; Eon's run is 25 films, Dr. No (1962) to No Time to Die (2021). Reveal verified: six actors, Craig 2006-2021 (15 years, 5 films). Position linear 10..60: (25-10)/50=0.300, matches. Prompt is date-pinned to the 2025 handover so future Amazon films cannot invalidate it — checked that specifically for drift. No dedupe flag supplied; no Bond question in the shipped pack.

verdicts.prompt: How many strings are stretched inside a modern grand piano?
verdicts.note: Answer, range and position all hold up — independent sources give ~230 strings (Classic FM: 'the 230-odd strings in a grand piano exert a combined force of 20 tonnes on the cast iron frame'; Merriam Music and piano-technician sources: typically 220-240, Steinway concert grands to ~243, under 10% spread and comfortably inside an 88..300 band). The first verifier's number-checking was sound. Where it stopped short: it validated the two FIGURES in the reveal and never checked the anatomical claim wrapped around them. 'The frame under the soundboard' is wrong twice over. In a grand, the cast-iron plate is installed OVER the soundboard — it is bolted to the rim and pinblock and deliberately does not touch the board, with nose bolts passing through holes cut in the soundboard (Chupp's Pianos, The Piano Deconstructed, Bechstein's own build guide). What actually sits under the soundboard is the wooden back beams and ribs — so the reveal names the one part of the structure that IS wood and calls it cast iron, inverting the fact it is trying to teach. A player who opens a grand lid sees the gold plate above the strings, so the reveal also contradicts what the reader can observe. Corrected reveal keeps both verified numbers and fixes the placement. Separately, not blocking and not part of the shipped text: the reasoning path says the two-string notes are 'the middle' of the keyboard, when the bichord section actually sits low in the bass (roughly notes 11-24); a representative split is ~10 single, ~14 double, ~64 triple = 230. Worth tightening if reasoning paths are ever surfaced. No dedupe collision found; nothing else piano-adjacent in the set.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Together they pull with roughly 20 tonnes of tension, which is why the gold-coloured frame the strings are anchored to is cast iron rather than wood.

verdicts.prompt: Orchestras tune to the A above middle C. What is its frequency in hertz?
verdicts.note: Agree with the first verifier that this is a fix, not a drop or keep, and independently confirmed its core finding — but its correctedReveal needs one repair of its own. Confirmed: answer 440 Hz correct; ISO adopted A440 in 1955, reaffirmed 1975 as ISO 16, so the source claim holds; May 1939 London conference at Broadcasting House agreed 440. Confirmed the candidate reveal is wrong: Wikipedia's Concert pitch article gives the 1740 Handel-associated fork as A = 422.5 Hz (a 1780 specimen is A = 409), and independent sources describe the fork Handel left at the Foundling Hospital in 1751 as C = 512, equivalent to A = 422.5. The candidate's 415 Hz is the modern baroque-performance convention — exactly one equal-tempered semitone below 440 (440/2^(1/12) = 415.3) — not a measured historical pitch, so the candidate both cites the wrong number and, at 1200*log2(440/422.5) = 70.2 cents, overstates the interval by calling it 'about a semitone'. Where I differ: the first verifier's correctedReveal says 'the tuning fork John Shore gave Handel sounds an A of about 422.5 Hz', fusing two separate claims. Shore invented the fork in 1711 and lore says he gave one to Handel, but the documented 422.5 artifact is the fork Handel left at the Foundling Hospital, evidenced by its box inscription; no source ties the measured fork to a Shore gift, and Wikipedia does not mention Shore here. Fixing a factual reveal by importing a weaker attribution is a half-fix, so my correctedReveal drops Shore, names the provenance that is actually documented, and states the interval in cents. Other checks: prompt unambiguous (A4 is unmistakably the A above middle C); log position ln(4.4)/ln(200) = 0.280, in band, and the very wide range is justified by the hearing-range framing in the reasoning path; reasoning path sound (A4 sits just above middle C, inside soprano range). No dedupe break found — the other frequency items are a microwave band and a hearing limit, different subject matter.
verdicts.correctedReveal: The pitch drifted for centuries — the tuning fork Handel left at London's Foundling Hospital sounds an A near 422.5 Hz, some 70 cents flat of today's — before a 1939 London conference settled on 440 and ISO adopted it in 1955.

verdicts.prompt: Roughly how many of Antonio Stradivari's instruments still survive today?
verdicts.note: Answer independently confirmed, but the verifier identified a defective reveal and supplied no replacement text. Dropped rather than shipped with a known-bad reveal. Recoverable as a fresh candidate in a later batch. Original note: Agree with the first verifier's call, with a tightened correction. ANSWER RE-VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY: Wikipedia (citing the Hill workshop census), Smithsonian and Britannica-adjacent sources all give ~1,116 instruments made and 'around 650 of these instruments survive, including 450 to 512 violins.' 650 is the standard figure; no competing number found. ORIGINAL REVEAL: the first verifier is substantially right that it is not supportable, though its own dating is slightly off. There IS a real late shrinkage — Tarisio documents that after 1725, and appearing around 1730, Stradivari introduced a narrower 'forma B piccola' cello model plus a shorter model (only ~6 'forma B piccola' cellos survive vs ~20 'forma B'). So the phenomenon is genuinely final-decade, not 1707 as the first verifier said. But it is confined to cellos: the late violins (late 1720s-1737) are standard-form and are described as showing advancing age and failing eyesight in workmanship, not reduced size. 'The instruments from his final decade are noticeably smaller and easier to handle' reads as a claim about the instruments generally, i.e. the violins, and is false there. Fix stands. CORRECTED REVEAL RE-VERIFIED: born c. 1644, died 18 December 1737, so 'about 93' is right and matches his own late labels ('de anni 89' on a 1732 violin, 'd'anni 92' on the 1736 'Muntz'); he was working in 1737 — his last violin is generally dated that year. Golden period is cited as 1700-1720 or 1700-1725, so 'roughly 1700 to 1720' is fine. One flaw in the first verifier's wording: 'it is the instruments of his golden period ... that now change hands for millions' implies late Strads do not, which is untrue — late instruments also sell in the millions. Reworded to 'fetch the highest prices', which is accurate (Lady Blunt 1721, Joachim-Ma 1714, Messiah 1716). RANGE: 650 in log 50..1200 sits at ln(13)/ln(24)=0.807, higher than ideal, but the ceiling is principled — it is roughly his total documented output (~1,116), i.e. the 'nearly all survived' bound — and the floor is the 'almost none survived' bound. Leaving the range as is rather than churning it. No duplicate: nothing on Stradivari, violins or instrument survival elsewhere in the set per the first verifier's dedupe check, and the prompt is portable and time-stable ('still survive today' moves by single digits per century). No drift from the category.

verdicts.prompt: How many different words did Shakespeare use across his complete works?
verdicts.note:
Independent check confirms the first verifier's core arithmetic but overturns its judgment on the reveal, which it explicitly waved through.

CONFIRMED: 31,534 word types is real, from Efron & Thisted, 'Estimating the number of unseen species: How many words did Shakespeare know?', Biometrika 63(3), 1976, pp. 435-447, of which 14,376 are hapax. Spevack's concordance (Riverside text) separately reports 29,066 different words, and Open Source Shakespeare gives 28,829 forms, so 31,000 sits sensibly in the middle of the type-count cluster. Answer stands. Range position also checks out: ln(31000/15000)/ln(800000/15000) = 0.726/3.977 = 0.183, and the 800,000 ceiling is a fair trap for anyone reaching for the ~884,647 token count. Keeping the range as shipped.

AGREE ON AMBIGUITY: the lemma count really is ~17,000-18,000 root words against ~31,500 forms, a 1.8x spread, so the prompt must name the counting rule. But the first verifier's fix used the jargon framing; I restated it in player-plain language ('every distinct spelling as its own word') so a non-specialist can act on it.

WHERE VERIFIER 1 IS WRONG: it declared the reveal safe because 'turn up in print for the first time' dodges the word 'coined'. It does not dodge the problem. The 1,700 figure is a count of OED first-citations, not of first appearances in print, and OED3's revision has been dismantling it: in one analyzed sample, 57 of 117 words once credited to Shakespeare now have documented earlier uses, and Schafer displaced over fifty attributions from Nashe alone. So the literal claim ('turn up in print for the first time in his plays') is false for a large and growing fraction of the 1,700, and the trailing clause 'as much a coiner of words as a user of them' is precisely the romantic myth the scholarship rejects — the streetlight effect of Cowden Clarke's 1845 concordance, not Shakespearean superhuman invention. A reveal cannot ship asserting the thing the field has spent forty years correcting. Replaced with the Efron-Thisted hapax result, which is from the same source as the answer, is not contested, and is more interesting anyway.

SOURCE: verifier 1 flagged this for the author but did not correct it. The shipped 'concordances of the First Folio' is wrong — the Folio omits the poems, Pericles and Two Noble Kinsmen; 31,534 comes from a complete-works concordance. Source should read: Efron & Thisted, Biometrika 63 (1976), counting from Spevack's complete-works concordance (Riverside text).

Dedupe: no collision. history48 is the death year — different category, different quantity, no shared answer surface.
verdicts.correctedPrompt: Counting every distinct spelling as its own word, how many different words appear across Shakespeare's complete works?
verdicts.correctedReveal: About 14,000 of those words appear exactly once in the entire corpus. That long tail of one-offs is what let two statisticians in 1976 estimate, from the shape of the frequency curve alone, that Shakespeare knew roughly 35,000 more words he simply never got around to using.

verdicts.prompt: How many tonnes did ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic computer, weigh?
verdicts.note: Second-pass check agrees with the first verifier on both the defect and the repair. Answer confirmed independently: ENIAC weighed more than 30 short tons = 27 tonnes (Wikipedia spec box; ARL Ordnance Corps history: '30 separate units, plus power supply and forced air cooling, weighed over thirty tons and occupied 1,800 square feet'). 1,800 sq ft = 167 m2, so the reveal's '170 m2' rounds honestly. Tube count 17,468 installed, 'almost 18,000' per CHM, so 'roughly 18,000' is fair. The original reveal's claim that engineers built a dedicated tester to hunt dead tubes is not sourceable: what the record shows is a 1950 tube surveillance/life-testing program at Aberdeen (statistical failure data, testing methods 'unique at the time') aimed at tube quality, not a purpose-built dead-tube locator, plus plug-in removable chassis for fast swaps. That is a different claim, so replacing rather than salvaging was right. I re-verified the replacement text directly at the Computer History Museum's ENIAC tube-change page: 'ENIAC lost one vacuum tube roughly every day or two... the maintenance team developed the skill to fix a problem in just 15 minutes,' with Eckert's own line 'We had a tube fail about every two days and we could locate the problem within 15 minutes.' Position on log 2..400 is ln(13.5)/ln(200) = 0.491, near centre; the 200x span is wide but appropriate for a quantity most players have no anchor for. Reveal leaks nothing about mass. Dedupe: no other weight-of-a-machine or ENIAC item in the set I was shown; the nearest computing neighbours (first transistor, candidate 40) ask different quantities. Keeping the first verifier's corrected reveal verbatim rather than re-wording it, to avoid churn.
verdicts.correctedReveal: One of its roughly 18,000 vacuum tubes burned out every day or two, though a practised crew learned to track the dead one down in about 15 minutes; the machine filled a room of some 170 m².
